Title: Artificial Intelligence applications for optimization control and decision making in Waste to Energy systems

Abstract: The increasing global generation of municipal, industrial, and agricultural waste, coupled with rising energy demand and stringent environmental regulations, has accelerated the development of intelligent Waste-to-Energy (WtE) systems. Although WtE technologies including incineration, gasification, pyrolysis, anaerobic digestion, and plasma conversion, offer significant potential for sustainable waste management and renewable energy production, their performance is constrained by feedstock heterogeneity, nonlinear process dynamics, emission control requirements, and economic uncertainty. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative enabler capable of addressing these challenges through advanced data-driven modeling, optimization, and decision-making frameworks. This review provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of AI applications across the WtE value chain, including feedstock characterization, process optimization, intelligent control, emission monitoring, predictive maintenance, and techno-economic planning. Techniques such as machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, evolutionary algorithms, and hybrid physics-informed models are systematically evaluated. The analysis shows that AI-based approaches can improve energy efficiency by 5–15%, reduce emissions by 10–25%, and decrease operational downtime by up to 40%, while enhancing prediction accuracy beyond 90% in key applications. Beyond summarizing existing studies, this review contributes a unified systems-level perspective and quantitative comparison of AI techniques, while identifying critical challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, cybersecurity, transfer learning, and regulatory integration. Emerging trends, including digital twins, edge AI, explainable AI, and large language model-driven decision support, are highlighted as key enablers of next-generation WtE systems. Overall, the integration of AI into WtE systems represents a paradigm shift from reactive operation to predictive, adaptive, and autonomous management, supporting circular economy strategies and global decarbonization goals. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Advances in slow pyrolysis reactors for sustainable biochar production: design principles, process optimization, and future perspectives

Abstract: Slow pyrolysis is a widely investigated thermochemical pathway for biochar production and long-term biogenic carbon sequestration. This review critically assesses the evolution and recent advances in slow pyrolysis reactor technologies from 1950 through December 2025, based on publication availability, focusing on reactor design, transport phenomena, product characteristics, scalability, and commercialization barriers. Four primary reactor configurations—fixed-bed, auger, rotary-kiln, and modified fluidized-bed systems—are systematically evaluated. The analysis indicates that reactor architecture strongly influences thermal management, residence-time distribution, and product selectivity. Under appropriate feedstock characteristics and operating conditions, rotary-kiln reactors can offer favorable prospects for large-scale continuous operation due to effective solids mixing, feedstock flexibility, and heat integration, whereas auger reactors may be particularly suitable for intermediate-scale and decentralized applications under appropriate operating conditions. Fixed-bed systems can remain advantageous for small-scale production, particularly where simple reactor configurations are preferred, although they are constrained by conductive heat-transfer limitations and low throughput. Conversely, fluidized-bed reactors, despite their high heat-transfer rates, require substantial hydrodynamic modifications for biochar-oriented slow pyrolysis and careful control of operating conditions to achieve the desired product characteristics. Biochar yield is strongly influenced by operating temperature, residence time, particle dimensions, and feedstock composition, with reported yields commonly falling within the range of approximately 25 to 45 wt% (dry basis) depending on these factors. Current industrial deployment is impeded by feedstock heterogeneity, thermal non-uniformity, process control limitations, and techno-economic uncertainties. Emerging digitalization strategies, including machine learning and digital twins, show potential for predictive monitoring and optimization, though their industrial implementation requires rigorous validation under transient operational conditions. Life-cycle and techno-economic assessments indicate that slow pyrolysis can contribute to carbon dioxide removal, while emphasizing the critical need for standardized evaluation frameworks. Ultimately, future commercialization will depend on the context-specific integration of advanced reactor engineering, intelligent process control, efficient energy recovery, and robust sustainability metrics. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Systematic data-driven genome-scale metabolic model reduction for bioprocess modeling: CHO culture case study
Affiliations: Sartorius Corporate Research, Royston, United Kingdom; Sartorius Corporate Research, Brussels, Belgium
Authors with affiliations: Antonakoudis A., Sartorius Corporate Research, Royston, United Kingdom; Richelle A., Sartorius Corporate Research, Brussels, Belgium
Abstract: Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) enable mechanistic insight into cellular metabolism, but their size and underdetermination hinder use in dynamic bioprocess simulation and real-time digital twins. Compact models are essential, yet existing reduction strategies either neglect experimental uncertainty, rely on simplistic rate estimates, or depend on manual assumptions, limiting robustness and scalability. Here, we present a metabolomics-driven reduction pipeline that integrates Bayesian flux estimation to propagate uncertainty from noisy and sparse exo-metabolomics data directly into the reduction process. Applied to time-course data from 12 fed-batch CHO cultures, the method produced a single reduced model that remained feasible across all conditions and accurately reproduced observed extracellular fluxes. Despite relying solely on exo-metabolomics, the reduced model preserved broad metabolic functionality, highlighting the strong predictive power of extracellular data. This establishes a systematic, uncertainty-aware framework for generating compact GEMs suited for dynamic bioprocess simulation and digital twin integration, demonstrated here in a CHO case study but generalizable across cell systems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Microstructure-based variational deep material networks for robust uncertainty quantification in materials digital twins
Affiliations: Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, United States; Theoretical Division, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Albuquerque, NM, United States; Department of Mechanical Engineering, Pohang University of Science and Technology, Pohang, South Korea

Abstract: Aleatoric uncertainties – irremovable variability in microstructure morphology, constituent behavior, and processing conditions – pose a major challenge to developing uncertainty-robust digital twins. We introduce the Variational Deep Material Network (VDMN), a physics-informed and microstructure-aware surrogate model that enables efficient and probabilistic forward and inverse predictions of material behavior. The VDMN captures microstructure-induced variability by embedding variational distributions within its hierarchical, mechanistic architecture. Using an analytic propagation scheme based on Taylor-series expansion and automatic differentiation, the VDMN efficiently propagates uncertainty through the network during training and prediction. We demonstrate its capabilities in two digital-twin-driven applications: (1) as an uncertainty-aware materials digital twin, it predicts and experimentally validates the nonlinear mechanical variability in additively manufactured polymer composites; and (2) as an inverse calibration engine, it disentangles and quantitatively identifies overlapping sources of uncertainty in constituent properties. Together, these results establish the VDMN as a foundation for uncertainty-robust materials digital twins. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Integrated monitoring models for dam health and safety: A review of methods and considerations
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, Sharif University of Technology, Tehran, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Moradi Sarkhanlou M., Department of Civil Engineering, Sharif University of Technology, Tehran, Iran; Toufigh V., Department of Civil Engineering, Sharif University of Technology, Tehran, Iran; Ghaemian M., Department of Civil Engineering, Sharif University of Technology, Tehran, Iran
Abstract: Dam safety and health monitoring are critical to ensuring the long-term reliability of water infrastructure, given the complex behavior of dams and the potentially severe consequences of failure. To evaluate current monitoring approaches, this study employs a structured literature review methodology that includes systematic database searching, screening, and qualitative synthesis of 215 relevant publications. The reviewed studies were organized into four major categories comprising artificial intelligence (AI)-based models, numerical models, hybrid models, and modern monitoring technologies. The review critically assesses the strengths, limitations, and application domains of these approaches, highlighting the increasing integration of AI techniques with numerical simulations to improve predictive accuracy while maintaining physical interpretability. Particular attention is given to methodological factors influencing model performance, including input variable selection, data quality, model validation strategies, and uncertainty management. The study also examines the role of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in improving transparency, interpretability, and engineering trust in safety-critical decision-making processes. Furthermore, emerging technologies such as digital twins, remote sensing systems, and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-assisted inspections are evaluated as key enablers of real-time monitoring and early warning systems. The review identifies major research challenges, including data scarcity, model generalization, computational demands, and interoperability across monitoring platforms. Future research directions are discussed, emphasizing the potential of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), foundation models, federated learning, and cyber-secure monitoring frameworks to support the next generation of intelligent dam monitoring systems. The findings provide practical insights for researchers and practitioners and help guide the development of more reliable and resilient dam monitoring frameworks. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Digital twin (DT) technology holds great potential for the lifecycle monitoring and prognosis of engineering assets; however, its practical implementation is still challenging under conditions of limited data, noisy measurements, and the need for physically consistent long-term predictions with reliable uncertainty quantification. Title: Geometric Fidelity Uncertainty in Cognitive Digital Twins: Automated Point Cloud Completion, Tessellation, and Industry Foundation Classes Recording for Maintenance
Source title: ASCE-ASME Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems, Part B: Mechanical Engineering

Abstract: Geometric fidelity is a fundamental prerequisite for reliable cognitive digital twins (CDTs). An inaccurate or incomplete as-is geometric foundation leads to model uncertainty, thereby undermining CDT reasoning and maintenance decisions. However, point cloud data (PCD) acquired through laser scanning is inevitably subject to occlusions caused by structural obstructions, sensor limitations, and complex mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) configurations, introducing geometric uncertainty that undermines the trustworthiness of as-is digital twin representations. Existing methods fail to address the high-precision full spectrum of occlusion scenarios in real-world Scan-to/versus-BIM (Building Information Modeling/Model) workflows, particularly for border truncations and irregular non-Manhattan geometries. This paper proposes a method that systematically reduces geometric uncertainty in CDT construction through three stages. First, a gap classification scheme categorizes incomplete point clusters by occlusion severity and object class, enabling targeted treatment of each scenario for both Manhattan and non-Manhattan geometries. The completed clusters are then tessellated into high-resolution meshes and converted into Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) models through a new purpose-designed data structure that embeds laser-scan timestamps and as-designed global identifier links. Together, these stages form a closed-loop geometric DT updating system that continuously reflects the as-is physical state of the building, directly reducing the geometric uncertainty that would otherwise propagate into CDT-based maintenance reasoning and risk assessment. The method is validated on various real-world datasets. The performance is evaluated with ground truth (GT) and Chamfer distance (CD), with results benchmarked against Level of Accuracy (LOA) requirements to confirm practical ability. The resulting timestamped IFC models provide a geometrically reliable foundation for CDT-based predictive maintenance and facility risk assessment. Copyright © 2026 by ASME.

Abstract: Groundwater underpins global water security yet remains one of the least observable and slowest-responding components of the Earth system. Cumulative abstraction, climate variability, land-use intensification, and energy-dependent pumping have intensified groundwater pressures, while artificial intelligence (AI) applications have expanded across diverse hydrogeological and socio-environmental settings, but most remain prediction-centric, with limited attention to delayed responses, structural heterogeneity, uncertainty, transferability, and techno-social equity. Drawing on literature published between 2000 and 2026, this narrative review reframes AI as a bounded decision-support intermediary for groundwater sustainable development (GSD). It synthesizes groundwater data foundations and observability constraints, major AI paradigms, and five sustainability functions: early warning, managed aquifer recharge and zoning, abstraction control, groundwater quality protection, and the groundwater–food–energy–climate nexus. Emerging directions, including scenario-conditioned inference, physics-informed learning, and digital-twin-like representations, offer opportunities for sustainability-oriented groundwater management but remain constrained by sparse observations, geological complexity, limited transferability, and institutional capacity. AI–GSD can support anticipatory groundwater stewardship by reconstructing hidden system stress, characterizing uncertainty, and informing decisions under changing conditions. Its long-term value depends on regulatory integration, uncertainty-aware deployment, interdisciplinary collaboration, and safeguards against unintended groundwater depletion. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Toward Self-organizing Production Logistics: A Multi-agent Approach
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Affiliations: KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Klein J.-F., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Jeong Y., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Flores-García E., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden; Wiktorsson M., KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm, 10044, Sweden
Abstract: Production logistics is increasingly exposed to variability, dynamic interdependencies, and operational disturbances that challenge conventional centralized planning and control approaches. Following a Design Science Research Methodology, this paper establishes a conceptual foundation for the design, implementation, and evaluation of Self-Organizing Production Logistics (SOPL) systems. First, key technological and systemic drivers motivating SOPL are identified, including autonomous logistics resources, advances in distributed AI-based decision-making, and the transition toward circular production systems, which further amplify operational uncertainty and complexity. Based on these drivers, system-level objectives and design requirements for SOPL are derived. Building on these requirements, the paper proposes an initial multi-agent architecture that integrates embodied and non-embodied agents, event-driven coordination, semantic knowledge structures, and digital twins. In addition, a three-phase demonstration roadmap is presented, progressing from an initial laboratory demonstrator toward increasingly distributed and adaptive SOPL systems. The Phase I demonstrator provides an experimental environment for investigating disturbance handling, human involvement, and supervisory coordination within an order-driven kitting and supply scenario. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Abstract: Engineered in vitro cardiac tissues are being developed and increasingly used for disease modeling and drug evaluation, but reproducing cardiac cell composition and three-dimensional architecture alone does not ensure physiologically meaningful function. Native myocardial performance arises from coordinated electrical activation, active force generation, and passive mechanical resistance governed by stiffness, anisotropy, nonlinear elasticity, and viscoelastic relaxation. Failure to reproduce these coupled properties can alter force transmission, tissue deformation, mechanosensitive cellular responses, and the interpretation of disease phenotypes or drug effects. Yet myocardial mechanics, computational modeling, biomaterial design, and biofabrication are commonly developed as separate domains. This review integrates these areas through a biomechanics-guided property–parameter–function framework. We first examine the multiscale structural determinants of myocardial mechanics and critically compare cellular, continuum, phenomenological, microstructure-informed, viscoelastic, and pathology-informed models with respect to predictive scope, computational demand, parameter identifiability, experimental validation, and engineering relevance. We then show how model-derived descriptors—including active stress, baseline and nonlinear stiffness, anisotropy, relaxation behavior, and remodeling-related parameters—can be translated into controllable biomaterial properties, scaffold architecture, fabrication and conditioning protocols, and mechanical boundary conditions. Emerging approaches involving artificial intelligence, inverse design, uncertainty quantification, and digital twins are discussed as routes toward adaptive and patient-relevant tissue models. By positioning computational biomechanics as a design and validation tool, this review provides a systematic basis for engineering cardiac tissues with more predictable mechanical function and more reproducible disease- and drug-response readouts. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) workflows for partial differential equations (PDEs) often require repeated simulations over many initial conditions, boundary conditions, or physical parameters. Although a single high-fidelity solve may be tractable on modern computing systems, large ensembles, optimization loops, uncertainty quantification studies, and digital-twin applications can make the aggregate computational cost substantial. This study presents a neural operator augmented with dynamic mode decomposition (DMD). The architecture combines a DeepONet-style branch–trunk mapping with additional branches that encode DMD modes and modal dynamics. The resulting model is intended as a trajectory-informed surrogate: DMD features are computed from states available before the prediction point and the subsequent state is reserved as the target. The method is evaluated for the Laplace, heat, and Burgers equations on 64×64 grids. On the heat benchmark, controlled five-seed comparisons include DeepONet, a parameter-matched DeepONet, FNO, and a KNO-style baseline; a capacity-controlled input ablation additionally evaluates the contribution of the DMD inputs without changing the trainable parameter count. Computational measurements separate classical solution time, DMD preprocessing, training, and network inference. The trained network has low evaluation latency, while case-specific DMD preprocessing dominates the present end-to-end path. Thus, the results support DMD-NO as a structured operator-learning approach for trajectory-conditioned prediction and identify modal preprocessing as the principal target for future parallel optimization, without claiming an end-to-end speedup over the classical solver. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Digital-twin-driven Adaptive Distance Protection for FACTS-compensated Transmission Lines under High Photovoltaic Penetration
Source title: International Journal of Intelligent Engineering and Systems
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Wasit University, Iraq; Department of Cyber Security, College of Computer Science and Information Technology, Wasit University, Iraq; Department of Renewable Energy Techniques, Technical Institute-Kut, Middle Technical University, Baghdad, Iraq
Authors with affiliations: Abbas Z.H., Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Wasit University, Iraq; Jabbar A.K., Department of Cyber Security, College of Computer Science and Information Technology, Wasit University, Iraq; Ahmed M.S., Department of Electrical Engineering, College of Engineering, Wasit University, Iraq; Mahmood H.R., Department of Renewable Energy Techniques, Technical Institute-Kut, Middle Technical University, Baghdad, Iraq
Abstract: When synchronous generation is replaced by grid-following photovoltaic plants, series-compensated lines lose distance-protection dependability: the metal-oxide varistor conducts during faults, and the converter's current-limited contribution corrupts the remote-infeed term at high fault resistance. This paper proposes a digital-twin-driven adaptive scheme in which the compensator drop is subtracted from direct measurement rather than from a model, and the infeed ratio is extracted from a superimposed-current Kirchhoff balance across synchronized terminals. Fault distance and fault resistance are separated by closed-form solution of a two-by-two real system, exact for an ideal two-source line, with the residual on the simulated line quantified against a fault-node ammeter. A first-order sensitivity law is applied online as the relay's own confidence bound, calibrated on data held strictly out of the evaluation grid. Over 250 enumerated fault episodes under a declared instrument chain (1% phasor-measurement-unit total vector error, 1.4% end-to-end per channel), the scheme is compared with four re-implemented methods published between 2021 and 2026, one of them from 2025, each run on the identical episodes, chain and two-cycle decision instant. Median reach error is lower by a factor of 3.0 than the strongest of them, dependability is 93.3% against 87.3%, and operating time is the same 44.8 ms at the median. That factor is pooled; stratified it ranges from 7.0 to 0.35, and at zero fault resistance the strongest comparators are as accurate, so the advantage lies in the resistive band. Across twelve measurement chains, high-resistance accuracy is shown to be instrument-limited rather than method-limited for the models tested. Title: Physics-based Digital Twin framework for electric vehicle battery health prediction and energy storage lifecycle management with reverse logistics optimization
Affiliations: Department of Management Science, Yanbu Industrial College, Royal Commission for Jubail and Yanbu, Yanbu, 45130, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Almuwallad M., Department of Management Science, Yanbu Industrial College, Royal Commission for Jubail and Yanbu, Yanbu, 45130, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Accurate state-of-health (SOH) prediction is central to managing the lifecycle of electric-vehicle lithium-ion batteries across both transport and second-life stationary energy storage, yet purely data-driven predictors generalize poorly across chemistries and operating histories. This paper presents a Blockchain-Enabled Digital Twin (BcDT), a proof-of-concept framework whose predictive core is a Doyle–Fuller–Newman (DFN)-constrained neural network that embeds electrochemical knowledge as structured regularizers, biasing the network toward physically consistent behavior without solving the full electrochemical partial differential equations. The digital twin is validated on 224 cells from five public datasets spanning four chemistries (NMC, NCA, LFP, LCO), achieving 1.82% mean absolute percentage error and statistically outperforming seven baselines (Wilcoxon (Formula presented), Cohen’s (Formula presented) ); L2-regularized and randomized-physics baselines confirm that the gain stems from correct electrochemical constraints rather than generic regularization. An uncertainty-aware grading scheme with calibrated 95% confidence intervals reduces misclassification of reusable batteries by 34 percentage points. A proof-of-concept simulation coupling the twin with a Hyperledger Fabric battery passport and a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming reverse-logistics model yields a 30.2% logistics-cost reduction, 92% material recovery, and an 8-percentage-point synergy premium beyond the sum of the individual technologies. These integration results are simulation-based rather than field-validated, and are offered as evidence that coupling physics-informed SOH prediction with governed data sharing can create non-additive value for energy-storage lifecycle management. The framework is aligned with the EU Battery Regulation (2023/1542) Digital Battery Passport, which enters force in February 2027. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: A digital twin framework for real-time probabilistic forecasting of permeable pavement performance

Abstract: Low Impact Development (LID), such as permeable pavements, mitigates some of the urban runoff effects. Their hydrologic response can be enhanced with real-time forecasting and management. Digital Twins (DT), which integrate physical models with sensor data, offer a solution, yet require methods to handle uncertainties in model inputs and observations. This study presents a DT framework for permeable pavement systems that couples a one-dimensional, explicit-state hydrologic model with a Particle Filter (PF) data assimilation scheme. The framework assimilates real-time underdrain outflow observations to refine model states and provide probabilistic forecasts. Uncertainty characterization revealed that sensor measurement error depends on the underdrain outflow, while rainfall forecast error from the High-Resolution Rapid Refresh model is a function of the magnitude of the rainfall event. The DT framework was evaluated against a baseline model using field data from four permeable pavement types. The data assimilation approach reduced the ensemble forecast error by an average of 20%, as measured by the Continuous Ranked Probability Skill Score (CRPSS), with positive skill scores in 96.2% of forecast events. The deterministic performance of the PF ensemble median, evaluated by Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), also exceeded that of the baseline model. The data assimilation framework yielded more accurate forecasts than a deterministic modeling approach and is computationally efficient for operational deployment. However, outflow forecast accuracy is constrained by the structural limitations of the baseline model, evidenced by poor prediction interval coverage during some high-intensity events, highlighting areas for future model development. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Integrated structural-thermal design and digital twin framework for satellite payload module

Abstract: Modern satellite payload modules require high structural stiffness, low mass, and thermal stability under coupled thermo-mechanical environments. Conventional separation of load-bearing and thermal-control subsystems often leads to inefficient heat transfer and degraded system performance. This study proposes an integrated structural–thermal design and data-driven digital twin framework combining CFRP honeycomb sandwich panels, a TC4 titanium-alloy ring frame, and integrated heat-transfer paths. Multiphysics simulations predict an in-plane temperature gradient of 3.2K and a maximum elastic thermal deformation of 0.075mm after removal of rigid-body motion. A literature-based comparison with conventional separated configurations indicates a 60%−80% shorter heat-transfer path and a 10%−20% lower structural mass. Model credibility was assessed through mesh-sensitivity analysis and independent analytical benchmarks, with differences of 1.48% in thermal resistance and 7.16% in structural displacement. The digital twin framework supports state prediction, parameter updating, uncertainty quantification, and health assessment. For maximum-displacement prediction, Gaussian process regression achieved R2=0.9996and an RMSE of 0.0136mm, while sequential data assimilation further reduced parameter uncertainty. Using precomputed FEM databases, the platform updated three-dimensional structural–thermal fields within 1.5s, enabling near-real-time response without online full-order FEM re-solution. Overall, the proposed approach provides an efficient and scalable solution for structural–thermal co-design, near-real-time monitoring, and health management of next-generation spacecraft payload modules. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Abstract: To address the growing complexity between the built environment and urban life, modern urban planning has increasingly relied on digital technologies for decision-making, including City Information Modeling (CIM). While CIM has matured from standards and data integration to real-time analytics and digital twins, most initiatives optimize physical systems while struggling to incorporate “intangible” citizen-generated data. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a replicable methodology to embed a customized Environment, Social, and Governance (ESG) framework with a CIM workflow by joining both tangible and intangible city layers to inform planning. The general methodology includes: (1) identifying a French priority neighborhood (QPV) and prioritizing local ESG indicators with a focus group, (2) conceptualizing and designing a data model that integrates urban geometry with subjective human perceptions, and (3) prototyping and developing the CIM model. This approach allows for a multi-scale assessment of socio-environmental sustainability, accounting for uncertainty in human perception. The novelty of this research lies in creating a replicable CIM method that converts non-geocoded citizen perceptions into spatially weighted and probabilistic indicators. Future work will complete the CIM workflow, detailing the integration of the ESG indicators in a practical CIM tool designed to inform decisions through reporting and recommendations. © 2026 The Author(s)

Abstract: Aging reinforced concrete (RC) bridges are susceptible to complex deterioration, yet conventional visual inspections yield qualitative condition ratings that cannot be directly translated into remaining service life predictions. Meanwhile, standard theoretical fatigue models often overestimate damage accumulation when site-specific loading and material degradation histories are not accounted for. To bridge this gap between physical inspection and numerical simulation, this study proposes an integrated assessment framework that synergizes Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry with nonlinear Finite Element Analysis (FEA). Applied to an 80-year-old RC bridge in Thailand exhibiting extensive cracking, the methodology features a novel two-stage calibrated fatigue assessment. In the calibration phase, an uncertainty-based matching algorithm systematically compares UAV-derived crack topologies (including flexural crack spacing and shear crack inclination) against simulated failure patterns across the full FEA loading history to determine the structure's equivalent fatigue age and current damage index. In the prediction phase, a structure-specific S-N curve is derived from multi-level cyclic FEA simulations and combined with Miner's rule to project the remaining service life under variable traffic scenarios. The calibration revealed that the bridge has consumed approximately 83.3% of its fatigue life, with the uncalibrated model overestimating the damage rate by predicting the same damage state at 54 years versus the actual 80-year service life. Scenario analyses estimate a remaining service life of approximately 7.5 years under baseline traffic conditions, while a load restriction policy prohibiting heavy trailers is estimated to extend operational life by approximately 0.8 years, within a range of 0.4–1.3 years reflecting the confidence interval on the fitted S-N exponent. The sign of this benefit is robust across that range; its magnitude is not tightly determined. While the calibration inputs, namely crack pattern, load history assumptions, and material properties, are specific to the case-study bridge, the underlying two-stage procedure, comprising uncertainty-based crack-pattern matching followed by structure-specific S-N characterization and Miner's-rule projection, is a generic pipeline applicable to any RC bridge for which UAV crack data and a nonlinear finite element model can be obtained, including structures with incomplete historical load records. The proposed framework thus demonstrates a transferable methodology for converting field-observed crack data into quantitative fatigue life predictions for aging RC structures. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Institution of Structural Engineers.

Abstract: Building height is a key variable for characterizing three-dimensional urban morphology, vertical development intensity, and spatial exposure, supporting applications in urban climate, air pollution, energy and carbon assessment, disaster risk, population mapping, planning, and digital twins. Remote sensing enables large-scale and updatable height mapping, but most sensors do not directly observe building height. Except for active measurements such as LiDAR, height is generally inferred from indirect cues, including shadows, stereo parallax, SAR scattering, street-view facades, spatial texture, and urban functional priors. Accordingly, remote sensing-based building height estimation should be viewed as a scale-dependent three-dimensional information retrieval problem constrained by observability, observation geometry, reference data, modeling approaches, and application requirements. This review examines data sources, height products, estimation methods, scale effects, uncertainty propagation, applications, and future challenges. We compare passive optical imagery, SAR, LiDAR, and street-view imagery in terms of height cues, applicable scales, and error mechanisms, and review representative products and methods, including geometry- and physics-driven approaches, statistical learning, deep learning, and multisource fusion. Particular attention is given to height definition, product comparability, accuracy assessment, scale transformation, and uncertainty propagation into environmental and socioeconomic applications. We argue that building height products should be evaluated not only by RMSE or MAE, but also by height definition, evaluation unit, reference data, aggregation strategy, uncertainty structure, and intended use. Future research should emphasize application-oriented reliability, standardized validation, cross-city generalization, interpretable modeling, dynamic mapping, and application-adaptive product generation. Title: Bridging idealized and operational models: an explainable AI framework for Earth system emulators
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, WI, United States; CEREA, ENPC, EDF R & D, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, Ile-de-France, France
Authors with affiliations: Behnoudfar P., Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, WI, United States; Moser C., Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, WI, United States; Bocquet M., CEREA, ENPC, EDF R & D, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, Ile-de-France, France; Cheng S., CEREA, ENPC, EDF R & D, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, Ile-de-France, France; Chen N., Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, WI, United States
Abstract: Computer models are indispensable tools for understanding the Earth system. While high-resolution operational models have achieved many successes, they exhibit persistent biases, particularly in simulating extreme events and statistical distributions. In contrast, coarse-grained idealized models isolate fundamental processes and can be precisely calibrated to excel in characterizing specific dynamical and statistical features. However, different models remain siloed by disciplinary boundaries. By leveraging the complementary strengths of models of varying complexity, we develop an explainable AI framework for Earth system emulators. It bridges the model hierarchy through a reconfigured latent data assimilation technique, uniquely suited to exploit the sparse output from the idealized models. The resulting bridging model inherits the high resolution and comprehensive variables of operational models while achieving global accuracy enhancements through targeted improvements from idealized models. Crucially, the mechanism of AI provides a clear rationale for these advancements, moving beyond black-box correction to physically insightful understanding in a computationally efficient framework that enables effective physics-assisted digital twins and uncertainty quantification. We demonstrate its power by significantly correcting biases in CMIP6 simulations of El Niño spatiotemporal patterns, leveraging statistically accurate idealized models. This work also highlights the importance of pushing idealized model development and advancing communication between modeling communities. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Engineering-practice-oriented digital twins for smart water management: Framework, enabling technologies, and future directions

Abstract: Urban water systems are increasingly challenged by climate extremes, aging infrastructure, and rising flood risks. Conventional water management practices remain fragmented across data, operations, and assets, limiting coordinated decision-making and scalable engineering deployment. Digital twins (DT) show great promise to overcome this fragmentation for resilient and efficient management. This review proposes an engineering-practice-oriented framework of digital twins for smart water management (DTSW). Utility demands are first structured through a scenario-oriented decomposition into points of interest (POIs), thereby linking practical engineering problems to digital variables. The review further summarizes a probabilistic graphical model-based scheme as the algorithmic backbone for POI implementation, and examines the key enabling technologies across organized data foundations, models, and real-time control. Particular attention is given to AI-empowered DTSW techniques, including soft sensing and data cleansing, hybrid modeling, and uncertainty-aware model deployment. Future development is discussed from the perspectives of proactive optimization, human-digital collaboration, and scalable engineering deployment. This review thus provides a structured framework for guiding the practical design and deployment of DT in urban water systems, facilitating coordinated, scalable and resilient water management. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Sparse measurement correction for full-field displacement prediction of nonlinear structures using reduced-order models and Gaussian process regression

Abstract: Online full-field displacement reconstruction from sparse measurements is an important task in nonlinear structural analysis, monitoring, and digital-twin applications. Direct finite element simulations are often too expensive for repeated online use, whereas input-only reduced-order model–Gaussian process regression (ROM-GPR) surrogate models may produce biased full-field predictions when the target structural state is insufficiently represented by offline training data. Sparse displacement measurements provide current-state information, but observation-only reconstruction is usually underdetermined or noise-sensitive under limited sensing conditions. To address this issue, this work develops a probabilistic correction strategy for ROM-GPR full-field displacement predictions by statistically weighting the input-informed surrogate estimate and sparse measurements according to their respective uncertainties. The Gaussian process regression (GPR) prediction provides a low-dimensional estimate with quantified regression uncertainty, while the measurement constraint uses an observation error covariance that accounts for sensor noise and the observation-space projection of reduced-order reconstruction residuals. Sparse measurements are incorporated through an error-covariance-weighted correction in the reduced-order space, with the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) and unscented Kalman filter (UKF) adopted as sampling-based implementations. Tests on two nonlinear 2D finite element examples and a 3D liver model show that the proposed correction reduces the mean reconstruction error by 55.92%–73.51% for autoencoder-based ROM-GPR and 72.48%–93.10% for proper orthogonal decomposition-based ROM-GPR. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Soil structure governs water storage, aeration, root growth, trafficability, nutrient transport, and carbon stabilization, but agricultural monitoring still relies largely on sparse, destructive, and labor-intensive measurements. Digital imaging, spectroscopy, geophysics, in situ sensors, proximal sensing, and remote sensing now provide multiscale observations, yet converting them into reliable structural information remains limited by sparse ground truth, scale mismatch, domain shift, and inconsistent validation. This structured narrative review synthesizes how artificial intelligence (AI) transforms these heterogeneous observations into useful soil structure information for agricultural monitoring and management. We organize the literature around a sensor-to-decision workflow: observation, representation, scaling, discovery, and decision-making. At the pore scale, deep learning improves image enhancement, segmentation, and reconstruction of pore and aggregate architecture from imaging technologies. At pedon and field scales, machine learning links spectra, geophysical signals, mobile proximal sensors, and in situ time series to structural proxies and subsurface states. At landscape scales, AI enables data fusion, downscaling, and transfer learning from UAV, satellite, LiDAR, and mobile sensing platforms. We further examine how physics-guided learning, uncertainty quantification, explainable AI, surrogate modeling, and soil digital twins can improve transferability and support management of transport processes, mechanical resilience, and biological carbon dynamics. By linking sensing modality, AI method, validation design, and management applications, this review provides practical guidance for selecting deployable soil structure monitoring workflows for compaction avoidance, irrigation management, trafficability assessment, carbon stabilization, and resilience monitoring. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Mechanism–AI fusion in refining simulation software: A module-level review
Affiliations: Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China; China Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), Beijing, 100728, China
Authors with affiliations: Han J., Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China; Zhao X., China Petrochemical Corporation (SINOPEC), Beijing, 100728, China; Han L., Petro-CyberWorks Information Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, 100007, China
Abstract: Refining simulation software has remained functionally static for decades: property calculation, reaction kinetics, unit-operation modeling, and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solving modules are hard-coded, unidirectional, and cannot be calibrated online against drifting plant conditions. Purely mechanistic approaches provide irreplaceable rigor but are constrained by computational cost; purely data-driven approaches offer speed and adaptivity but lack the interpretability, generalization, and physical guarantees required for safety-critical deployment. This review examines how mechanism–AI fusion—encompassing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), reduced-order models (ROMs), operator learning, and closure-model augmentation—is reshaping these functional modules at the architectural level. We propose a module-level taxonomy that maps each fusion strategy to the specific simulation module it transforms, and we distinguish this paradigm from related concepts (hybrid modeling, physics-informed machine learning, grey-box modeling, and digital twins) by specifying the bidirectional information flows between mechanistic and AI components. A systematic literature survey following PRISMA-style methodology identified 133 references from Web of Science, Scopus, and IEEE Xplore (2000–2025). We provide enhanced comparative tables that include training cost, data requirements, extrapolation ability, uncertainty quantification (UQ), scalability, and industrial maturity for each method class. Industrial software benchmarking is presented as a qualitative comparison rather than a subjective ranking. Three industrial case studies (gasifier, FCC unit, distillation column) are analyzed with explicit baselines, deployment durations, and performance indicators, clearly identifying vendor-reported versus independently verified data. We discuss emerging topics—AI-native scientific software, foundation models for scientific computing, autonomous engineering agents, trustworthy and explainable AI, verification & validation (V&V), and MLOps for scientific applications—that will shape the next decade. The review concludes with graded findings (verified, supported, emerging, conceptual, and policy-level) to clearly distinguish established results from industrial observations and conceptual proposals. The central finding is that mechanism–AI fusion transforms refining simulation software from a fixed-algorithm tool into an adaptive multi-fidelity platform, but the transition from advisory and optimization applications to safety-critical closed-loop control requires standardized V&V protocols, UQ frameworks, and process-industry-specific safety governance that do not yet exist. Title: Key technologies for digital twin-driven second-level targeted early warning in flood detention basins: a coupled method of flood routing and spatiotemporal population heatmap

Abstract: Conventional flood detention basin warning chains often operate at minute-to-hour latency and treat hydraulic hazard and population exposure as separate layers, leaving a gap between hydrodynamic forecasts and village-level warning decisions. This study develops a digital twin platform for second-level targeted early warning in the Chengdong Lake Flood Detention Basin on the middle Huai River. The platform couples a GPU-accelerated two-dimensional shallow-water model with a mobile-signaling-based population heatmap through a cell-level risk index that integrates normalized inundation depth, flow velocity, and dynamic population density. The hydraulic model was retrospectively evaluated using lake-stage records and 72 surveyed high-water marks from the 2003, 2007, and 2020 events, yielding Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency values of 0.78–0.91, an RMSE of 0.27 m for water depth, and an inundation-extent fit of 0.83 for the 2020 event. The hydrodynamic core advanced one 30 s simulation step in 11.4 s on a single RTX A6000, corresponding to a 28-fold speed-up over a 16-core CPU baseline. The median observation-to-village-alert latency was 47 s, with a 95th percentile of 58 s. Compared with a conventional warning chain, the digital twin provided at least 30 min of potential lead time for about 60% of the 380 administrative villages, compared with about 25% under the conventional chain. A first-order sensitivity analysis showed that the main warning outputs remained stable across plausible risk-weight perturbations. The results indicate that integrating hydraulic state, dynamic population exposure, and geofence-based dispatch within a common grid and update clock can improve the timeliness and spatial targeting of detention-basin warnings, although prospective validation of evacuation response and full uncertainty propagation remain future work. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: This paper presents a hybrid methodology to combat endemic time and cost overruns in construction, particularly in emerging markets. The study fills a critical gap by integrating three advanced techniques into a single, coherent framework. First, the project schedule is determined by a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that elastically optimizes time and costs, moving beyond simplistic linear models to account for realistic, nonlinear costs and diminishing returns associated with accelerating project activities. Second, this optimized schedule is rigorously validated through Monte Carlo simulation, which models and quantifies the probabilistic risk of meeting contractual deadlines under real-world uncertainty, transforming a deterministic plan into a risk-informed one with quantifiable confidence levels. Finally, this combined optimization-simulation engine is integrated into a digital twin (DT) platform, which operates as a dynamic system by integrating real-time field data to enable dynamic replanning when conditions change and, importantly, to generate a traceable, data-rich audit trail. This approach, applied to a Moroccan real estate project, provides more realistic cost-time tradeoffs than traditional assumptions, and becomes legally defensible and invaluable for supporting claims, justifying resource allocation, and strengthening a party's position in contractual disputes.  © 2026 This work is made available under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license,.

Abstract: Natural frequencies of large-scale machine tools exhibit strong position dependence across the workspace. Accurate real-time prediction of position-dependent natural frequencies is essential for avoiding resonance and optimizing cutting parameters. However, existing methods face high testing costs, overlooked measurement uncertainties, and difficulty in achieving both accuracy and real-time performance under simulation uncertainty. This study proposes a probabilistic Key Conditional Quotient (KCQ) method that integrates a small amount of noisy vibration data with finite element simulations under parameter uncertainty to enable accurate real-time prediction. Quotient-form expressions for the conditional probability density function (PDF), conditional mean, and conditional variance are derived, transforming the prediction task into the computation of conditional statistical quantities. To solve this efficiently, a non-equal-weight generalized quasi-Monte Carlo (GQMC) method and Gaussian smoothing of the Dirac delta function are employed. An offline–online coupled KCQ framework is developed to support millisecond-level real-time performance. Validation on the JR-2203Q gantry machine tool, as a digital-twin-oriented application scenario, demonstrates prediction errors below 3% and computation times under 5 ms, confirming the method’s effectiveness in both predictive accuracy and computational speed. © 2026 CIRP.

Abstract: Smart polymer composite actuators are emerging as enabling materials for next-generation soft robotics by combining mechanical compliance, multifunctionality, and programmable responsiveness within lightweight architectures. Their ability to convert electrical, thermal, magnetic, optical, and chemical stimuli into controlled deformation provides advantages for adaptive interaction with complex environments. Advances in three-dimensional (3D) and four-dimensional (4D) printing have expanded their design space through multimaterial integration, spatially programmed architectures, functional gradients, and time-dependent shape transformation. Concurrently, machine learning (ML) offers new opportunities for material discovery, structure–property prediction, fabrication optimization, actuator modeling, inverse design, sensing, and intelligent control. This review critically examines the integration of polymer composites, 3D/4D printing, computational modeling, and ML across the materials-to-device development chain, from formulation and architecture to manufacturing, actuation, sensing, control, and lifecycle monitoring. Particular attention is given to printability–functionality trade-offs, multimaterial interfaces, manufacturing scalability and reproducibility, dataset limitations, uncertainty, simulation-to-reality transfer, and model generalization. Emerging strategies, including physics-informed ML, multiscale density functional theory–molecular dynamics–ML frameworks, digital twins, closed-loop design–print–test optimization, and sustainable composite systems, are discussed as pathways toward more predictive and efficient development. The review emphasizes that high ML accuracy does not necessarily ensure transferability or reliable physical performance and highlights the need for standardized validation and experimentally grounded models. Finally, opportunities for increasingly autonomous, self-adaptive, and closed-loop soft robotic systems are outlined, providing a roadmap toward reliable, scalable, sustainable, and application-ready intelligent soft robotic technologies. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Dynamic monitoring of railway bridges via coupling digital twins with deep reinforcement learning

Authors with affiliations: Xu X., Sichuan University Jinjiang College, Sichuan, Meishan, 620860, China; He G., Sichuan Tourism University, Sichuan, Chengdu, 610100, China; Liu C., Sichuan University Jinjiang College, Sichuan, Meishan, 620860, China; Ding X., Sichuan University Jinjiang College, Sichuan, Meishan, 620860, China
Abstract: Railway-bridge anomaly detection during retrofitting is a core structural health monitoring (SHM) task, requiring timely alarms for safety. It is challenging because responses are strongly nonstationary and distorted by environmental and operational variability, while sensing budgets constrain what can be observed. Classical feature-and-threshold pipelines are interpretable but fragile to operating-condition drift, yielding unstable alarms without compensation. Deep time-series detectors are effective, but data-only scores are hard to calibrate into risk cues and usually assume fixed sensing. Digital twin (DT) approaches provide uncertainty-aware belief tracking, yet twin-only alarming may respond slowly and may ignore sequential accuracy–cost optimization. We propose Residual Digital-Twin Monitoring with Branching Dueling Q-learning (RDTM-BDQ), coupling an event-triggered Bayesian DT, a mask-aware residual Mamba encoder, and a Branching Dueling Double Deep Q-Network (BDQ) policy. Hybrid evidence fuses DT innovation energy and a normalized safety-margin index with an inverse-projection inconsistency score from the Mamba embedding, forming a belief-augmented state representation for joint alarm and sensing decisions. Training is off-policy with prioritized replay, using a reward that penalizes delay, false alarms, misses, and sensing cost, plus a consistency loss for the inverse projection head. Experiments on the public KW51 and Z24 datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of RDTM-BDQ: on KW51 it achieves 0.95 F1-score (F1) and 0.98 precision, and on Z24 it reaches 0.92 F1-score, confirming robustness to both retrofit-induced and environmentally-induced nonstationarity. Operating-point analysis on KW51 further shows an explicit accuracy–burden–cost trade-off, e.g., reducing detection delay from 41.4 h to 3.9 h with controllable monitoring cost. Ablations confirm that DT cues, residual Mamba encoding, and branching Q-learning each improve accuracy and stability. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Accurate modelling of the performance of a vapor-compression cycle across broad operating ranges is essential for the design, optimization and supervisory control of refrigeration systems. But traditional data-driven surrogate models can perform poorly out of training distribution and do not guarantee thermodynamic feasibility. Here we introduce a physics-guided Fourier-transformer surrogate model to model a single-stage vapor-compression cycle with R1234yf and nano-lubricant additives, such as alumina, graphene, and carbon nanotubes. The model leverages Fourier feature lifting for smoother non-linear interactions, Transformer blocks to learn interactions across the four thermodynamic states, and physics-guided soft penalties designed to encourage physically plausible predictions by penalizing violations of output bounds and a prescribed monotonicity prior, without explicitly enforcing the governing thermodynamic conservation equations. To facilitate a systematic evaluation, a Koopman-inspired physics-guided state-space model is also proposed and compared with ANN, PIML, PGML, and PG-FNT models. The novelty of this study lies in its combination of spectral, relational, and physics-guided learning within a single compact architecture and its comparison with a specially designed state-space model under explicit distribution shift testing. To the authors’ knowledge, this combination has not been previously investigated for vapor compression refrigeration systems using nanolubricants with low GWP refrigerants. In the original five-fold cross-validation benchmark, PG-FNT[full] achieved a mean validation RMSE of 0.005202 and MAE of 0.003895, corresponding to reductions of approximately 55.5% and 55.7%, respectively, compared with the conventional ANN baseline under the same evaluation protocol. PG-KSSM also demonstrated competitive predictive performance, achieving up to 28.7% lower RMSE than ANN in the corresponding benchmark. Furthermore, under a high-condenser-temperature operating-envelope shift within the same experimental campaign, PG-FNT achieved a mean R2 of 0.9541 ± 0.0082 across five initialization seeds following few-shot adaptation with 10 labelled observations. Performance was evaluated on a separate 20-sample held-out test set, with no overlap between adaptation and test observations. These findings demonstrate the strong predictive capabilities of the proposed architectures and highlight the effectiveness of limited-data adaptation for maintaining accurate thermodynamic performance prediction under changing operating conditions. This work presents a transferable benchmarking and cross-validation, out-of-dispersion assessment, perturbation analysis, and significance testing protocol applicable to other thermofluidic systems with limited small and noisy datasets for the scientific community. The proposed framework provides a physics-guided, data-driven approach for predicting vapor-compression-cycle performance, demonstrating improved accuracy relative to the evaluated machine-learning baselines. Its comparative performance against conventional thermodynamic cycle solvers remains to be established. Title: A shared-latent probabilistic digital twin for BLI fan-blade forced response with physics-anchored stress fields
Affiliations: School of Aerospace Engineering, Xiamen University, Fujian, Xiamen, 361005, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhang X., School of Aerospace Engineering, Xiamen University, Fujian, Xiamen, 361005, China; Zhang B., School of Aerospace Engineering, Xiamen University, Fujian, Xiamen, 361005, China
Abstract: Boundary-layer ingestion (BLI) fans operate under severe three-dimensional, non-axisymmetric inlet distortion that induces low engine-order excitations and multi-harmonic blade vibration, posing major challenges for prediction and health monitoring. We develop a probabilistic digital twin (PDT) that embeds physics-consistent cyclic harmonic response synthesis (CHRS) into neural surrogates for (i) forward full-field stress prediction, (ii) inverse identification from sparse multi-harmonic measurements, and (iii) online drift tracking. Physics labels are generated from a reusable database of prestressed cyclic-symmetry finite-element models combined with CHRS, enabling low-cost multi-harmonic modal-superposition evaluations in resonance-critical regimes. A dual-path network learns a shared latent stress manifold that unifies parameter-to-field mapping, sensor-to-parameter inference, and sensor-to-field reconstruction. Manifold-alignment regularization ties the sensor embedding to the physical-parameter manifold, improving identifiability. To stabilize learning in sharply varying resonant regimes, stochastic weight averaging (SWA) is adopted, while conformalized quantile regression (CQR) provides calibrated prediction intervals with near-nominal 95% coverage under independent and identically distributed conditions. On a representative BLI fan case, the PDT predicts peak stress accurately (R2=0.9997) and improves inverse identification across parameters (average MAPE=0.22%, mean R2=0.9936). Drift tests track time-varying parameters (R2 up to 0.94) and peak-stress history (R2 up to 0.74), motivating drift-aware recalibration to sustain coverage for uncertainty-aware integrity monitoring. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Probabilistic Graphical Modeling for Machine Tool Dynamics With a Case Study in 3D Printer Vibration Compensation
Source title: Journal of Manufacturing Science and Engineering
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Victoria, Victoria, V8W 2Y2, BC, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Mehrabi M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Victoria, Victoria, V8W 2Y2, BC, Canada; Ahmadi K., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Victoria, Victoria, V8W 2Y2, BC, Canada
Abstract: This article presents a new framework for modeling machine tool dynamics to enable their integration into machine tool digital twins. The framework is formulated as a dynamic Bayesian network, in which model parameters, sensor and process observations, and decision variables are represented explicitly and updated sequentially using Bayesian inference. The framework incorporates a library of candidate models and enables model selection, uncertainty quantification, and physical system state estimation through probabilistic inference. These properties enable scalable digital twin creation at both the machine and fleet levels. The proposed framework is designed to be broadly adoptable across a wide range of machine tool dynamics problems. In this article, we demonstrate its implementation through a case study in feed-drive dynamics, where the generated model interfaces with a 3D printer’s controller to adaptively produce optimal trajectories that compensate for structural vibrations during printing. Bidirectional digital–physical communication loop is established and experimentally validated, confirming the framework’s ability to predict and adapt to system variations. Results indicate improved vibration compensation and enhanced surface quality under varying dynamic conditions in this case study, while computational challenges for enabling general implementation are discussed. Title: Benchmarking of multi-order equivalent-circuit models with empirical ageing for Li-ion battery digital-twin workflows
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Cagliari, via Marengo 2, Cagliari, 09123, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Carcangiu S., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Cagliari, via Marengo 2, Cagliari, 09123, Italy; Paramasivam S., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Cagliari, via Marengo 2, Cagliari, 09123, Italy; Kumar A., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Cagliari, via Marengo 2, Cagliari, 09123, Italy; Pilo F., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Cagliari, via Marengo 2, Cagliari, 09123, Italy; Gatto G., Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, University of Cagliari, via Marengo 2, Cagliari, 09123, Italy
Abstract: Accurate and computationally efficient battery models are essential for battery management systems and battery digital-twin workflows. However, model selection requires careful evaluation of the trade-off between dynamic voltage fidelity, computational effort, energy accounting, and ageing representation. This paper presents a reproducible MATLAB-based benchmarking workflow for comparing equivalent-circuit models (ECMs) at battery-pack scale under common parameterisation and ageing assumptions. A SAFT-type RC model and first-, second-, and third-order Thevenin models are evaluated using open-access state of charge (SoC)/state of health (SoH)-dependent parameter surfaces, an empirical calendar–cycling ageing law, and automated post-processing through the DATTES toolbox. The benchmark is performed on a 64s29p LiFePO₄ battery pack under a repeated synthetic 24-h current profile over a three-year equivalent operating horizon at fixed 25 °C. The results show that higher-order ECMs improve agreement with the third-order Thevenin internal reference, but the incremental benefit diminishes beyond the second-order model. Within the investigated model family, duty cycle, and MATLAB implementation, the second-order Thevenin model provides the most favourable compromise between internal-reference voltage fidelity and per-step computational cost. The ageing outputs show identical SoH and internal-resistance-growth trajectories across ECMs because the adopted ageing law is driven by common daily stress metrics rather than ECM-specific polarization states or transient overpotential histories. Therefore, these ageing results should be interpreted as a property of the implemented modular ageing-coupling strategy, not as a general proof that ECM order has no influence on degradation in real batteries. The study provides a transparent and reproducible benchmarking workflow for controlled ECM comparison, while experimental validation, electro-thermal coupling, and estimator-in-the-loop testing remain necessary before predictive deployment in operational BMS or digital-twin systems. © 2026 The Authors. Title: A Hybrid Framework for Managing Uncertainty in Digital Twins Information Processing
Source title: ASCE-ASME Journal of Risk and Uncertainty in Engineering Systems, Part B: Mechanical Engineering
Affiliations: Valencian Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Universitat Politècnica de València, Camino de Vera s/n, Valencia, 46022, Spain
Authors with affiliations: Giret A., Valencian Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Universitat Politècnica de València, Camino de Vera s/n, Valencia, 46022, Spain
Abstract: In the context of industry 4.0 and industry 5.0, digital twins (DTs) are key and useful elements for monitoring and adjusting physical entities in manufacturing systems. Although this approach offers clear and well-demonstrated advantages, DTs are affected by inaccuracies and uncertainties coming from multiple sources, such as data sensing, biases introduced by data processing, and model abstraction. Adequately managing uncertainty in DT is crucial for the efficient operations of manufacturing systems. This paper proposes a hybrid framework (i.e., a human-in-the-loop supported by AI techniques) for uncertainty management. The proposed framework uses AI approaches to identify and quantify uncertainties and to propose actions to the human user to reduce the risk of unsafe and/or inaccurate reasoning in DT information processing. The proposed approach incorporates a continuously running module that monitors the DT throughout its life cycle to identify emerging sources of uncertainty. This module is a mechanism for tracking how uncertainties propagate through the model, and for registering how these uncertainties influence and modify the resulting outcomes. Also, the proposed hybrid approach helps identify the DTs risky components and enables human users to manually intervene, facilitating informed and transparent decisions. A simplified case study of predictive maintenance for machine resources in the production line of a lumber factory producing medium-density fiberboard is used to illustrate and validate the proposal. The objective in this case study is to assess whether the proposed framework is able: (i) to identify uncertainty values out of the given confidence threshold defined by the user, (ii) to support the refinement and adaptation of the training phase of the AI approach implemented by the DT to reduce uncertainty, and (iii) to adequately detect malfunctioning sensors requiring replacement. Title: A strip-wise curvature integration deformation reconstruction framework using strain measurement from fiber optic sensors
Affiliations: Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States
Authors with affiliations: Li Y., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Wang X., Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States; Yang X., Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States; Ding J., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Hu R., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States; Huang Y., Department of Civil, Construction, and Environmental Engineering, North Dakota State University, Fargo, ND, United States; Tao C., Bowen School of Construction, Purdue University, West Lafayette, IN, United States
Abstract: Distributed fiber optic sensing (DFOS) provides spatially continuous strain measurements and is increasingly used in infrastructure monitoring applications. However, structural deformation, a key response parameter for performance assessment, is not directly available from measured strain data alone. To enable deformation evaluation from distributed strain measurements, this study develops a curvature integration deformation reconstruction framework based on Kirchhoff-Love plate theory specialized for DFOS applications in thin plate structures. This study is designed to accommodate the intrinsic measurement characteristics of DFOS, in which strain data are obtained along discrete fiber paths. Given the number restriction of DFOS, the reconstruction formulation is modified to enable strip-based calculations compatible with DFOS layouts. The reconstruction is formulated as an inverse problem grounded in Kirchhoff-Love plate theory. DFOS measured surface strains are converted into bending curvatures and subsequently integrated along Kirchhoff-Love strips to recover full field displacement. Spline interpolation and boundary correction are incorporated to enhance numerical stability and mitigate measurement uncertainty. To verify the reliability of the method, multiple representative loading conditions on thin plates are conducted, including bending, impact, and buckling. The results are validated through comparison with finite element analysis (FEA) and experimental measurements. In the bending test, the predicted transverse deflection closely matches the imposed displacement, with a relative error of less than 9%. For the impact and buckling conditions, the reconstructed peak transverse deflections also show strong alignment with FEA outputs. These results indicate that the Kirchhoff-Love strips method (KLSM) framework, leveraging DFOS measurement data, provides a reliable and efficient solution for deformation reconstruction in thin-plate structures with limited sensor coverage, supporting potential applications in real-time structural health monitoring and digital twin systems. © 2026 Institution of Structural Engineers. Abstract: Verification of digital twins, especially in the presence of distributed components and asynchronous communication, remains a fundamental challenge. Uncertainty arises not only from the physical environment and virtual representations, but also from the bidirectional flow of data between them. This paper presents a formal verification methodology that captures these dynamics by translating a digital twin’s probabilistic elements into a finite state machine, augmented with explicit models of message delay and concurrent evolution. Using the Temporal Logic of Actions (TLA), we specify and verify temporal properties that ensure system-level correctness despite communication disorder and component-level asynchrony. We demonstrate this approach on a digital twin of an unmanned aerial vehicle, showing how to verify synchronization properties that govern end-to-end coherence between the physical and virtual components. Our case study highlights how formal specification clarifies system modeling choices, including which guarantees must hold, how system behaviors should be represented, and what assumptions are essential. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: A cyber–physical digital twin for secure and optimal operation of smart energy grids under deep uncertainty
Affiliations: University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Yordanova Z., University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria; Nozari H., University of National and World Economy, Bulgaria
Abstract: Smart energy networks, as critical cyber-physical infrastructures, face simultaneous challenges such as conflicting operational objectives, data uncertainty, and increasing cyber threats. Decision-making in such environments requires frameworks that can manage system dynamics, information ambiguity, and security risks in an integrated manner. In this study, an innovative decision-making framework is presented that enables adaptive and resilient optimization of energy networks by combining digital twin and fuzzy goal modeling. As an active component, the digital twin dynamically updates the decision-making process and reflects the impact of different cyber-attack scenarios on decisions. The results of various analyses show that the proposed framework is able to significantly improve the quality of decisions, performance stability, and system resilience under uncertain conditions. This study provides a new path for the development of smart and secure decision support systems in the energy sector. © 2026 The Authors

Title: GNN-RL: Multi-objective HPC scheduling with graph neural networks and reinforcement learning
Affiliations: Department of EECS, University of Kansas, 2001 Eaton Hall, 1520 West 15th Street, Lawrence, 66045, KS, United States
Authors with affiliations: Adimora K.C., Department of EECS, University of Kansas, 2001 Eaton Hall, 1520 West 15th Street, Lawrence, 66045, KS, United States; Sun H., Department of EECS, University of Kansas, 2001 Eaton Hall, 1520 West 15th Street, Lawrence, 66045, KS, United States
Abstract: High-performance computing (HPC) systems face escalating challenges in resource allocation as workloads grow increasingly heterogeneous and computational demands reach exascale levels. Traditional scheduling methods struggle to effectively manage diverse and fluctuating workloads, while recent machine learning approaches fail to fully capture the complex interactions between jobs, resources, and system states. We present GNN-RL, a framework that integrates Graph Attention Networks (GAT) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to address fundamental limitations in HPC scheduling. Our approach complements recent uncertainty-aware and digital twin-based schedulers by providing efficient graph-structured state representations that capture complex job dependencies and resource topologies. Through multi-head attention mechanisms and sophisticated state representations, GNN-RL simultaneously optimizes resource utilization, job throughput, makespan, and system fairness. A comprehensive evaluation of 377,234 jobs from three Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF) systems, Polaris, Mira, and Cooley, demonstrates significant improvements over EASY-backfilling: 13.8%–20.2% resource utilization gains, 15.0%–50.0% throughput increases, and 12.1%–12.8% makespan reductions, with statistical validation confirming significance and large effect sizes. Job-level analysis reveals that medium-sized batch jobs (16–128 nodes) benefit most from graph-based scheduling (＋15.3 percentage points utilization), while large jobs ((Formula presented) nodes) show smaller gains with a slight fairness trade-off. The framework maintains 76% effectiveness at 50K concurrent jobs, demonstrating strong potential for practical application in HPC environments. © 2026 The Authors. Published by Elsevier B.V.
