Title: Adaptive Bayesian learning for stability characterization of re-entry vehicles
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, 37996, TN, United States; School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, 74078, OK, United States
Authors with affiliations: Tiwari B., Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, 37996, TN, United States; Musharrat L., Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, 37996, TN, United States; Romeo S.A.S., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, 74078, OK, United States; Kassem A., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, 74078, OK, United States; Kara K., School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Oklahoma State University, Stillwater, 74078, OK, United States; San O., Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, University of Tennessee, Knoxville, 37996, TN, United States
Abstract: Accurate characterization of aerodynamic stability coefficients is essential for predicting the dynamic behavior of atmospheric re-entry vehicles. Estimating these coefficients from free-flight data is challenging due to nonlinear flow–structure coupling, limited data, and high computational costs. Existing nonlinear parameter estimation methods often provide only discrete results without full uncertainty quantification, emphasizing the need for a continuous and uncertainty-aware framework. This study introduces an adaptive Bayesian surrogate approach that combines differential evolution (DE), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), and Gaussian process regression with an upper confidence bound adaptive-sampling strategy to infer both static and dynamic stability coefficients from computational fluid dynamics data. The approach first uses DE–MCMC to estimate baseline aerodynamic coefficients at discrete control-points and then iteratively refines smooth, uncertainty-bounded functional curves through adaptive learning. Demonstrations on one-degree-of-freedom free-flight simulations of the Genesis re-entry capsule at Mach 1.10–1.50 show that the refined surrogates capture physically consistent trends across the angle of attack range, reduce epistemic uncertainty by more than 50 percent, and achieve mean reconstruction errors below 0.7 for training and within 1.5 for validation cases. The framework provides an efficient, data-driven route for constructing continuous aerodynamic-stability response surfaces with quantified confidence, supporting predictive modeling and digital-twin development for re-entry systems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: LLM-augmented semantic edge intelligence in wireless sensor networks and IoT: a review-led evidence synthesis and conceptual framework
Affiliations: Department of Computing and Information Technology, Faculty of Science and Technology, The University of the West Indies, St. Augustine, Trinidad and Tobago
Authors with affiliations: Khan K., Department of Computing and Information Technology, Faculty of Science and Technology, The University of the West Indies, St. Augustine, Trinidad and Tobago
Abstract: Wireless sensor networks (WSNs) increasingly support sensing-to-decision loops in which the value of a transmission depends on task utility, freshness, uncertainty, privacy, and safety rather than on bit fidelity alone. This article presents a review-led evidence synthesis and, as a secondary contribution, an author-proposed conceptual framework; it does not report a validated control algorithm. The review analyzes a 178-record evidence corpus, complemented by seven separately logged mathematical-outlook references, across WSN and IoT foundations, semantic communication, TinyML and split inference, federated learning, generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), digital twins, wireless foundation models, and language-model-assisted operations. The supplementary materials release a machine-readable extraction sheet with one row per record, a field codebook, a reference and screening ledger, qualification and completeness audits, and an integrity manifest. A work qualifies as LLM-augmented semantic edge intelligence only when an identifiable large language model (LLM) consumes task-relevant WSN/IoT state or operator intent and can affect sensing, communication, diagnosis, resource allocation, or control through a typed and auditable path. Under this boundary, only one retained work supplies direct E2 simulation evidence of an LLM-mediated communication or control path. Most LLM/RAG evidence is bridging or adjacent and remains at E0–E2. The synthesis therefore distinguishes the roles and maturity of the component technologies instead of treating them as an interchangeable stack. It identifies bounded examples of LLM/RAG utility in communication-policy generation, cross-task networking adaptation, global evidence synthesis, tool orchestration, and natural-language formulation for an external solver. It does not support a general claim of superiority over rules, exact optimization, structured retrieval, or task-specific machine learning and reinforcement learning. To translate the documented gaps into testable requirements, the article proposes an IoT-native reference architecture, a seven-axis taxonomy, a threat model, a formal synthesis and selection/cost model, typed cross-layer interface contracts, and an eight-phase benchmark protocol. These normative artifacts are proposed by the author. They are not established methods extracted from the corpus, consensus standards, a deployable solver or controller, or experimentally validated results. An explicitly hypothetical wildfire-monitoring case makes the formalism inspectable: it defines semantic distortion, normalizes and elicits the penalty weights, evaluates a finite candidate set under hard constraints, applies the non-dominance and LLM-admission rules, reports switch-point sensitivity, and exercises one LLM-to-optimizer interface contract. Its values are tutorial inputs, not measurements. A provenance audit separates cited evidence, author-defined review and coding constructs, conventional notation, and proposed framework artifacts. Each contribution is linked to measurable outcomes and a minimum support condition, but these quantities define future tests rather than imply new performance gains. An LLM is retained only when it closes a declared open-vocabulary or heterogeneous-knowledge capability gap, satisfies hard energy, deadline, privacy, safety, and verifier constraints, and provides positive incremental value over the strongest feasible simpler baseline. Resource-constrained nodes continue to handle sensing, routing, medium access control, and lightweight inference. Grounded LLM/RAG components operate at gateway, edge, cloud, or digital-twin tiers, and their outputs are limited to evidence-linked, tool-checked, reversible proposals. The review remains the evidentiary core; the conceptual framework converts its gaps into falsifiable design and evaluation requirements for future semantic IoT systems. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: A modular Digital Twin architecture for the data-driven reactive planning of disassembly systems

Abstract: Disassembly is key to circular production, enabling end-of-life products to be recovered through reuse, remanufacturing, or recycling. However, disassembly is characterized by high uncertainty about product condition and process feasibility, which requires dynamic, product-specific planning. While predictive disassembly planning anticipates uncertainties, disassembly systems must additionally be able to adapt their plans in real time when deviations occur. This is addressed by Reactive Disassembly Planning (RDP), which enables the dynamic adaptation of disassembly processes and schedules during disassembly. However, unlocking RDP's full potential requires complex decision-making based on comprehensive real-time data. To support such data-driven RDP, a modular Digital Twin architecture is presented that integrates all decision-making steps into an automated, real-time planning pipeline. The architecture is instantiated and deployed as a Digital Twin in a learning-factory disassembly system to demonstrate the feasibility and end-to-end operation of the proposed modules and connectors. Its potential is illustrated in a representative scenario, in which the instantiated Digital Twin achieves a 78% reduction in lead time and a 2% increase in profit compared to operating without RDP, and a 529% profit increase compared to a rule-based process-termination strategy. These results serve as illustrative proof of applicability, indicating that data-driven RDP via Digital Twins can support efficient, resilient disassembly operations and thereby strengthen the business case for circular factories and the transition to more sustainable production. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Transition-Based Digital Twin Modelling for Alzheimer’s Disease Under Sparse Longitudinal Data

Abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) progression is highly heterogeneous and is typically observed through sparse and irregularly sampled longitudinal data, posing challenges for reliable prediction and individualised monitoring. Existing machine learning approaches have improved AD prediction using multimodal data, yet they often focus on static classification or cohort-level risk estimation, providing limited support for subject-specific trajectory modelling and uncertainty-aware reasoning. To address these limitations, we present a personalised digital twin framework for Alzheimer’s disease prediction and scenario-based analysis using multimodal longitudinal data. The proposed approach integrates complementary modelling strategies to capture both short-term clinical transitions and longer-range temporal dependencies across follow-up visits. Using data from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), including cognitive assessments, clinical variables, and MRI-derived structural phenotypes, the framework predicts future cognitive status and diagnostic categories while quantifying predictive uncertainty and enabling patient-specific what-if trajectory analysis under controlled perturbations of clinically meaningful variables. Experimental evaluation on leak-free subject-level splits demonstrates strong performance in both cognitive score forecasting and diagnosis classification. Importantly, in this sparse and irregular ADNI setting, transition-based modelling of adjacent visits achieved higher predictive accuracy than the sequence-based branch, suggesting that local transition modelling may be more data-efficient under the present data constraints. While sequence models remain valuable for uncertainty-aware trajectory forecasting, local transition modelling offers a more data-efficient and robust predictive strategy in this setting. These findings highlight the importance of aligning temporal modelling strategies with the structure of real-world clinical data and suggest that transition-based digital twin formulations may provide a practical and interpretable approach for personalised disease forecasting and monitoring in neurodegenerative disorders. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Prognostics and health management (PHM) is essential for reliable unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operation, yet its transition from laboratory development to real platforms is hindered by scarce fault data, low-fidelity simulations, and the lack of cross-scenario validation mechanisms. This paper proposes a consistency-driven digital twin (DT) paradigm for scalable and deployment-oriented UAV-PHM by unifying physical modeling, uncertainty reconstruction, and cross-domain validation within a closed-loop physical-digital workflow. Structure-aware system identification establishes dynamic consistency for physically grounded virtual models, while distribution-aligned residual modeling reconstructs stochastic sensing discrepancies to ensure statistical and measurement consistency. These components are further integrated into an executable DT infrastructure that preserves control-flow and uncertainty characteristics, enabling reliable algorithm training, verification, and seamless Simulation-to-Reality (Sim2Real) migration across virtual and real UAVs. Extensive real-virtual experiments demonstrate near-lossless Sim2Real transfer, robust cross-domain generalization, and stable diagnostic performance even under extreme data scarcity, significantly reducing reliance on large-scale fault flight campaigns. Finally, the complete DT toolkit, consistency enhancer, interface protocols, and validation platform are open-sourced at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Mask-F727/README.md to provide a reproducible and extensible foundation for standardized twin-enabled PHM development. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Atomic and mesoscale simulations of silicon anodes in lithium-ion batteries: A review of methodologies and degradation mechanisms

Abstract: Silicon offers high theoretical capacity but undergoes coupled chemical and mechanical degradation, including large volume change, particle and electrode fracture, repeated solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) renewal, and irreversible lithium trapping. This review examines atomic and mesoscale methods used to study these processes, covering density functional theory (DFT), ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), density-functional tight-binding (DFTB), the embedded-atom method (EAM), the modified embedded-atom method (MEAM), the reactive force field (ReaxFF), and machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). For each method, we distinguish the quantities it can resolve, its typical spatial and temporal domain, the assumptions that control reliability, and the degradation questions that remain inaccessible. Beyond cataloguing methods, the review links common failure signatures to simulation outputs and experiment-comparable observables, and it explains how validated atomistic quantities may be transferred to particle-, electrode-, and cell-scale models. Emerging directions are assessed conditionally, with emphasis on uncertainty-aware MLIPs, bidirectional simulation-experiment validation, controlled cross-scale coupling, and evidence thresholds for future digital-twin applications. © 2026 Science Press and Dalian Institute of Chemical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Abstract: Additive manufacturing is relying more and more on artificial intelligence for prediction, control, and real-time decisions. Deployment, however, is still difficult. The main reason is that the underlying thermal, flow, and microstructural behavior can shift as the process changes, which makes reliable model performance hard to maintain. This review examines how trustworthy artificial intelligence (TAI) can be used to close that gap in digital twins for additive manufacturing across both metallic and ceramic systems. It frames trustworthiness as a technical condition for deployment and translates it into an AM-specific operational framework. From that point onward, it examines how current workflows handle reliability, uncertainty quantification, interpretability, explainability, robustness, generalizability, fairness, and transparency. A structured evaluation of sixty studies in metallic and ceramic additive manufacturing systems reveals a distinct trend. Robustness and generalizability receive much more attention than transparency, explainability, and fairness. The coverage is also stronger in metallic systems than in ceramic ones. To move beyond binary classification, the review further applies a structured evidence-depth rubric that distinguishes absent coverage, limited or implicit evidence, method-level evidence, and operational evidence for each TAI attribute. We further show that trustworthy deployment depends on more than predictive accuracy. It also depends on physically consistent models as well as updates that account for uncertainty. Decision support has to remain interpretable as well. Model transfer across machines and materials should be treated as controlled adaptation, where reusable physics, sensing, and validation elements are separated from material-specific features that require recalibration. The validation path must also support qualification and industrial deployment, leading to a more cohesive digital twin framework. It brings together physics-based models, reduced-order models, learning-based surrogates, multimodal sensing, and trust-aware evaluation. The main finding is that trustworthiness is the missing technical link between digital twins that can be confidently used in advanced manufacturing and promising AI-enabled demonstrations. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Trustworthy and physics-informed artificial intelligence for food processing operations: validation, control relevance, and industrial readiness
Source title: Trends in Food Science and Technology
Affiliations: Department of Biosystems Engineering, Faculty of Agriculture, Bu-Ali Sina University, Hamedan, Iran; Department of Engineering, Faculty of Agriculture, Dalhousie University, Truro, NS, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Alaei B., Department of Biosystems Engineering, Faculty of Agriculture, Bu-Ali Sina University, Hamedan, Iran; Chayjan R.A., Department of Biosystems Engineering, Faculty of Agriculture, Bu-Ali Sina University, Hamedan, Iran; Martynenko A., Department of Engineering, Faculty of Agriculture, Dalhousie University, Truro, NS, Canada
Abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications in food processing are mostly limited to data-driven prediction models, while industry needs AI for trustworthy operational use. Much of the evidence still rests on dataset-level performance, whereas validation quality, physical credibility, uncertainty, interpretability, control relevance, and industrial readiness of AI models are examined less consistently. Scope and approach: This critical review uses structured evidence mapping strategy to appraise recent reviews, methodological papers, and direct evidence studies across drying, thermal processing, extrusion, fermentation, cleaning, quality monitoring and process systems enabled by AI models. Related nonthermal, membrane, separation, and rheology-oriented studies are used only when they inform validation, process physics, monitoring, control, or industrial readiness. The final reference list contains 73 cited sources; 69 of these were coded as records in the structured evidence map, while the remaining sources supported background, conceptual framing, methodological context, or boundary positioning. Key findings and conclusions: Predictive modeling and soft sensing are comparatively mature, especially when spectral, imaging, acoustic, or process data are used to estimate quality attributes or state variables. However, external validation across batches, products, equipment, and production periods remains inconsistent. Uncertainty is rarely quantified, and many claims involving digital twins or advanced control remain limited to conceptual frameworks, simulations, or laboratory-scale demonstrations. Physics-informed machine learning, hybrid mechanistic data-driven models, reduced-order models and digital twins offer promising pathways toward transferable and robust process AI, but only when underlying physical assumptions, validation domains, and deployment constraints are clearly defined. Future research should better align model claims with rigorous validation strategies, explicit physical grounding, uncertainty quantification, and measurable process-level benefits. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Digital twin modelling of shield tunneling undercrossing existing tunnels: A case study

Abstract: Shield tunneling undercrossing existing tunnels presents significant challenges for deformation control due to complex ground-structure interactions and geotechnical uncertainties. While digital twin modeling offers a promising solution for real-time decision-making, its reliability is often limited by soil spatial variability and sparse monitoring data. To address this challenge, this paper presents a comprehensive digital twin modeling framework designed for shield tunneling undercrossing existing tunnels. First, a data-driven multi-conditional random field for the undercrossing zone is constructed using the three-dimensional multi-output sparse Bayesian learning method to account for spatial variability in soil properties. The constructed random field is then integrated into a stochastic finite-difference model to simulate deformation responses under uncertainty arising from soil spatial variability. Subsequently, Bayesian sparse dictionary learning is employed in conjunction with field monitoring data to enable accurate prediction and uncertainty quantification of existing tunnel deformations under sparse data conditions. Finally, based on Monte Carlo simulations, system reliability indices of the existing tunnels during the undercrossing process are calculated using deformation as performance indicators, and shield operational parameters are optimized accordingly. The proposed framework is validated using the Nanjing Metro Line 11 undercrossing Line 10 project as a case study. Systematic analysis of field monitoring data is first conducted, based on which computational modeling and analysis are performed to verify the framework's applicability and effectiveness. The results demonstrate good agreement between predicted and measured deformations, confirming the model's accuracy. Reliability analysis reveals that the Line 10 right-line tunnel is more susceptible to heave failure, with the overall system failure probability reaching 5.58%. By appropriately reducing the mean earth chamber pressure in the undercrossing section to 250 kPa, the system failure probability can be effectively reduced to 3.46%. The findings demonstrate that the proposed digital twin modeling framework can effectively assess tunneling-induced deformation risks during undercrossing operations and support risk-informed optimization of shield operational parameters. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A digital-twin framework for rapid field-level prediction using parametric POD-ROM and phase-locked transient analysis

Abstract: A digital-twin framework for efficient prediction of field-level quantities in pump-turbine systems using a reduced-order modeling (ROM) approach is presented in this paper. The framework couples a steady parametric proper-orthogonal-decomposition reduced-order model (POD-ROM) with a phase-locked Fourier representation of transient blade loading, enabling fast reconstruction of blade-surface pressure and velocity distributions across operating conditions. Pressure and velocity are used only as representative demonstration variables; the same workflow applies to other monitored scalar or vector quantities, provided the field of interest admits an accurate low-rank (linear) approximation. Under leave-one-out validation at the design condition, the steady POD-ROM reproduces the CFD reference with a global relative (Formula presented) error of 0.55% for pressure and 3.0% for velocity, with coefficients of determination R2of 0.997 and 0.991, respectively; the larger pointwise velocity percentiles are confined to low-momentum regions and do not affect the global or mechanical-integrity-relevant fidelity. The model extrapolates accurately for small excursions beyond the sampled range, is well-conditioned against input-parameter uncertainty (normalised sensitivity below unity), and inherits an intrinsic denoising capability from POD truncation. For transient loading, the phase-locked Fourier "twin state" compresses rotor-synchronous pulsations—at the design and two off-design conditions—into a compact, physically interpretable coefficient set, reconstructing the phase-resolved loading with sub-percent error while retaining cycle-to-cycle variability. Once the offline stage is complete, online inference reduces a full CFD evaluation from hours to seconds or less, making the framework well suited to real-time digital-twin deployment for predictive maintenance and operational optimization. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Digital Twin Hydration Intelligence for Wearable Atmospheric Water Generators: A Microclimate-Conditioned, Closed-Loop Advisory Architecture

Abstract: This study proposes and evaluates a digital twin framework for personalised, microclimate-conditioned hydration support integrated with a Smart Wearable Atmospheric Water Generator (SWAWG). Urban heat exposure increases dehydration risk, yet most wearable hydration devices remain reactive and rarely account for local microclimate. The framework predicts individual hydration risk from physiological signals and temperature–humidity context, then generates advisory operating targets for the SWAWG. The twin synchronizes on-body sensing with edge–cloud processing to maintain an updated wearer–device state, forecasts near-term hydration trajectories, and applies conservative uncertainty-aware rules to output guidance that can prompt intake or adjust water-generation duty cycling within safety constraints. The framework is design- and architecture-oriented; contributions include a control-oriented closed-loop sensing-to-actuation pipeline, a microclimate–physiology co-modelling scope with explicit boundary conditions, and an edge–cloud operational design with indicative latency and energy targets as engineering goals. To illustrate expected system behaviour, we present scenario-based simulations under contrasting climate conditions (hot–humid and mild), reporting conceptual fluid deficit adaptation and hydration tracking performance as proof-of-concept results rather than empirically validated outcomes. The approach aims to improve hydration decision support, support energy-aware actuation planning, and motivate privacy-preserving population analytics in urban heat-risk deployments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Closing the learning loop in lithium–sulfur batteries through physics-informed and trustworthy artificial intelligence

Abstract: Lithium–sulfur (Li–S) batteries combine a high theoretical specific energy with low-cost active materials, yet their development remains constrained by coupled reaction pathways, mobile intermediates, lithium-metal instability, and a large design space that changes with loading, electrolyte inventory, temperature, format, and cycling history. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a way to connect these variables, but most published demonstrations remain isolated within small computational datasets, literature-derived tables, or single-laboratory cell series. This review develops an evidence-first, closed-loop framework for AI-enabled Li–S research that links observation, learning, decision, validation, and model updating. It critically examines data infrastructure, text and multimodal extraction, descriptor learning, catalyst and electrolyte design, physics-informed state inference, degradation prognosis, autonomous experimentation, and digital twins. The available evidence shows that machine learning (ML) can compress high-dimensional calculations, recover useful structure–property relations, and predict selected cell outcomes within bounded domains. However, ML has not yet demonstrated robust transfer across laboratories, cell formats, or practical operating conditions. The main barriers are incomplete metadata, non-independent data splits, uncertain labels, weak uncertainty calibration, and limited prospective validation. To address these gaps, the review introduces a minimum data schema, an evidence-fidelity pathway that separates proxy prediction from decision-grade evidence, task-specific benchmarking requirements, and a minimum viable digital-twin architecture for Li–S cells. The central conclusion is that AI becomes decision-grade only when its predictions are physically credible, uncertainty-aware, experimentally actionable, and iteratively validated. © 2026 The Authors. Abstract: This letter presents a novel model predictive control (MPC) approach for autonomous pick-and-place between moving platforms with a hook-equipped aerial manipulator. First, for accurate and rapid modeling of the complex dynamics, a digital twin model of the quadcopter equipped with a hook-based gripper, implemented in MuJoCo, is constructed and used as the predictive model for the MPC. To handle uncertainties of the predictive model (e.g. due to aerodynamics and uncertain payloads), a robust adaptive MPC approach is proposed. By systematic integration of zero-order robust optimization (zoRO) based uncertainty propagation and an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for parameter estimation, the MPC algorithm ensures robust constraint satisfaction, high performance, and computational efficiency. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated in complex simulated scenarios and in real-world flight experiments. © 2016 IEEE.

Abstract: Efficient control of industrial bioprocesses requires robust mathematical models capable of predicting microbial dynamics under different environmental conditions. This study evaluates the Dynamic Energy Budget (DEB) theory for predicting Escherichia coli metabolism during sudden transitions between different carbon sources. We focused on assessing the sensitivity and identifiability of model parameters to determine substrate-specific factors and evaluate predictive limits. The DEB model demonstrated high in-sample precision and accuracy. The observed decrease in out-of-sample prediction accuracy was most likely caused by an accumulating systematic error. This error arose from the emergence of unmodeled factors during the final stage of the experiment, which can be mitigated by either preventing these factors experimentally or explicitly incorporating them into the model. Consequently, leveraging its mechanistic foundations derived from mass and energy balances, the DEB model provides application-useful accuracy even with limited data, showing great potential to be utilized as a Soft Sensor within Digital Twin technologies for bioprocess monitoring. © 2026 The Author(s). Abstract: Spinal deformities, including adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, adult spinal deformity, and early-onset scoliosis, are three-dimensional disorders that may evolve over time through interacting biological, developmental, and biomechanical processes. Although radiography, CT, MRI, and EOS imaging remain central to diagnosis and surgical planning, they provide static anatomical information rather than longitudinal, biomechanical, or intraoperative representations of deformity behaviour. This narrative review examines the transition from static image-based assessment to dynamic intelligence in spinal deformity care. Early AI applications have focused on vertebral segmentation, landmark detection, Cobb angle measurement, Lenke classification, and radiographic workflow automation, but these static models remain limited by annotation variability, domain shift, and a lack of temporal modelling. Emerging longitudinal approaches, including recurrent neural networks, temporal transformers, graph neural networks, and neural ordinary differential equations, may support trajectory-based prediction of deformity progression. Biomechanics-constrained methods, including finite element analysis, physics-informed neural networks, and patient-specific digital twins, may further enable individualised prediction of correction response, implant loading, fixation biomechanics, and junctional risk. Robot-assisted platforms have improved navigation-guided pedicle screw placement, but current systems remain surgeon-directed assistance tools rather than autonomous deformity-correction systems. Dynamic, temporally aware, and biomechanics-constrained intelligence may reshape spinal deformity care, but the maturity of the supporting technologies remains uneven. Static imaging is clinically established, and automated measurement has the strongest evidence among the AI applications reviewed here; longitudinal prediction and patient-specific simulation remain under validation; continuous-time models, closed-loop autonomous correction, and neuromorphic control remain conceptual. Clinical translation will require longitudinal multicentre datasets, temporal validation, uncertainty quantification, explainability, adaptive AI governance, and meaningful surgeon oversight. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Hybrid Digital Twin Framework for Predictive Maintenance and Operational Optimization of Marine Propulsion Systems
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, AMET University, Chennai, India; Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, SSN School of Engineering, Shiv Nadar University, Chennai, India; Faculty of Data Science and IT, INTI International University, Nilai, 71800, Malaysia

Abstract: Marine propulsion systems operate under highly variable environmental and mechanical conditions, making conventional threshold-based monitoring and calendar-based maintenance insufficient for early degradation detection and operational optimization. This study proposes a hybrid Digital Twin framework for a Panamax-class container vessel equipped with a MAN B&W ME-GI propulsion system. The framework integrates multi-rate operational and sensor data, time synchronization and preprocessing, a physics-based Mean Value Engine Model, machine-learning residual analysis, anomaly detection, Remaining Useful Life estimation, uncertainty quantification, and PMS/EMS-based decision support. A twelve-month simulated dataset was generated to represent variations in engine load, vessel trim, draft, sea state, hydrodynamic resistance, and progressive machinery degradation. The proposed framework was evaluated against a baseline Planned Maintenance System using Specific Fuel Oil Consumption, unplanned maintenance events, advisory latency, and false-alarm rate. Results show that the Digital Twin reduced Specific Fuel Oil Consumption from 184.6 to 176.9 g/kWh, equivalent to a 4.17% improvement. Unplanned maintenance events decreased from 11 to 9 per year, advisory latency was reduced from 20.0 to 8.5 seconds, and the false-alarm rate declined from 6.1% to 2.1%. The framework also enabled earlier identification of scavenge-cooler fouling, cylinder leakage, injector-response delay, turbocharger deterioration, and bearing degradation. These findings demonstrate that combining physics-based modelling with temporal residual analysis can improve propulsion-performance estimation, diagnostic reliability, and condition-based maintenance planning. However, further validation using real shipboard data and multiple vessel configurations is required before operational deployment. © Authors retain all copyrights.

Title: SHINE: An Entropy-Guided Digital Twin Framework for 3D Myocardial Scar Reconstruction from Sparse CMR

Abstract: Accurate reconstruction of the arrhythmogenic myocardial substrate—specifically the conducting isthmuses essential for ventricular tachycardia (VT) ablation—depends on capturing fine-scale scar topology from sparse, anisotropic Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) MRI. Given the pronounced anisotropy (e.g., 1.2 × 1.2 × 8.0 mm) and limited slice sampling, volumetric reconstruction constitutes a highly ill-posed inverse problem, often leading to aliasing artifacts and discontinuous “staircase” geometries under discrete interpolation schemes. To address this challenge, we propose substrate reconstruction as a continuous function learning task defined on a patient-specific anatomical manifold. We introduce SHINE (Scar Heterogeneity via Implicit Neural Encoding), a framework that constructs a mathematically consistent “Digital Twin” of the diseased myocardium. The pipeline integrates automated biventricular segmentation with a Statistical Shape Model (SSM) to establish a continuous anatomical prior. To reconstruct detailed scar morphology, we employ a Bayesian SIREN architecture with sinusoidal activation functions, enabling the representation of high-frequency geometric structures and mitigating the spectral bias persistent in conventional Neural Fields. Importantly, we introduce an Entropy-Weighted Dirichlet Energy loss, which uses epistemic uncertainty to adaptively enforce smoothness in data-sparse regions while preserving high-fidelity details in data-rich regions. Evaluated on a clinical VT cohort of 40 patients, SHINE significantly outperformed discrete interpolation and weakly supervised benchmarks, achieving a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.93 and a volumetric error of 3.1%. Notably, our method effectively addresses the Nyquist sampling gap, enabling recovery of sub-voxel conducting channels within a unified, topology-preserving 3D framework to support precision electrophysiology planning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Integrating passive design, renewable energy, thermal flexibility, and intelligent control in net-zero energy buildings: A system-level review

Authors with affiliations: Refaey H.A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia, Department of Mechanical Engineering, Faculty of Engineering at Shoubra, Benha University, Cairo, 11629, Egypt; Alsharif A.M.A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, College of Engineering in Yanbu, Taibah University, Yanbu Al-Bahr, 46421, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Net-zero energy buildings require coordinated decisions across passive design, active systems, renewable generation, storage, occupants, and control. This article presents a structured evidence map and a focused critical review of these interactions. Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, and ScienceDirect were searched for English-language journal articles and reviews published from January 2015 to 11 August 2026. Database searches returned 4385 query-level records; the imported files contained 4423 occurrences due to a duplicate 38-record Scopus audit subset. Cleaning and cross-database deduplication produced 3180 unique records. Title-and-abstract screening retained 2622 records in a broad evidence map, while 66 sources were selected using predefined relevance criteria to support the focused synthesis. This source set represented the principal evidence types, performance dimensions, and system interactions rather than a statistically representative sample. Evidence was examined across energy performance, indoor environmental quality and well-being, flexibility, resilience, and whole-life carbon and cost. Reported performance depended strongly on climate, building type, occupancy, baseline, system boundary, and control strategy. Passive and hybrid envelope measures reshape building loads, whereas heat pumps, thermal and electrical storage, and predictive control provide operational flexibility. Their effectiveness depends more on coordinated sizing and operation than on individual component efficiency. Field evidence remains less common than simulation and short-term demonstrations, particularly for cyber-physical building systems. The review proposes a performance-oriented co-design and operation framework that integrates contextual conditions, design and control variables, and practical constraints within a coupled building-system model. Research priorities include long-term field validation, semantic interoperability, uncertainty-aware control, occupant-centered operation, resilience assessment, and whole-life evaluation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: The digital twin (DT) of battlefield environment is a cornerstone for real time, high fidelity decision support in modern joint operations. Traditional numerical simulation methods face inherent trade offs between computational speed, accuracy for nonlinear multi scale phenomena, and robust uncertainty quantification. This paper investigates physics informed machine learning as a paradigm to overcome these limitations, focusing on two representative techniques: adaptive physics informed neural networks (PINNs) for underwater acoustic field reconstruction, and graph neural network (GNN) based weather forecasting (GraphCast) for global atmospheric simulation. For underwater acoustics, we analyze an adaptive PINN framework that dynamically balances data fidelity and physics constrained losses, enabling accurate reconstruction of multimodal pressure fields from sparse hydrophone measurements; the method reduces inference time by two orders of magnitude compared to traditional parabolic equation solvers while maintaining relative errors below 5% in complex shallow water environments. For global weather, GraphCast generates 10 day deterministic forecasts at 0.25° resolution in under one minute, outperforming the ECMWF high resolution system in more than 90% of atmospheric variables when verified against operational analyses. A side by side comparison highlights complementary strengths, applicability boundaries, and common challenges including forecast smoothness, bias accumulation, and lack of intrinsic uncertainty quantification. Drawing on recent advances in conformal prediction and adversarial uncertainty quantification, we discuss pathways to produce statistically valid prediction intervals. Finally, we propose a layered simulation architecture for military digital twin environments that integrates global GNN based forecasting with local PINN based high resolution refinement, and we address verification, validation, and accreditation (VV&A) considerations based on DoD and U.S. Navy guidelines. The results demonstrate that physics guided artificial intelligence provides a viable, scalable path toward intelligent, real time battlefield environment digital twins. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Authors with affiliations: Zhang Y., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Ren F., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Liu H., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Meng F., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Li Q., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Wang J., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Zhu R., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Wu H., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China; Wu W., School of Electrical Engineering, Shandong University, Jinan, 250061, China
Abstract: Safety-critical energy infrastructures require high-fidelity digital twins (DTs) for reliable dynamic risk assessment. However, conventional state estimation faces trade-offs between computational efficiency and uncertainty calibration accuracy under degraded sensor data. To address this challenge, we propose a spatially selective Bayesian inference framework for real-time uncertainty quantification (UQ) in inverse heat transfer problems (IHTPs). By dynamically decoupling the physical domain into localized region-of-interest (ROI) subgraphs via graph neural networks (GNNs), the framework eliminates redundant far-field computations and isolates measurement anomalies. Validated on a million-node converter transformer, it compresses MCMC latency from 3631.44 s (restricted to a single serialized chain under the full mesh baseline) down to 217.23 s for a 6-chain parallel 5000-step execution, while maintaining a minimal memory footprint of 332.50 MB. Under extreme overloads and high measurement noise, the framework achieves stable parameter tracking and well-calibrated posterior uncertainty estimation. Furthermore, resolved uncertainty profiles are rapidly propagated for full-field thermal reconstruction and solid insulation aging prognostics. The results quantify heavy-tail degradation risks, providing grid operators with rigorous probabilistic safety margins to support proactive Condition-based Maintenance Plus (CBM+) and dynamic load rating (DLR) decisions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Uncertainty-aware hybrid framework for melt pool geometry prediction and process map development in Laser Powder Bed Fusion of Inconel 718
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical and Civil Engineering, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL, United States; Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, United States; Department of Mechanical, Materials, and Aerospace Engineering, Illinois Institute of Technology, IL, United States
Authors with affiliations: Saghaian S.E., Department of Mechanical and Civil Engineering, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL, United States; Hemmati M., Department of Mechanical and Civil Engineering, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL, United States; Hernanz A.C., Department of Mechanical and Civil Engineering, Florida Institute of Technology, Melbourne, FL, United States; Yang L., Department of Industrial Engineering, University of Louisville, Louisville, KY, United States; Saghaian S.M., Department of Mechanical, Materials, and Aerospace Engineering, Illinois Institute of Technology, IL, United States
Abstract: Melt pool geometry governs porosity formation, inter-layer bonding, microstructural evolution, and residual stress development in Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), making its accurate prediction central to process qualification and process-window development. However, experimental qualification is resource-intensive, high-fidelity multi-physics simulations remain computationally expensive for large-scale parameter exploration, and reduced-order analytical models often lose accuracy near melting-regime transitions. Existing machine learning (ML) approaches provide deterministic predictions but do not explicitly address uncertainty or systematic prediction bias, limiting their reliability across different operating conditions and experimental datasets. This study presents an uncertainty-aware hybrid ML framework for melt pool geometry prediction and process qualification in L-PBF of Inconel 718 (IN718). Single-track and multi-track specimens were fabricated over a broad range of laser powers, scan speeds, hatch spacings, and layer counts and characterized using optical and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed framework combines k-fold ensemble regression with physics-informed directional classification, where the ensemble standard deviation serves as a physically interpretable uncertainty signal and is subsequently converted into a targeted bias-correction mechanism. The melt pool depth-to-width ratio (D/W) was adopted as a unifying descriptor linking melt pool morphology, thermal-gradient-driven grain growth direction, melting-regime transitions, and process-map development. The framework was trained using 68 experimentally measured melt pools and evaluated using an external dataset of 54 measurements compiled from published L-PBF IN718 studies, including validation and independent test datasets. Compared with established analytical models and polynomial curve-fitting baselines, the proposed approach improved predictive accuracy, enhanced cross-study generalization, and provided useful ensemble-based uncertainty estimates. Multi-track experiments further validated the maximum hatch spacing criterion for predicting lack-of-fusion onset from single-track measurements, achieving prediction errors below 6% and enabling the identification of defect-free processing windows. The results demonstrate that ensemble prediction uncertainty contains information related to regime-dependent model sensitivity and can be exploited to improve prediction reliability near conduction-transition-keyhole boundaries. Beyond the specific IN718 case, the proposed framework provides a potentially transferable strategy for uncertainty-aware process qualification and rapid process-window development and offers a computationally efficient foundation for digital twin development, in-situ monitoring, and future closed-loop control of metal additive manufacturing (AM). © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Modeling of Movement Planning Process for Autonomous Mobile Robot in the University Technopark

Abstract: This paper examines the problem of modeling and planning the movement of an autonomous mobile robot in a university technology park characterized by high uncertainty, a multi-zone structure, and intensive interaction with personnel. It is shown that classical route planning algorithms do not provide the required adaptability and safety in an environment with variable human density and dynamic production priorities. A two-level algorithm for planning the motion of an industrial mobile robot is proposed, including fuzzy decision-making and classical navigation. The fuzzy model considers task urgency, distance to the target, population density, technology park zone type, and safety restrictions, generating an integrated route assessment and recommended speed. The technology park structure, robot status, and fuzzy rule base are formalized, enabling adaptive route selection in real time. Simulation experiment on 100 routes was conducted, comparing the proposed approach with the A* and Dijkstra algorithms. The simulation results showed that the fuzzy algorithm reduces the integrated risk indicator by an average of 40–45% and the number of route replanning. This confirms the feasibility of using fuzzy-logic and hybrid planning methods for mobile robots operating in the multifunctional environments of university technology parks. The results obtained can be used in the design of intelligent logistics systems integrated with MES/ERP and digital twins of production complexes. © European Alliance for Innovation 2027.

Title: Smart manufacturing of nanocomposites: Digital twins, process engineering, and translational industrialization

Abstract: Carbon nanotubes, graphene derivatives, MXenes, metal oxides, nanocellulose, and hybrid nanofillers exhibit outstanding reinforcement properties, such as mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, thermal transport, barrier properties, and multifunctionality, in thermoplastic and thermosetting matrices. However, the ability to produce these materials on an industrial scale is still hindered by many challenges, such as the variability of the raw materials, degradation of the properties when the materials agglomerate, high-throughput processing challenges due to the instability of the dispersion, high energy consumption of dispersion processes, limited window of manufacturability, quality control requirements, recycling limitations, and uncertainty regarding regulatory requirements. This review introduces a manufacturing framework to translate nanocomposites on the basis of a process-driven and systems engineering approach rather than just a material design perspective. This review addresses the processing methods that can be used on a large scale, such as melt compounding, reactive extrusion, solution-assisted processing, additively manufactured components, and roll-to-roll fabrication, and explores the dispersion behaviour, interphase evolution, orientation of the fillers, percolation behaviour, formation of defects, and functional reproducibility under different processing conditions. Special emphasis is placed on the coupled relationships between transport phenomena, rheological evolution, and multiscale structural organization, which are responsible for manufacturing scalability and deployment readiness. Emerging Industry 4.0 technologies, such as process analytical technologies (PATs), inline metrology, machine learning, digital twins, and autonomous process control, have been tested for their potential to predict and control important manufacturing metrics, such as dispersion quality, rheological behavior, filler-network formation, defect occurrence, and process consistency, through real-time data integration and adaptive feedback systems. The review also incorporates technoeconomic analysis, life cycle assessment, circular manufacturing approaches, and regulatory aspects to assess industrial feasibility for various application fields, such as aerospace, electronics, energy, biomedical, and multifunctional coatings. Finally, future directions include designs for manufacturing compatible nanomaterials, predictive multiscale modelling, certification structures enabled by digital, autonomous production systems, and sustainable industrial ecosystems. This review offers a complete overview of the challenges of scaling up the industrialization of advanced nanocomposite materials to be reproducible and economically viable while maintaining nanomaterial engineering, manufacturing science, digitalization, and lifecycle sustainability. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Digital twin stackelberg bayesian coordination of mobile storage for uncertainty-resilient renewable integration in offshore and coastal green hydrogen energy hubs
Affiliations: Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran
Authors with affiliations: Shayeghi H., Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran; Mohamadi B., Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran; Zare P., Energy Management Research Center, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, Ardabil, Iran
Abstract: The rapid deployment of renewable energy in offshore and coastal regions increases the need for storage systems that can manage intermittency, spatial mismatch, and grid integration constraints. Coordinated operation across offshore, coastal, and land-based energy hubs remains insufficiently developed when mobile storage logistics, green hydrogen pathways, multi-carrier coupling, and market mechanisms are considered together. This study proposes a digital twin-enabled optimization framework for mobile and hybrid storage management in offshore and coastal multi-energy communities. The architecture integrates electrical, thermal, cooling, hydrogen, and water subsystems, while offshore energy transport vessels relocate mobile storage units and support dynamic energy exchange among distributed hubs. A mixed-integer optimization model determines storage scheduling, inter-hub exchange, desalination operation, grid interaction, and market participation. A Stackelberg-Bayesian structure captures hierarchical interactions and information asymmetry among hubs, while a Wasserstein distance-based robust optimization framework handles uncertainty in renewable generation, demand, and market prices. Carbon emission trading and green certificate trading are embedded as market-based decarbonization incentives. Numerical results show that coordinated mobile storage operation improves renewable utilization and flexibility, eliminates curtailed electrical loads, and reduces operating costs by up to 21% compared with non-coordinated operation. Under environmental constraints, groundwater extraction is fully eliminated, with the cost increase partly offset by carbon and green certificate revenues. Coordinated operation increases carbon trading revenues by approximately 27% and green certificate revenues by up to 54%. These findings show that digital twin Stackelberg-Bayesian coordination of mobile storage can strengthen uncertainty-resilient renewable integration in offshore and coastal green hydrogen energy hubs. © 2026

Title: C³M-OMMT twin: A causal process–structure–property digital twin for morphology-aware mechanical optimization of OMMT-Modified PLA in fused-filament fabrications

Sant Gadge Baba Amravati University, Maharashtra, Amravati, India; Bhore N., Shri Shivaji Education Society Amravati's College of Engineering and Technology Akola. Sant Gadge Baba Amravati University, Maharashtra, Amravati, India
Abstract: Mechanically reliable fused-filament-fabricated (FFF) PLA/OMMT parts depend not only on filler fraction and nominal printing settings, but also on the coupled evolution of clay dispersion, melt rheology, thermal healing, void topology, and strain localization. This study develops C³M-OMMT Twin, a six-stage causal process-structure-property digital twin comprising ExfoRheo-MAP, ThermoBond-Sense, MorphoFrac-3D, CauPSP-Net, ConBayes-Pareto, and CounterTwinV. Approximately 60 D-optimal material-process combinations were used for model development and 20 Bayesian-selected trials were reserved for experimental closure. The design space covered 0–5 wt% OMMT, 195–225 °C nozzle temperature, 0.10–0.25 mm layer height, 25–55 mm s⁻¹ print speed, raster orientation, and infill. A directly characterized condition at 2 wt% OMMT, 215 °C, 0.15 mm, and 35 mm s⁻¹ produced 62.5 MPa tensile strength and approximately 2.2% void fraction. On held-out data, CauPSP-Net achieved R²= 0.974, RMSE= 1.72 MPa, MAE= 1.29 MPa, and MAPE= 2.53%; 90% conformal intervals achieved 90.7% empirical coverage with a 4.46 MPa mean width. Model-based multi-objective optimization identified the same operating neighborhood, with predicted Young's modulus of 3.82 GPa, flexural strength of 94.1 MPa, and CVIFSI of 0.162, while CounterTwinV reported a 3.1% validation discrepancy. The originality lies in retaining physically interpretable intermediate states from exfoliation and rheology through thermal bonding and three-dimensional defect morphology, then separating direct and morphology-mediated effects under calibrated uncertainty. The resulting manufacturing window is intended for reproducible, morphology-aware optimization of lightweight PLA/OMMT FFF components rather than unrestricted extrapolation beyond the validated material and process domain. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Toward autonomous infrastructure management: Agentic AI for structural health monitoring, robotics, and digital twins
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States
Authors with affiliations: Khan M.A., Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States; Hong P., Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States; Lin Z., Department of Civil Engineering, University of Texas at Arlington, Arlington, 76010, TX, United States
Abstract: Modern sensing, robotics, artificial intelligence (AI), and digital twins (DTs) are reshaping the design, construction, operation, and maintenance of civil infrastructure. This review examines the evolution of structural health monitoring (SHM) from predictive models toward agentic AI for autonomous infrastructure management. Current research has achieved substantial progress in vibration-based monitoring, vision-based inspection, robotic sensing, and transformer-enabled analytics; however, most workflows remain diagnostic and lack autonomous reasoning and decision-making capabilities. This review defines the emerging concept of Agentic SHM, synthesizes recent advances in reinforcement learning, large language models, robotics, and DTs, and proposes layered architecture integrating perception, reasoning, planning, execution, and governance. Key challenges, including trustworthy autonomy, uncertainty-aware decision-making, reproducibility, standards compliance, and multi-agent coordination, are identified. The review concludes that progressively validated, human-supervised agentic AI provides a practical pathway toward safer, more resilient, and lifecycle-oriented infrastructure automation, while providing a roadmap for future research and practical implementation across infrastructure. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Digital twin–based multi-scale framework for seismic integrity assessment of deep underground caverns
Affiliations: Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering, Hanyang University, Seoul, 04763, South Korea; Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering College of Engineering, King Faisal University, Al-Ahsa, 31982, Saudi Arabia
Authors with affiliations: Sharafat A., Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering, Hanyang University, Seoul, 04763, South Korea; Tanoli W.A., Department of Civil & Environmental Engineering College of Engineering, King Faisal University, Al-Ahsa, 31982, Saudi Arabia
Abstract: Deep underground caverns have attracted considerable interest in recent years due to their critical role in hydropower and energy infrastructure systems. However, reliable post-earthquake assessment remains challenging due to the complexity of multi-scale seismic response, uncertainty in rock mass properties, and difficulties in interpreting heterogeneous monitoring data. Despite the importance of seismic integrity assessment, there remains a paucity of systematic frameworks that integrate modeling and monitoring in a unified manner. This study therefore proposes a Digital Twin–driven multi-scale framework for seismic integrity assessment of underground caverns, integrating analytical, two-dimensional, and three-dimensional numerical modeling with real-time monitoring data. The aim of this study is to develop a comprehensive framework that enables consistent integration and interpretation of model predictions and monitoring observations. Within this framework, model outputs are defined as Project Intent Information, while monitoring data are defined as Project Status Information, allowing structured comparison through a unified data and knowledge ontology. This study introduces three performance metrics to assess the seismic response, namely the Seismic Integrity Index, Model Consistency Index, and Sensor Consistency Ratio, which collectively provide a quantitative basis for evaluating structural performance and model reliability. In addition, a rule-based multi-sensor consistency logic is developed to distinguish between local anomalies and global structural response, thereby improving the reliability of post-earthquake interpretation. Furthermore, a feedback-based model updating mechanism is implemented to refine numerical models using monitoring-informed interpretation within an integrated Digital Twin-based assessment framework. The proposed approach demonstrates the applicability of an integrated Digital Twin-based framework for model–monitoring-based seismic assessment under the investigated conditions. The results demonstrate that seismic-induced deformation remains limited under high confinement conditions, while the Digital Twin framework enables accurate interpretation of monitoring data and identification of local anomalies. These findings suggest that the proposed approach provides a systematic and scalable methodology for integrating modeling and monitoring in underground seismic assessment. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Carbon offset-aware economic scheduling using echo state enhanced variational mode decomposition and ARIMA forecasting for P2X-based city energy ecosystems with joint green-carbon certificate and socio-financial welfare

Abstract: Urban energy systems in sustainable cities are facing increasing challenges due to the simultaneous integration of hydrogen-based conversion, carbon regulation, renewable energy uncertainty, and emerging electric mobility demands. This paper develops a low-carbon optimization framework for a Multi-Energy Distribution Network that coordinates electricity, gas, heat, and hydrogen infrastructures while incorporating Power-to-X technologies, hydrogen-enriched gas utilization, carbon capture, and aerial electric mobility. The proposed framework integrates ADTAN-driven Electric Taxi Drone demand modeling, Digital Twin synchronization, Blockchain-based trusted coordination, ARIMA-based source-load forecasting, and a hybrid Stackelberg Game, Mechanism Design, and Nash Game structure within a unified scheduling framework. A mixed-integer optimization model is formulated considering green certificate trading, ladder-type carbon trading, and socio-financial welfare to achieve coordinated multi-energy management. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is evaluated through a large-scale urban energy system case study. Numerical results demonstrate that coordinated hydrogen blending and environmental market mechanisms reduce operating costs by 25.2% and carbon emissions by 17.2% compared with the baseline case. Moreover, wind power utilization increases from 71.5% to 98.8%, while renewable curtailment penalties decrease by more than 95%. The integrated Digital Twin and Blockchain layers further enhance operational transparency, synchronization capability, and coordination reliability, supporting the development of resilient and low-carbon urban energy management strategies. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Artificial intelligence in hydrogen safety: A Comprehensive review of methods, applications, and future directions
Source title: Journal of Loss Prevention in the Process Industries
Affiliations: Maria Curie-Skłodowska University in Lublin, Department of Neuroinformatics and Biomedical Engineering, Lublin, Poland; Warsaw University of Technology, Institute of Heat Engineering, Faculty of Power and Aeronautical Engineering, Warsaw, Poland

Abstract: Hydrogen is rapidly emerging as a cornerstone of the global clean energy transition, yet its unique physicochemical properties — wide flammability range, low ignition energy, high diffusivity, and invisible flame — pose substantial safety challenges across the entire value chain. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques may augment established safeguards through data-driven leak detection, real-time risk assessment, predictive maintenance, and physics-informed simulation. Following a structured, semi-systematic methodology, this review analyses the role of AI in hydrogen safety by examining applications in six key domains: (i) leak detection and sensor intelligence, (ii) dispersion modelling via ML–CFD surrogates, (iii) explosion and consequence prediction, (iv) probabilistic risk assessment, (v) fuel cell diagnostics and prognostics, and (vi) digital twin frameworks. The paper further evaluates physics-informed learning, reinforcement learning, natural language processing, and explainable AI from a process-safety perspective. Throughout, we distinguish demonstrated hydrogen-specific evidence from methods transferred from adjacent domains, and appraise reported performance critically, noting that high headline accuracies seldom address false-negative rates, dataset imbalance, uncertainty, or out-of-distribution behaviour. Key challenges including data scarcity, model interpretability, real-time deployment, and regulatory integration are discussed, and a research roadmap is proposed. Language-model applications are treated as expert-supervised knowledge assistance rather than substitutes for formal safety studies or regulatory decisions. © 2026

Title: AI for EV battery health: Statistical meta-analysis and Autonomous Intelligence Pyramid
Affiliations: Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India
Authors with affiliations: Tanala S., Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India; Venkatesh A., Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Anil Neerukonda Institute of Technology and Sciences, Sangivalasa, Andhra Pradesh, Visakhapatnam, 531162, India
Abstract: The transportation sector accounts for approximately 21% of global CO2 emissions (≈[jls-end-space/]8.4Gt CO2 in 2024), and the electrification of road transport is a critical lever for decarbonisation. Annual global EV battery deployment reached 1.2TWh in 2025, making accurate battery health monitoring essential for both performance and sustainability. This review, conducted via a PRISMA-based protocol over 531 peer-reviewed studies (2018–2026), provides a statistical meta-analysis of all major AI families deployed in battery management: classical machine learning, ensemble methods, deep sequential networks, hybrid CNN architectures, Transformers, Physics-Informed ML (PIML), Explainable AI (XAI), Federated Learning, and Large Battery Foundation Models. A DerSimonian–Laird random-effects meta-analysis with 95% confidence intervals and I2 heterogeneity statistics confirms that CNN–LSTM achieves a pooled RMSE of 0.47% (95% CI: 0.41%–0.53%, (Formula presented) vs EKF baseline) and Transformer architectures reach 0.42% (0.36%–0.48%, (Formula presented) ). The Foundation Model group, based on only nine studies at TRL 2–3, yields a preliminary pooled RMSE of 0.42% that is sensitivity-dependent on a single influential study; this figure should not be directly compared with the more robustly supported Transformer estimate. Critical limitations of all emerging methods are explicitly characterised. Environmental and social impacts of battery energy systems, including CO2 lifecycle analysis, are discussed. Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly being developed to support monitoring, prediction, optimization, and control in thermal and energy conversion systems operating under variable loads, uncertain boundary conditions, degradation, and strict safety and efficiency constraints. Their relevance is especially strong in internal combustion engines, gas turbines, batteries, fuel cells, heat exchangers, thermal energy storage, buildings and heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, and renewable- and hydrogen-integrated energy platforms, where real-time or near-real-time decision support can improve performance, reliability, and operational flexibility. This review examines how digital twins are being constructed and deployed across these domains, with emphasis on the requirements for trustworthy and practically usable implementations. It synthesizes the main methodological foundations of deployable twins, including reduced-order physics-based modeling, surrogate and scientific machine learning, data assimilation and state updating, uncertainty propagation, and real-time optimization and control. The review shows that progress has been substantial but uneven. Buildings and HVAC systems and battery-related applications appear closest to practical deployment, while many other domains remain limited by insufficient synchronization, sparse field validation, weak uncertainty treatment, and incomplete integration of prediction with operational decision-making. Based on this cross-domain synthesis, the review identifies the main barriers to wider adoption and proposes a framework for next-generation trustworthy digital twins built on physics-grounded reduced models, adaptive data linkage, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and decision-oriented deployment © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled digital twins are increasingly used to improve monitoring, prediction, control, and sustainability assessment in circular biorefineries. However, the literature remains fragmented, with many studies focusing on isolated prediction tasks rather than validated, decision-oriented digital-twin systems. This review critically examines AI-enabled digital twins for circular biorefineries that convert heterogeneous bioresources into biogas, hydrogen, volatile fatty acids (VFAs), microbial products, algal products, bio-oil, syngas, and biochar. The review differs from earlier studies by linking digital-twin architecture with soft sensing, hybrid modeling, constrained control, embedded techno-economic analysis (TEA), life-cycle assessment (LCA), and deployment-readiness requirements. Particular attention is given to VFA-platform biorefineries, where product speciation, pH control, separation energy, product routing, and uncertainty strongly influence process value. Across the reviewed literature, the most useful digital-twin functions are early detection of instability, estimation of hard-to-measure variables, feedstock-adaptive optimization, energy-intensity reduction, and transparent cost-emission trade-off analysis. The main barriers are limited online observability, weak external validation, poor transferability across sites, incomplete reporting of uncertainty, and insufficient integration between AI models and TEA-LCA decision layers. Future work should move from stand-alone predictive models toward validated hybrid twins with transfer learning, auditable data pipelines, constrained model predictive control (MPC), and carefully governed large-language-model interfaces to support operators and interpret scenarios. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: In the context of climate change, robust operational strategies are required to mitigate water supply depletion and ensure the reliable operation of decentralized water infrastructure systems. Rainwater Harvesting, Treatment and Reuse Systems (RHTRSs) are a feasible option, especially for non-drinking purposes, but their effectiveness depends on maintaining service continuity and compliance with water quality standards under uncertain environmental and operating conditions. In this study, a reliability-oriented Digital Twin (DT) was developed and implemented to simulate the RHTRS of a commercial building, combining the Building Information Modeling (BIM)-based geometry, hydrological study, physical-chemical treatment, Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) modeling, and an immersive Mixed Reality (MR) interface. The DT enables dynamic reliability assessment under uncertainty of system operation under stochastic environmental and demand variability by coupling structural data, hydraulic behavior, and time-series predictions of critical variables, including water availability and total suspended solids. The joint application of BIM, DT, ARIMA-based forecasting module supporting future soft sensing (e.g., turbidimeter), and MR visualization of a real-world, building-scale RHTRS is novel and provides a decision-support system to enhance the reliability, resilience, and safety of complex constructed infrastructure. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Digital Twin-oriented optimizer selection for volatility-sensitive manufacturing scheduling
Affiliations: Department of Business Administration, University of Patras, Patras, 26504, Greece
Authors with affiliations: Nearchou A.C., Department of Business Administration, University of Patras, Patras, 26504, Greece
Abstract: The increasing adoption of Digital Twin (DT) technologies in smart manufacturing has created the need for adaptive scheduling intelligence capable of operating under volatile and uncertain energy environments. Existing studies typically assume that a single optimization algorithm can effectively operate across all manufacturing conditions. However, optimization effectiveness is strongly influenced by energy volatility, uncertainty and production-context characteristics. This paper proposes a DT-oriented hyper-heuristic framework for adaptive optimizer selection in manufacturing scheduling. An offline Pareto optimization knowledge repository is constructed using nine representative multi-objective optimization (MOO) paradigms evaluated under multiple industrial energy scenarios with different volatility regimes. The resulting optimization knowledge is subsequently exploited to train a hyper-heuristic selector capable of recommending suitable optimization paradigms according to the prevailing DT operating conditions. To evaluate cross-environment robustness, a leave-one-scenario-out (LOSO) validation strategy is adopted using previously unseen energy conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that optimizer effectiveness is highly context-dependent and that the proposed framework consistently identifies near-optimal optimization paradigms associated with relatively low regret. Explainable decision-landscape analysis further reveals structured optimizer-selection transitions across different volatility regions, highlighting the strong interaction between energy-market dynamics and adaptive optimization behavior. © 2026 The Author

Title: Prediction of cooking-induced food transformations: A survey and outlook towards machine learning
Affiliations: Multitel Research & Innovation Center, Artificial Intelligence Department, Belgium; Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB), Transfers, Interfaces and Processes (TIPs), Belgium; Wallonia Institute of Food Science and Technology (WIFST), Belgium

Abstract: Cooking induces coupled physical, chemical, and biological transformations that jointly determine food safety, nutritional value, and sensory quality. Predicting cooking-induced food transformations is therefore a central challenge, receiving growing attention across applications including process optimisation in the food industry, product design, quality control, personalised cooking, and the development of smart appliances and digital twins. Despite extensive progress in food process engineering, robust prediction across foods, geometries, and operating conditions remains difficult due to the multiscale heterogeneity of food matrices, substantial process variability, and experimental data that are often sparse, noisy, or destructive to acquire. To stimulate future research, this survey provides a comprehensive review of modelling approaches for cooking-induced transformations and articulates a structured outlook towards machine learning (ML). We first consolidate the scientific background on food cooking processes. We then introduce a principled taxonomy of conventional models and analyse how their encoded structure can act as inductive bias for data-driven learning. Building on this foundation, we formalise cooking prediction as learning mappings from initial product state and process descriptors to time-resolved or endpoint outcomes, and synthesise data modalities and evaluation protocols required for trustworthy generalisation under distribution shift. Finally, we systematically map existing ML-based predictors, review hybrid and physics-informed integration strategies, and propose a research roadmap towards data-efficient, physically consistent, and uncertainty-aware models that enable robust decision-making and scalable digital twins for cooking processes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.
