Abstract: Reliable quality of transmission (QoT) prediction is essential to ensure that services operate near their optimal working point, maximizing network capacity and efficiency while avoiding large design margins. A major source of QoT prediction error lies in the uncertain modeling of nonlinear fiber impairments, particularly the Kerr effect and stimulated Raman scattering, which are difficult to monitor with existing hardware. Accurate modeling of these effects requires knowledge of fiber insertion loss. Additionally, the gain spectrum of optical amplifiers, which governs amplified spontaneous emission noise, is not directly monitored. Further uncertainties stem from service end-to-end impairments, including wavelength selective switch (WSS) filtering-induced noise and from device-specific back-to-back (B2B) transponder performance, both of which are typically unknown at deployment time. To address these challenges, we propose incremental learning-based input refinement (IIR), a parameter estimation method that leverages multiple network snapshots to jointly refine fiber insertion losses, amplifier gain spectra, and end-to-end offset noise (comprising WSS filtering and transponder B2B contributions). IIR is applied incrementally during routine, live network (re-)optimization, requiring no intrusive measurements. The proposed method is validated through (1) simulations using experimental data on a C-band ring network and (2) experimental validation on a C-band mesh network. Results show that IIR significantly improves the estimation of key physical-layer parameters, enhancing QoT prediction accuracy and enabling effective closed-loop power optimization. © 2009-2012 Optica Publishing Group.

Title: Large language models, ChatGPT, and beyond: A new paradigm for condition monitoring and prognosis in power and energy systems
Affiliations: University of Brest, UMR CNRS 6027 IRDL, Brest, France
Authors with affiliations: Benbouzid M., University of Brest, UMR CNRS 6027 IRDL, Brest, France
Abstract: Large language models and related foundation models offer new capabilities for interpreting heterogeneous information, retrieving engineering knowledge, and supporting high-level decision processes in power and energy systems. This Perspective examines their role in condition monitoring and prognostics and health management, with particular emphasis on remaining useful life estimation. To support language and multimodal model interpretation of structured and validated estimates, we propose a digital twin-centric architecture comprising physics-guided hybrid estimation, digital twin synchronization, rule-governed semantic translation, foundation model reasoning, output validation, and human supervision. The specific contribution is threefold. First, the proposed layering principle distinguishes physically consistent estimation, system integration, and higher-level reasoning functions. Second, an auditable semantic interface is defined to encode health indicators, degradation states, remaining useful life distributions, uncertainty information, operating context, provenance, retrieved evidence, and permitted reasoning scope. Third, a deployment-oriented reliability framework relates physical consistency, digital twin consistency, explanation fidelity, uncertainty preservation, robustness, traceability, safe deferral, latency, data sensitivity, and computational requirements to edge, on premises, cloud, and hybrid implementations. An illustrative battery state-of-health and remaining useful life use case demonstrates the resulting information flow. The foundation model layer is primarily intended for slow-timescale, human-supervised functions such as diagnostic explanation, degradation interpretation, maintenance prioritization, inspection planning, and fleet-level assessment, rather than protection or real-time control. The Perspective also examines complementary roles for small language models, tiny recursive models, world models, large language models, and multimodal foundation models and identifies priorities for their reliable evaluation and deployment in power and energy prognostics and health management. © 2026 The Author(s). Abstract: Digital twin-enabled robotic surgery is emerging at the intersection of surgical robotics, patient-specific simulation, artificial intelligence, extended reality, teleoperation, and surgical autonomy. However, its global research structure and translational trajectory remain insufficiently defined. This study mapped the bibliometric landscape, intellectual structure, and thematic evolution of this field. Publications were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed, and Scopus on 5 June 2026, covering 2010–2026. After deduplication, screening, and eligibility assessment, 508 publications were included. Bibliometric and knowledge-mapping analyses were conducted using bibliometrix/Biblioshiny, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace.The final corpus comprised 508 publications from 328 publication sources, spanning 2011–2026, with an annual growth rate of 35.38%, 2102 contributing authors, 76,871 cited references, 4091 database-supplied index keywords, and 1844 author keywords. Publication activity accelerated markedly after 2022, with 438 records published during 2022–2026, accounting for 86.2% of the corpus. Exploratory life-cycle modeling was consistent with an early rapid-growth phase, although its estimates should be interpreted cautiously. The International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery was the most productive publication source, while China, the United States, and Italy led national scientific production. International co-authorship remained limited at 4.13%. Keyword and network analyses highlighted digital twin modeling, virtual and augmented reality, artificial intelligence, robotics, teleoperation, simulation, and human–robot interaction as prominent and increasingly interconnected themes.Overall, digital twin-enabled robotic surgery remains a rapidly expanding but formative research domain. Its focus is shifting from static virtual representation and simulation toward patient-specific modeling, surgical training, extended-reality interaction, teleoperation, scene understanding, and supervised robotic assistance. Future progress will require clearer definitions, interoperable data structures, real-time model updating, uncertainty-aware methods, multicenter validation, and clinically meaningful outcome evaluation. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag London Ltd., part of Springer Nature 2026.

Abstract: Coordinating the complex coupling of uncertain renewable energy supply with dynamic industrial production loads presents a significant challenge in the operation of multi-energy smart industrial parks. Existing solutions often fail to capture the intricate interdependencies of these systems and lack the adaptability to evolve and accommodate operational conditions. To address these issues, this research proposes the large language model-enhanced digital twin multi-agent system (EnergyDTMAS). By leveraging advantages in large language models and multi-agent systems, EnergyDTMAS improves decentralized decision-making through the integration of domain knowledge and dynamic adjustments to operational contexts. The framework incorporates three key innovations. First, a multi-agent self-organizing negotiation mechanism is developed to enable autonomous perception of renewable energy supply and dynamic production loads, facilitating real-time coordinated resource scheduling. Second, a dual-sided uncertainty modeling framework is proposed to enhance the prediction accuracy for renewable generation and industrial loads, thereby improving the flexibility and robustness of scheduling strategies. Lastly, a dynamic production load-oriented coordination mechanism is designed to optimize multiple objectives, including operational costs, carbon emissions, and reliability under variable conditions. A case study demonstrates the effectiveness of this research, showing EnergyDTMAS reduces grid electricity purchase, carbon emissions, and operating costs by up to 22.35%, 44.07%, and 34.12%, respectively, compared to benchmark models. These results highlight EnergyDTMAS’s capability to effectively coordinate multi-energy supply and dynamic industrial loads, thus enhancing energy utilization efficiency, reducing costs, and mitigating environmental impacts. This provides a scalable and adaptive solution for sustainable smart industrial park operations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Navigating uncertainty in digital twin ecosystems: A unified framework and key challenges
Affiliations: Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering, Multimedia University, Persiaran Multimedia, Selangor, Cyberjaya, 63100, Malaysia
Authors with affiliations: Tan A.H., Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering, Multimedia University, Persiaran Multimedia, Selangor, Cyberjaya, 63100, Malaysia; Chuah T.C., Faculty of Artificial Intelligence and Engineering, Multimedia University, Persiaran Multimedia, Selangor, Cyberjaya, 63100, Malaysia
Abstract: Digital twins have emerged as a transformative paradigm for real-time representation, management, and integration of complex physical systems. Traditional uncertainty classification may be insufficient to address the complexities of uncertainty in digital twin ecosystems. A new class is proposed, referred to as ontological uncertainty, which comprises a novel category arising from the dynamic reconfiguration of the frame of discernment in evolving digital twin ecosystems. A random set representation and an update mechanism are introduced to model this category, enabling both frame reconfiguration and focused exploitation of the current frame. Key systemic drivers shaping the interaction, propagation, and amplification of uncertainties in digital twin ecosystems are determined, with an illustration using an autonomous electric vehicle (AEV) example. A six-layer pyramid framework, constructed from hybrid, adaptive, probabilistic, collaborative, quantum and human-in-the-loop digital twins, is introduced to mitigate uncertainty. A case study is presented using real data on a battery system that represents an important component in an AEV. Significant computational advancements remain necessary to address the challenges of navigating uncertainty in dynamic and complex digital twin ecosystems. © 2026

Title: A physics-assisted digital twin of a village-scale solar dryer: Cross-site validation and propagated calibration uncertainty in rural Tripura, India

Abstract: Post-harvest losses remain a persistent burden for smallholder spice producers in humid tropical regions, where open-sun drying degrades both yield and quality. This work presents a physics-assisted machine learning digital twin for a forced-convection solar dryer deployed at four Self-Help Group sites in West Tripura, India, for turmeric drying. Five thermal models were calibrated on 105 multi-site field records and evaluated under a leave-one-group-out protocol that withholds entire sites, where Random Forest reached a cross-site R2 of 0.430. A latent-heat correction couples the thermal model to a calibrated Lewis drying-kinetics model in a closed hourly loop and constrains cumulative thermal exposure rather than peak temperature. For a rated 50 kg batch, the twin predicts a peak cabinet temperature of 84.9 °C, a moisture-based thermal efficiency of 21.3 % and a drying duration of 276 h to 372 h depending on start month. Because the rated load exceeds the mean operated field load by about sixteen times, these are reported as model projections, with calibration uncertainty propagated through to the outcomes. A triple-bottom-line assessment gives a payback period of 2.3 to 5.0 years, a benefit-cost ratio of 1.35 to 2.87 and 99 kg to 195 kg of CO2-equivalent avoided per unit annually, with benefits shared predominantly among women members. Uncertainty in the kinetic calibration, derived from a single 27 h window, lengthens every batch by about a quarter and, unlike seasonal variation, does not average out over the year, making a full-load drying trial the highest-value measurement. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: Guidelines for managing scientific data have been established under the FAIR principles, requiring that data be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. In many scientific disciplines, especially computational biology, both data and models are key to progress. For this reason, and recognizing that such models are a very special type of “data”, we argue that computational models, especially mechanistic models prevalent in medicine, physiology and systems biology, deserve a complementary set of guidelines. We propose the CURE principles, emphasizing that models should be Credible, Understandable, Reproducible, and Extensible. We delve into each principle, discussing verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification for model credibility; the clarity of model descriptions and annotations for understandability; adherence to standards and open science practices for reproducibility; and the use of open standards and modular code for extensibility and reuse. We outline recommended and baseline requirements for each aspect of CURE, aiming to enhance the impact and trustworthiness of computational models, particularly in biomedical applications where credibility is paramount. Our perspective underscores the need for a more disciplined approach to modeling, aligning with emerging trends such as Digital Twins and emphasizing the importance of data and modeling standards for interoperability and reuse. Finally, we emphasize that given the non-trivial effort required to implement the guidelines, the community should strive to automate as many of the guidelines as possible. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Finite element model updating method for mesh antennas based on adaptive evolution and Gaussian correction

Abstract: Mesh antennas play an important role in the space communication field. Affected by uncertainty factors, including the dynamic evolution of mesh antenna cable sensitivity and model simplification, a certain deviation often exists between the initial FEM and the real physical structure. In response to this, this paper proposes a model updating method based on adaptive evolution and Gaussian correction. First, an iterative framework based on the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) is constructed. By dynamically updating the sensitive cable set, it overcomes the optimization failure under tension redistribution, realizing the global optimization of high-dimensional cable forces. Second, targeting the inherent model uncertainties brought by simplifying assumptions, including finite element meshing, a physics-enhanced Gaussian process regression (GPR) surrogate model is introduced to compensate for the residual coordinate deviations of the front net nodes. The experiment based on the 3-m aperture hoop-column antenna prototype demonstrates that the front net node RMS error decreases from 9.8664 mm to 1.5278 mm after updating. Under varying cable force deduction operating conditions, the normalized topological correlation coefficients reach 0.853 and 0.805, effectively capturing the dominant deformation mode of the system. This research provides an effective approach for the digital twin construction of large space structures. © 2026 IAA. Published by Elsevier Ltd. Title: Neural network-assisted unscented Kalman filtering with unknown inputs for joint parameter identification and temperature prediction in RC thermal models

Abstract: Accurate online identification of building thermal states, model parameters, and unknown thermal disturbances is essential for reliable building thermal modeling and advanced energy management. However, conventional Kalman filter-based approaches are highly dependent on manually adjusted noise covariance matrices, making them sensitive to non-Gaussian and time-varying uncertainties commonly encountered in building operations. To address this challenge, this study proposes a neural network-assisted unscented Kalman filter under unknown input (UKF-UI-Net) for the joint estimation of thermal states, RC model parameters, and unknown heat inputs. The proposed framework combines a recurrent neural network with an unscented Kalman filter under unknown input (UKF-UI), enabling adaptive learning of the evolution patterns of process and measurement uncertainties from filtering residuals. RC parameters are augmented into the state vector for simultaneous online identification, while unknown heat inputs are reconstructed through weighted least-squares estimation. This hybrid physics-data framework eliminates the need for manual covariance tuning and enhances adaptability to complex noise environments. The framework is evaluated against fixed-covariance UKF-UI and Sage–Husa-UKF-UI under Gaussian, t-distributed, and nonstationary noise conditions using 35 Monte Carlo trials, and is further validated through experiments conducted in a south-facing test room. Compared with the baseline methods, the proposed method generally improves the overall accuracy and stability of parameter and unknown-input identification while maintaining reliable temperature estimation under complex noise conditions. These results demonstrate that UKF-UI-Net improves the robustness and accuracy of building thermal model identification under uncertainty conditions, providing a practical solution for online model calibration, digital twins, and model predictive control applications. Abstract: The accelerated transition toward renewable energy, sustainable infrastructure, and circular economies is driving adoption of advanced materials, including bio-based composites, recycled polymers, nanostructured coatings, and hydrogen-resistant alloys. While critical for net-zero goals, these materials often exhibit heterogeneous architectures, interface-controlled transport, and evolving degradation pathways that complicate reliability, safety, and certifiable long-term performance. Conventional micro- and nano-scale characterization provides indispensable mechanistic insight but frequently relies on destructive sampling and limited coverage, restricting applicability to in-service assets. Nondestructive testing (NDT) therefore provides a complementary life-cycle evidence layer for characterization, monitoring, and qualification under realistic operating conditions. Advances in ultrasonics, eddy currents, infrared thermography, X-ray computed tomography, and optical-fiber sensing enable in situ and real-time assessment across composites, metals, and multifunctional coatings. Combined with artificial intelligence, multimodal sensor fusion, and digital-twin frameworks, NDT is moving beyond diagnostic defect detection toward predictive state estimation that informs design, manufacturing control, maintenance planning, and circular reuse decisions. This Review synthesizes progress across sustainable composites, battery and hydrogen storage systems, smart and self-healing polymers, and nanomaterial-enabled coatings, and distills evidence requirements for credibility at scale, including calibration transfer, robustness to variability and environmental drift, and uncertainty-aware reporting for reuse certification. We also address the sustainability paradox of inspection by highlighting evidence-efficient workflows that balance confidence against energy, resource, and computational costs. Finally, we outline a roadmap toward Inspection Science as a foundational pillar that aligns materials innovation with scalable, decision-grade characterization across full life cycles. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Author full names: Bartoloni, Alessandro (35285626700)
Title: AMS-02 Through a Research-Infrastructure Lens for Space Radiobiology Translation
Affiliations: EP Department, CERN, 1211 Geneva 23, Geneva, Switzerland; INFN Sezione di Roma, Rome, Italy
Authors with affiliations: Bartoloni A., EP Department, CERN, 1211 Geneva 23, Geneva, Switzerland, INFN Sezione di Roma, Rome, Italy
Abstract: The Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer (AMS-02), operating on the International Space Station since May 2011, is widely recognized for its flagship contributions to astroparticle physics, including precision measurements of cosmic-ray leptons, antiprotons, and nuclei over more than a solar cycle. In this article, I present AMS-02 through the lens of a research infrastructure (RI): a long-lived, globally networked, and continuously evolving capability that produces curated data products, technical documentation, calibration knowledge, and operational experience that remain valuable beyond the original physics drivers. I argue that AMS-02 has matured into a reference infrastructure-like resource for characterizing the space-radiation environment in low Earth orbit (LEO) and for translating charged-particle measurements into space radiobiology and astronaut health risk assessment. I describe the instrument architecture and detector suite, the ISS-to-ground operational chain centered at CERN, and the data lifecycle practices that enable reproducibility and long-term technical memory. I then review how the collaboration’s Physical Review Letters Manuscripts (PRLM) can be interpreted as a sequence of validated RI outputs spanning time-averaged spectra and fine time-structure measurements. Finally, I outline a practical translation pathway from AMS fluxes and charge-resolved spectra to quantities relevant to radiobiology, including spectral inputs to transport codes, dose and quality proxies, and uncertainty budgets, and highlight interfaces with terrestrial medical physics, digital twins, and ontology-driven knowledge organization. The article concludes with recommendations for improving interoperability, FAIRness, and cross-mission benchmarking, positioning AMS-02 as a case study of how a fundamental-physics mission can generate RI-like functions and sustained societal value in “Space for Health”. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Building a Deep Temporal Emulator of an Ocean Carbon Uptake Model
Affiliations: University of Kiel, Kiel, Germany; GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, Kiel, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Mohanty S., University of Kiel, Kiel, Germany, GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, Kiel, Germany; Kazempour D., University of Kiel, Kiel, Germany; Göhring A., University of Kiel, Kiel, Germany; Rath W., GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, Kiel, Germany; Patara L., GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel, Kiel, Germany; Kröger P., University of Kiel, Kiel, Germany
Abstract: The global ocean carbon sink is a critical component of the Earth’s climate but current ocean models are limited in their predictive capabilities because of the high computational cost that a biogeochemical (BGC) model, required to simulate air-sea CO2 fluxes, entails. Our research investigates the reconstruction of ocean CO2 flux focusing on local physical oceanographic drivers, such as sea surface temperature, salinity, and sea-ice coverage, which are outputs of the simulations conducted with a global ocean BGC model. We frame the flux estimation problem as a temporal sequence problem and evaluate the efficacy of both Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN) architectures augmented with attention mechanisms. The models ingest eight different physical parameters over a six-month sliding window at each grid point without explicit spatial information, and are designed to identify and weigh the historical physical states that most strongly influence current ocean-atmosphere carbon fluxes. Our framework employs LSTMs to capture sequential dependencies through recurrent hidden states. Moreover, we evaluate TCNs as a distinct alternative that uses dilated convolutions to identify multi-temporal patterns. Besides, we build a probabilistic framework utilizing Gaussian Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss to account for aleatoric uncertainty in the dynamical drivers of ocean CO2 flux. To ensure credible reconstructions, we apply Conformal Prediction as a post-hoc calibration layer. This methodology yields calibrated uncertainty intervals with guaranteed 95% coverage. Our results show that for most oceanographic regimes deep temporal models can function as reliable digital twins for point-wise carbon flux estimates. The proposed framework provides a data-driven foundation for reconstruction of air-sea carbon fluxes through an AI emulator built upon dynamic physical parameters. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: In order to address health monitoring issues on offshore wind turbines, while taking into account engineering know-how and constraints, we propose a robust model identification procedure based on reliability of information for such structures. The procedure leans on the modified Constitutive Relation Error concept, which naturally considers sensing and modeling uncertainties. The concept is here extended to a multi-physics framework involving nonlinear fluid–structure interactions. In this framework, each individual interface is seen as a specific and potentially nonlinear constitutive relation, assumed unreliable and relaxed in the identification process, with suited error metric. Parameters associated to these constitutive relations are then identified to close at best the gap between operational observations and model predictions, and to detect modeling incompatibilities by means of error indicators. Considering classical engineering modeling and simulation approaches dedicated to offshore wind turbines, with inherent idealization and model bias, the performance of the approach is numerically analyzed. This is done first on academic examples with synthetic data, then in a more practical context by processing real in situ measurements coming from an industrial demonstrator equipped with various multiphysic sensors. Results notably illustrate the capability of the approach to cope with crude models by means of its bias-aware formulation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Automated and robust system discovery in power systems assets using physics-informed machine learning
Affiliations: Hitachi Energy Research, Montreal, Canada; Hitachi Energy Research, Baden-Dätwil, Switzerland; Hitachi Energy Research, Västerås, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Chakravorty J., Hitachi Energy Research, Montreal, Canada; Ripamonti N., Hitachi Energy Research, Baden-Dätwil, Switzerland; Laneryd T., Hitachi Energy Research, Västerås, Sweden
Abstract: System discovery, such as parameter estimation or model reconstruction, in complex power system assets can play crucial roles in condition monitoring, troubleshooting and root cause analysis. However, robust system discovery in presence of noisy or sparse data is a challenging problem that requires solving an inverse problem and quantifying uncertainties. In this paper we address this problem and propose an approach to find the solution by using Physics-Informed Machine Learning approach for modeling cause and effect in power systems assets with polynomial dynamics. In a probabilistic setting we establish the merits of the proposed approach using empirical results. In particular, we benchmark our proposed end-to-end method with a baseline that uses Bayesian Neural Network with dropout and show that our approach outperforms baseline by 79% of reduction of validation error, 34% reduction of training time and 97.5% reduction of inference time. © 2026

Title: Latency-robust corridor supervisory control for hybrid nuclear–HVDC–renewable power systems under communication-constrained low-inertia operation
Affiliations: Electrical, Instrumentation and Automation Department, Doris Engineering UK Co. (ODE), London, United Kingdom; AAU Energy, Aalborg University, Esbjerg, Denmark

Abstract: Hybrid nuclear–HVDC–renewable transmission corridors introduce new supervisory coordination challenges due to reduced inertia, heterogeneous asset dynamics, and non-negligible bounded communication delay. Conventional coordination approaches typically assume ideal communication or treat latency as a secondary implementation issue, limiting robustness under wide-area supervisory operation. This paper proposes Latency-Robust Corridor Supervisory Control (LR-CSC), a reproducible engineering framework for delay-robust supervisory coordination under bounded communication delay. The methodology integrates a compact corridor-level state-space representation, a delay-embedded min–max supervisory formulation, and a digital-twin-based feasibility screening engine. Rather than relying on continuous online optimisation or centralised control authority, LR-CSC evaluates candidate supervisory actions over an admissible state envelope and enforces constraint satisfaction for all delays within a specified design bound. Validation is conducted using a fully specified synthetic nuclear–HVDC–renewable corridor benchmark under disturbance variation, stochastic bounded communication delay, and inertia degradation. Results demonstrate three principal outcomes. First, embedding bounded communication delay directly within supervisory feasibility expands the stable inertia–delay operating region relative to delay-blind coordination strategies. Second, delay-embedded feasibility screening suppresses oscillatory interaction between fast converter dynamics and slower synchronous response, yielding improved frequency nadir, reduced peak RoCoF, and faster settling behaviour. Third, robustness improvements persist across Monte-Carlo disturbance and communication uncertainty scenarios, indicating that performance gains arise from structural delay-embedded supervisory coordination rather than scenario-specific tuning. The proposed framework is intentionally positioned as a supervisory feasibility layer for low-inertia corridor coordination and provides a transparent balance between bounded computation, reproducibility, and practical implementability under communication-constrained operation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: This study synthesizes the rapidly expanding evidence base on machine learning that links renewable variability to green-hydrogen production optimisation and proposes an integrated PM–CFL–OPT architecture that embeds uncertainty handling, safety constraints, and interpretability across the decision chain. The architecture represents a synthesis-derived and testable functional hypothesis rather than a quantitatively validated superior pipeline. Because the included studies use heterogeneous datasets, horizons, system boundaries and performance measures—and only three studies are primarily classified as CFL—the present corpus cannot support a pooled estimate of the framework’s incremental performance over standalone alternatives. A PRISMA-aligned, feedback-loop workflow was executed across Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Taylor & Francis, and SpringerLink, yielding 244 records; 48 duplicates were removed, and 129 critical studies were retained for synthesis. Bibliometric profiling revealed a transition from early exploratory contributions during 2016–2019 to a marked acceleration after 2022, with publication output peaking in 2025 and expanding geographically across established research economies and emerging regions. A systems-map synthesis organises the literature using an Energy/System Vector–Machine-Learning Method–Application/Decision Domain (E–M–A) framework and overlays it with three functional roles: predictive modelling (PM), clustering and feature learning (CFL), and optimisation and control (OPT). E–M–A locates each study by physical context, computational method and decision task, whereas PM–CFL–OPT identifies how ML contributes to the forecast–representation–action chain. Persistent gaps include limited transferability across climates and grids, weak decision-focused learning pipelines, and under-specified safety cases for real-time and market participation. The review concludes with a deployment-oriented roadmap for climate-robust, privacy-preserving, and auditable ML that can scale hydrogen-integrated renewable operations. Findings clarify maturity, trust, and transferability bottlenecks for deployment. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: Nuclear power plants (NPPs) generate virtually carbon-free baseload electricity and occupy a strategic role in the global energy transition, yet their potential as a context for sustainable data-driven innovation remains underexplored in the energy analytics literature. This paper presents a comprehensive integrative review grounded in the 2026 IAEA technical report NR-T-1.22 as its primary authoritative source, enriched by 78 peer-reviewed studies (2018–2026) spanning the full NPP lifecycle across sixteen query clusters. The review delivers: (i) a seven-paradigm AI/ML/DS taxonomy with explicit boundary definitions, a hierarchical structure, and regulatory compatibility ratings under IEC TR 63468:2023; (ii) a cross-domain performance evidence synthesis across fourteen application domains, classified under a four-level data-environment scheme (synthetic / simulator / integral test facility / operating plant) that separates laboratory results from genuine field validation; (iii) a six-barrier adoption analysis with quantified mitigation pathways and a mechanism-level account of why the simulator-to-field gap persists; (iv) a reliability-oriented synthesis of uncertainty quantification, false-positive behaviour, and robustness reporting; and (v) a five-layer AI-NPP integration framework applied diagnostically across domains. Reported performance is strong in simulator settings—high simulator-based classification accuracy in anomaly detection and fault diagnosis, large thermal–hydraulic simulation speed-ups, and economically material fuel-optimisation benefits—and fleet-scale field deployments are documented across 68 NPP units in the IAEA annexes. Critically, however, 53 of the 78 peer-reviewed studies (68%) report synthetic or simulator-only results and only 12 (15%) use operating-plant data; the high headline metrics therefore evidence simulator-stage feasibility rather than demonstrated real-world readiness, and the IAEA field figures are practitioner-reported without an independent non-AI baseline. The paper establishes that systematic AI/ML/DS deployment can advance SDG 7 and SDG 13 through four quantified mechanisms—extended plant lifetimes, improved fuel efficiency, reduced unplanned outages, and accelerated advanced-reactor development—while arguing that the binding constraints are regulatory and institutional rather than algorithmic. Ethical dimensions including algorithmic bias, liability allocation, and safety–critical deployment thresholds are addressed with concrete regulatory and operational specifics. © 2026

Title: Machine learning for wind farm wake modeling: Output-driven taxonomy, architectural inductive biases, and benchmarking
Affiliations: Department of Civil Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong
Authors with affiliations: Dong Z., Department of Civil Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong; Zeng W., Department of Civil Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong; Deng X., Department of Civil Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong; Yang K., Department of Civil Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong
Abstract: Accurate plant-scale wake modeling is essential for wind-farm design, control, and digital-twin operation, yet practical prediction remains constrained by the fidelity–deployability trade-off between fast engineering wake models and physics-rich computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Machine learning (ML) has expanded rapidly as a route to low-latency wake prediction and multi-fidelity correction, but existing studies remain difficult to compare because they differ in learned outputs, data provenance, and validation claims. This review reframes ML wake modeling around the predicted physical quantity rather than the algorithm alone. Four task families are distinguished: scalar response or key performance indicator (KPI) prediction, static wake-field or wake-state emulation, dynamic wake evolution, and turbine–turbine interaction-operator learning. For each family, we examine how representative architectures, including tabular surrogates, convolutional and recurrent models, graph neural networks, neural operators, reduced-order models, and physics-informed learning, embed inductive biases for spatial locality, temporal memory, directional coupling, coherent wake structure, and discretization-aware mapping. We further synthesize data regimes spanning engineering models, CFD, aero-servo-elastic simulation, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA), light detection and ranging (LiDAR), and wind-tunnel measurements, emphasizing how label fidelity, sample independence, operational confounding, and solver-specific assumptions shape the sim-to-real gap. Building on this taxonomy, we propose claim-driven benchmarking that aligns hold-out design, physics-aware diagnostics, uncertainty calibration, and deployment evidence across regime, layout, control-policy, site, discretization, and fidelity shifts. The review identifies where current ML wake models are mature, where validation remains weak, and how future work can support robust layout optimization, wake steering, load-aware control, and wind-farm digital twins. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Integrating artificial intelligence into nuclear reactor safety: ML-augmented CFD, AI-enabled PSA, and cybersecurity

Abstract: This review provides a structured synthesis of how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping safety-critical analysis in nuclear power plants through three complementary technical domains and cross-cutting enablers. First, we examine machine learning (ML) augmentations to computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and reduced-order thermal–hydraulic models, focusing on boiling and critical heat flux (CHF) closures, interfacial transport, transient emulation, and containment-scale mixing. Particular attention is given to physics-constrained surrogates, verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ), and best-estimate plus uncertainty (BEPU) practices that enable credible acceleration of high-fidelity analyses. Second, we review AI integration within probabilistic safety assessment (PSA), covering Bayesian and hybrid graphical models, dynamic event and fault trees, human reliability analysis enhanced by learning-based support, and digital-twin frameworks that embed online updating of risk metrics. Third, we examine cybersecurity in digital instrumentation and control (I&C) systems, including threat pathways, AI-enabled detection and response, adversarial model robustness, and the coupling of cyber–physical consequences with PSA. These technical strands are complemented by recent developments in uncertainty quantification and resilient AI, together with a dedicated assessment of multi-unit and multi-hazard PSA covering inter-unit and inter-module dependencies, shared structures, systems, components, and recovery resources, multi-unit accident sequences, and single, combined, and cascading external hazards. Across all domains, we consolidate comparative evidence, highlight regulatory and explainability requirements, and identify open challenges linked to data scarcity, plant heterogeneity across small modular reactor (SMR), pressurized water reactor (PWR), and boiling water reactor (BWR) designs, and physics–data integration. The outcome is a consolidated map of methods and datasets, together with a lifecycle governance framework for AI-enabled PSA that links intended use, data and model qualification, PSA integration, configuration control, operational monitoring, requalification, and human oversight to auditable decision gates. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Nanofluids are innovative materials consisting of a suspension of nanoparticles in a fluid, such as water or oil. They are commonly used in engineering and medicine because of their thermal conductivity, which makes them particularly efficient for cooling, heat transport, and tumor treatment. In recent times, the unique properties of nanofluids have led to their use for environmental application. This includes oil extraction processes, the treatment of contaminated water and soil, and the improvement of the seismic response of the soil during strong seismic events. Although these applications are very different from each other, it is necessary in all cases to inject the nanoparticles into the soil. However, predicting the distribution of particles a priori, considering the injection parameters, is very difficult due to the intrinsic complexity of the subsoil and uncertainty regarding parameters such as porosity and elastic properties. One possible solution is to use numerical simulations on digital twins of the area of interest. These simulations are computationally expensive, and are affected, in the specific case, by a high level of uncertainty, due to the lack of specific information on soil stratigraphy. In this paper, we present and discuss a mathematical model that describes the injection of nanofluid into the soil, taking into account its natural poroelasticity, which is often neglected. The subsequent drift and diffusion of the particles, as well as their interaction with the surrounding medium through absorption and desorption processes, can be described using the same model, but with different boundary and initial conditions. After introducing the model, we discuss in detail the effects of poroelasticity and the role of injection parameters on particle distribution. We also present some (semi−)analytical representations of the model that could be useful for the preliminar calibration of the numerical simulations and, potentially, of the injection process. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Efficient and reliable full-state temperature estimation is critical for condition monitoring and digital twin applications of enclosed high-voltage equipment, yet it remains challenging due to sparse measurements and the high computational cost of multiphysics simulations. This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware workflow for full-state temperature estimation of a 550 kV gas-insulated switchgear (GIS) disconnector under contact degradation scenarios, based on a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) reduced-order representation. A probabilistic forward surrogate enables posterior-driven data augmentation, while a lightweight inverse surrogate is trained to infer POD coefficients from only three temperature measurements on the enclosure surface, followed by full-state reconstruction with uncertainty quantification. Numerical results on the evaluated cases show favorable reconstruction accuracy and noise tolerance, with lower errors than gappy POD under the reported settings despite using fewer sensors. These results indicate the potential of the proposed workflow for digital twin-oriented temperature-field estimation in GIS. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Flood events clearly induce significant impacts in urbanized regions. Over the last decades, advances in computational capacity, high-resolution digital elevation data, and open-access geospatial datasets have enabled the development of Evacuation Models (EM). However, many EMs are often not so suitable for operational use by civil protection authorities, due to their significant data requirements, high computational burden and complex parametrisation. In this context, this work aims to bridge this gap by proposing a screening-level, operational tool based on a simplified probabilistic methodology, that integrates pedestrian movement under uncertainty with a streamlined representation of flood arrival time, and then produces evacuation-time distributions and spatially explicit estimates of floodwater-pedestrian interaction probability. The approach is applied to a flood-prone urban area in Rome (Italy). Results highlight the role of network topology, route branching and behavioural variability in determining evacuation performance, revealing critical areas where existing Evacuation Plans (EPs) may require revision. Finally, we state the need for integrating simplified evacuation models into emergent decision-support frameworks, including Digital Twins for urban flood management. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Artificial intelligence in traffic accident analysis: A comprehensive review

Abstract: Road traffic accidents continue to be a significant problem in terms of public health and transport safety. Whilst traditional statistical methods are of fundamental importance for drawing conclusions and evaluating policies, certain approaches have limitations stemming from predefined functional structures, distribution assumptions, limited forms of interaction, and difficulties in processing heterogeneous, high-dimensional or continuously updated data. This review critically synthesises artificial intelligence (AI) applications that directly support safety decisions through accident detection and prediction, the determination of accident frequency and risk, and the assessment of injury severity and duration. The literature is organised within a two-dimensional framework. In the first dimension, studies are classified as vision-based approaches, data-driven AI techniques and spatiotemporal AI models. The second dimension focuses on the roles of these studies in detection, prediction, explanation and decision support. The framework highlights developments ranging from standalone machine learning, convolutional and recurrent models to multimodal fusion, graph-based learning, transformers, foundation models, generative AI and digital-twin-supported simulations. However, the increase in predictive power gives rise to various trade-offs in terms of interpretability, robustness, computational cost, scalability, transferability, data requirements, fairness and readiness for deployment. Consequently, this study focuses not only on performance but also on the explanatory capacity of model families, their applicability and their contribution to engineering and policy decisions. Cross-regional comparison, causal and uncertainty-aware modelling, rare event learning, vision-language reasoning, synthetic scenario generation, digital twin validation and human-supervised decision support systems have been identified as key research priorities. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: To ensure the stability of three types of heterogeneous vehicles with different information acquisition capabilities, control mechanisms, and delay effects, this paper proposes a mixed vehicle group cooperative consensus control strategy based on subgroup division rules by employing digital twin technology. Firstly, the mixed vehicle group consisting of connected autonomous vehicles (CAVs), autonomous vehicles (AVs), and traditional human-driven vehicles (HVs) is taken as the research object; it is divided into multiple logical subgroups to facilitate analyzing the cooperative driving relationship among heterogeneous vehicles within each subgroup and between subgroups. Thereafter, to guarantee that heterogeneous vehicles can quickly track different desired inter-vehicle distances, a heterogeneous spacing strategy is designed. Meanwhile, the improved HV, CAV, and AV models are established by considering the randomness and uncertainty of human drivers, as well as the impact of heterogeneous delays. Subsequently, to mitigate the impact of heterogeneous delays on the stability of mixed vehicle groups, a cooperative consensus control strategy is developed based on the delay compensation mechanism under a digital twin network. Lastly, the conditions of string stability among heterogeneous vehicles within subgroups and between subgroups are derived to ensure the stability of cooperative driving of the mixed vehicle group composed of CAVs, AVs and HVs. The simulation results show that the proposed method can ensure collision-free tracking of heterogeneous desired intervehicle distances of 13 m, 14 m, and 16 m for CAVs, AVs, and HVs within approximately 24 s, 17 s, and 28 s within the mixed vehicle group consisting of 13 heterogeneous vehicles. This result further verifies the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed method. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Nanoindentation enables the high-resolution characterization of mechanical properties and the study of advanced materials. However, in the measurement practice, several influence factors affect nanoindentation, introducing bias or increasing measurement uncertainty. Some influence factors are internally sourced (force–displacement noise), others are induced by the environment (electro-mechanical vibrations, indenter-sample thermal equilibrium), and some depend on interactions with the measurand (sample surface integrity, indenter tip wear). Digital twins are simulation models that replicate physical systems in a virtual environment, dynamically updating the virtual model to match the observed state of its real counterpart, enabling physical control of the latter. Digital twins allow predicting system response and highlighting anomalies, while identifying critical influence factors causing such out-of-control conditions, and deploying control actions to avoid malfunctions through predictive maintenance, while avoiding wasting resources. However, to ensure appropriate equipment monitoring and decision-making, traceable digital twins that consider measurement uncertainty are needed. While discussing the advantages of alternative modelling pathways, the work demonstrates the creation of a traceable digital twin for nanoindentation on reference materials based on physics-based data-driven approach. Validation strategies for synthetic and real datasets are implemented, and the capability to detect the most common measurement errors in nanoindentation is highlighted. Strategies to eliminate or compensate for sources of identified measurement errors by the digital twin are discussed, outlining a route towards traceable digitization in nanoindentation. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: Research on edge-intelligent IoT collaborative perception and adaptive spatial design optimization for urban digital twins
Affiliations: Institute of Marxism, Hubei Institute of Fine Arts, Wuhan, 430000, China
Authors with affiliations: Ruan Y., Institute of Marxism, Hubei Institute of Fine Arts, Wuhan, 430000, China
Abstract: Edge collaborative perception for urban digital twins requires timely state maintenance under constrained communication resources. Existing collaborative perception methods mainly optimize detection accuracy and communication compression, whereas urban-scale 3D reconstruction methods generally assume that observations have already been acquired or transmitted. Neither directly addresses how limited edge communication resources should be allocated according to their expected contribution to persistent twin-state maintenance. To address this gap, this paper proposes a twin-update-aware communication-allocation framework for edge-enabled urban digital twins. Candidate perception queries are selected under a fixed bandwidth budget according to their predicted twin-state variation, uncertainty reduction, spatial-feedback relevance, and communication cost. An event-driven semantic Gaussian backend then performs localized semantic and identity-preserving updates in event-affected regions, while a spatial-feedback estimator derives protocol-defined operational indicators and sensitivity signals from the updated twin state. The propagated sensitivity is explicitly used in the next time step to adjust subsequent query priorities, forming a feedback-coupled communication process rather than a post-hoc feedback module. Under a multi-dataset hierarchical proxy protocol, the proposed method achieves a favorable perception–communication trade-off and improved twin-maintenance utility. On V2X-Real, it achieves 72.4% 3D mAP and 77.6% recall at 4.4 Mb/frame, while the fixed-backend evaluation yields a TSUG of 0.312 and a DSCE of 0.103. Sequential experiments further show that dynamic sensitivity propagation reduces cumulative twin-state error relative to static or sensitivity-free variants. These results concern protocol-defined twin maintenance and feedback-aware communication utility and should not be interpreted as evidence of complete urban spatial-design optimization. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping alloy research and development by extending its role from conventional data-driven property prediction to a broader set of functions embedded in physical models, manufacturing workflows, characterization pipelines, and service assessment frameworks. This review summarizes recent progress in AI-enabled alloy development across four interconnected stages: multiscale computational simulation, intelligent manufacturing, high-throughput characterization, and service-life prediction. In computational simulation, machine learning interatomic potentials, CALPHAD-assisted models, discrete dislocation dynamics, phase-field modeling, crystal plasticity finite element methods, and ICME are discussed with emphasis on simulation acceleration, closure-relation learning, parameter inversion, and multi-scale coupling. In intelligent manufacturing, applications of AI in casting, forging, additive manufacturing, rolling, heat treatment, and metallurgical refining are reviewed, highlighting multi-source sensing, physical-field reconstruction, defect detection, process optimization, and digital-twin-based control. High-throughput characterization based on SEM, EBSD, TEM/STEM, and automated microstructure quantification is further considered as a critical data-feedback layer that links processing history, microstructural descriptors, and model calibration. For service assessment, AI-assisted prediction of corrosion, fatigue, creep, and coupled damage is summarized to clarify how composition, microstructure, defects, residual stress, environment, and loading history can be integrated for lifetime prediction and reliability evaluation. Finally, key challenges are discussed, including data scarcity and heterogeneity, insufficient physical consistency, limited extrapolation reliability, weak interoperability among models and scales, and the lack of uncertainty-aware decision-making. Future perspectives are proposed toward physics-informed learning, standardized databases, autonomous laboratories, digital twins, and closed-loop alloy development systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: Increasing demands for Reliability, Availability, Maintainability, and Safety (RAMS) are fostering design innovations in modern nuclear facilities. High Temperature Gas-cooled Reactor (HTGR) is an advanced technology characterized by inherent safety features, where significant core degradation can be practically eliminated through the robust ceramic-coated fuel particles, high-temperature resistant graphite matrix, inert helium coolant, and passive heat removal. The novel technological concepts and first-of-a-kind engineering solutions introduce, however, methodological challenges in conducting RAMS assessments for HTGRs and collocated facilities. This article opens a series of works derived from the original results of the RAMS analyses performed for the newly designed high-temperature reactor HTGR-POLA (POLish Atomic). Initiated at an early stage of the reactor's design, these studies have yielded broadly applicable outcomes relevant to the field of reliability engineering and system safety. This work introduces an integrated framework for the Reliability-Centered Design (RCD) process, incorporating digital twin modeling, lifetime simulations of the RAMS parameters, Monte Carlo-based uncertainty assessment, and Sobol’s index-driven quantification of sensitivity measures. This approach, preceded by traditional methods such as Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) and Fault Tree Analysis (FTA), aims at optimizing the design of HTGR-POLA in terms of RAMS while minimizing its complexity. The findings of this work highlight the effectiveness of the new RCD framework in balancing competing design objectives, as shown by the example of the electrical power system, where the design complexity and Forced Outage Rate (FOR) were jointly considered. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Knowledge-Driven Parameter Optimization for Combat Experimentation Simulation Models: Evolution, Mechanisms, and Application Prospects
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Affiliations: Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; People’s Liberation Army Unit 63677, Xinjiang, Urumqi, 830000, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang D., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China, People’s Liberation Army Unit 63677, Xinjiang, Urumqi, 830000, China; Lyu M., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; Liu Z., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China; Wen M., Institute of War Studies, Academy of Military Sciences, Beijing, 100091, China
Abstract: With the transition of combat experimentation from scheme demonstration to intelligent decision support, the computational efficiency and credibility of simulation model parameter optimization have become key bottlenecks in system-of-systems wargaming. Traditional black-box optimization methods face severe challenges, including high computational cost, high-dimensional mixed-variable spaces, and deep battlefield uncertainty. To address these challenges, knowledge-driven parameter optimization integrates military domain knowledge, physical mechanisms, tactical rules, and historical simulation data into the optimization process, thereby reducing ineffective search spaces and improving the feasibility of candidate solutions. This paper systematically reviews knowledge-driven parameter optimization methods for combat experimentation simulation models. First, it clarifies the conceptual boundaries between parameter calibration and parameter optimization, and summarizes a four-stage technological evolution from offline heuristic search to surrogate-assisted optimization, online closed-loop assimilation, and cognitive optimization assisted by large models. Second, it analyzes the core mechanisms of heuristic and evolutionary optimization, high-dimensional Bayesian optimization, multi-fidelity surrogate modeling, physical-prior injection, Kalman-filter-based data assimilation, reinforcement learning, and large-language-model-assisted semantic reasoning. Third, it compares the advantages, limitations, applicable scenarios, and validation requirements of different mechanisms, and summarizes their applications in simulation experiment design, combat entity behavior modeling, system-of-systems effectiveness evaluation, and digital twin battlefield construction. Finally, it discusses future research directions, including multimodal foundation models, simulation resource sharing, heterogeneous multi-task collaborative optimization, and human-machine hybrid cognitive simulation. The review aims to provide a structured reference for method selection and trustworthy application of parameter optimization in combat experimentation simulation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Abstract: Preferential seepage becomes evidence of internal erosion only when the hydraulic response can be linked to particle detachment and transport. This critical review examines that distinction in embankment dams and levees, considering how transient loading, storage, and geological structure affect both the physical process and its observation. Hydraulic records establish the response to changing loads, while thermal and geophysical surveys help constrain possible pathways. Particle sampling and investigation of sediment sources provide evidence of material loss that these indirect observations cannot establish alone. Joint interpretation of lag, attenuation, hysteresis, recession, and spatial coherence helps distinguish regional groundwater and bank-storage responses from localized seepage. The comparison of sensing and inverse methods shows why resolution, uncertainty, and verification must be assessed for the particular question being asked. We propose an evidence hierarchy and an observation-conditioned event tree to connect these interpretations with engineering decisions. For learned models and digital twins, testing on unseen events and assets, independent physical checks, and the consequences of false and missed alarms are central to evaluating practical benefit. The review emphasizes physically grounded, site-specific interpretation and verification as the basis for diagnosis and warning. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: From Aging-Aware Operation to Circular Value Retention: A Circular Battery Digital Twin for Electric Bus Fleets
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Affiliations: DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden
Authors with affiliations: Fattouh A., DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden; Dahlquist E., DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden; Chirumalla K., DigiCircle Research Group, Mälardalen University, Eskilstuna, Sweden
Abstract: The electrification of public transport has introduced new challenges in managing lithium-ion battery degradation, operational efficiency, and lifecycle sustainability. While battery digital twins (BDTs) have emerged as a promising solution for monitoring and prediction, most existing approaches remain limited to short-term state estimation and do not exploit lifecycle data for circular decision-making. This paper proposes a Circular Battery Digital Twin (CBDT) framework that integrates aging-aware operation, predictive lifecycle modeling, and circular value retention within a unified architecture. The framework combines real-world operational, environmental, and maintenance data to continuously calibrate a semi-empirical degradation model supporting multiple use cases, including route reassignment and second-life assessment. The framework is demonstrated using a multi-year dataset from a real electric bus operating in Sweden. The bus operates with a 60 kWh LFP battery pack and relies exclusively on pantograph charging at terminus stops. The results show that CBDT enables consistent degradation estimation, supports cost-aware operational decisions, and provides a pathway toward circular battery management. The framework successfully identified an optimal reassignment threshold at 70% load that extends operational life by 45%. The study demonstrates how integrating multi-source data and lifecycle intelligence enables the transition from reactive battery management to proactive and circular decision-making. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Title: A Monte Carlo enhanced agent based model for Tokenized BIM Twin (TBT) resource reallocation in construction projects
Affiliations: School of Engineering, Cardiff University, Cardiff, United Kingdom; Department of Architecture, Artvin Coruh University, Artvin, Turkey; Department of Statistics, Cumhuriyet University, Sivas, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Celik Y., School of Engineering, Cardiff University, Cardiff, United Kingdom, Department of Architecture, Artvin Coruh University, Artvin, Turkey; Cadirci M.S., Department of Statistics, Cumhuriyet University, Sivas, Turkey
Abstract: Construction projects involve a complex relationship of interdependence among numerous parties, which often leads to delays and significant coordination costs among contractors. While approaches based on Building Information Modeling (BIM) and Digital Twin (DT) technologies have enhanced monitoring and visualization capabilities, they remain limited in their ability to enable autonomous, decentralized, and tamper-proof resource reallocation. This paper proposes and computationally evaluates a three-layer Tokenized BIM-Twin (TBT) framework under controlled simulation conditions. The framework combines a static IFC-based BIM layer for resource tokenization, a real-time Digital Twin layer to detect anomalies and measure deviations, and a blockchain-based smart contract layer that has the potential to minimize disputes and reallocate resources automatically and transparently under the modelled conditions. The framework is evaluated using an agent-based simulation model defined on an eight-parameter uncertainty space. A total of 150 Monte Carlo iterations per scenario (n = 450 observations) are performed across three configurations: Baseline (traditional management), Centralized BIM + DT, and the TBT framework. The results are assessed using one-way ANOVA, Welch’s t-tests, and effect size analysis (Cohen’s d), indicating statistically significant differences across all evaluated performance dimensions under the modelled conditions. Schedule overrun is reduced within the simulation environment from a mean of 38.90% (± 6.24) to 3.30% (± 1.38) (F = 2672.5, p < 0.001, d = 7.88). Resource idle rates decline from 35.52% (± 3.22) to 20.04% (± 3.02) (d = 4.96), while disruption response time is reduced from 5.45 days (± 1.23) to 0.44 days (± 0.17) (d = 5.69). In addition to its conceptual contribution, the framework has practical implications, as the framework demonstrates the potential to improve coordination efficiency, reduce disputes, and increase transparency under the modelled conditions. The results suggest that the approach has potential for projects characterized by high uncertainty and complex stakeholder interactions, although empirical validation is still required before real-world performance can be confirmed. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Agent-based, immune system-inspired supply chain automation for disruption management
Affiliations: Berlin School of Economics and Law, Department of Business Administration, Berlin, 10825, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Ivanov D., Berlin School of Economics and Law, Department of Business Administration, Berlin, 10825, Germany
Abstract: Resilience in supply chains resembles immune system mechanisms in protecting against disruptions and recovery deployment. Addressing a gap in the literature for models that conceptualize supply chain resilience from an immune-system perspective and in response to growing interest in supply chain automation, this article introduces a multi-agent system (MAS) informed by molecular biology and immunology. The proposed models conceptualize supply chain resilience as comprising both preparedness and recovery, analogous to the innate and adaptive components of immune systems. An immune system-inspired mechanism is implemented in the MAS, integrating innate and adaptive responses and incorporating discrete-event and agent-based simulation methods. In a nutshell, the article presents an agentic AI framework combined with supply chain analytics and develops a MAS model readily available for practical applications. The models are developed using AnyLogic software. From a theoretical standpoint, we contribute to resilience theory and its methodological frameworks for uncertainty modeling in supply chains by proposing an agent-based AI environment that replicates immune system mechanisms acting without a priori information about disruptions and so enhancing adaptability to multiple future scenarios. From a practical perspective, the proposed framework and its operationalization in the MAS model supports automated disruption detection, impact assessment, and response coordination through interacting agents that emulate immune-system functions. It can be deployed as part of a supply chain digital twin to assist managers in evaluating recovery alternatives, activating contingency measures, and improving resilience under disruption scenarios. © 2026 The Author(s)

Abstract: Predictive multiscale cellular modeling is emerging as a consequential direction in precision medicine, converging hypothesis grammars, digital twins, and integrative genomics to interrogate tumor-immune dynamics, therapeutic resistance, and cellular plasticity. This perspective synthesizes recent progress across these domains and critically maps their translational potential alongside their current limitations. Hypothesis grammars translate mechanistic theories into executable agent-based models (ABMs) and hybrid ODE-PDE systems, enabling rapid in silico hypothesis testing while lowering the authoring barrier for domain scientists. Patient-specific digital twins, driven by multi-omics data, employ stochastic ensemble methods to simulate clonal evolution and microenvironmental interactions, though prospective clinical validation of these capabilities remains at an early stage. Integrative genomics, leveraging algorithms such as SCODE and SimiC, infers causal gene regulatory networks (GRNs) using Bayesian variational autoencoders, embedding dynamic intracellular logic into tissue-scale simulations. Emerging applications include in silico oncology trials for optimizing checkpoint blockade and combination therapies. Large language models are being explored to enhance rule induction, while FAIR-compliant digital cell repositories aim to ensure reproducibility and reuse. Verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ) via Sobol sensitivity analysis and Kennedy-O’Hagan calibration are identified as essential components for addressing non-identifiability and supporting regulatory credibility. Federated learning is discussed as a means of mitigating privacy and bias concerns in multi-institutional settings. Together, these converging approaches outline a plausible pathway toward virtual clinical trials and adaptive theranostics, contingent on the prospective validation, data infrastructure, and governance frameworks that clinical deployment will require. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Digital twin–driven energy optimization in food manufacturing systems
Source title: International Journal on Interactive Design and Manufacturing
Affiliations: University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria
Abstract: This research presents an integrated framework for energy and sustainability optimization in food production systems, which is based on a combination of digital twin simulation, multi-objective fuzzy optimization, and an Agentic AI layer for contextual selection of operational decisions based on Pareto solutions. The framework evaluates the trade-off between energy consumption, operating cost, carbon emissions, and product quality under operational uncertainty. The empirical analysis of the research is based on data from an industrial food production line and is complemented by digital twin-based simulations to cover a wider range of operating conditions and decision-making scenarios. The results show that the proposed approach reduces energy consumption by about 6–8% and carbon emissions by about 5%, while maintaining product quality stability. These findings indicate that the proposed framework can support more reliable and implementable energy and sustainability decisions in complex food production environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag France SAS, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Physics-guided multi-fidelity framework for probabilistic deformation prediction of concrete arch dams under digital twin-based monitoring

Abstract: Digital twin-enabled safety monitoring of concrete arch dams requires deformation prediction models that are continuously updateable, physically informed, and uncertainty-aware. Nevertheless, existing approaches often struggle to effectively integrate simulation knowledge with monitoring data, especially under the dual constraints of limited response time and previously unseen real operating conditions. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a physics-guided multi-fidelity Bayesian neural network (PGMF-BNN) framework for digital twin-oriented probabilistic deformation prediction. Low-fidelity data are generated from a three-dimensional finite element model to represent the dominant deformation behavior under hydrostatic loading initially. A multi-input multi-output (MIMO) architecture is constructed to capture spatial dependencies among monitoring points and enable collaborative prediction. The model is subsequently pre-trained using low-fidelity data to learn a mechanically consistent response skeleton, followed by a two-stage transfer learning process using prototype monitoring data to achieve virtual–physical alignment. Finally, Bayesian inference is incorporated to quantify epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties and to produce calibrated prediction intervals. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated using a real concrete arch dam case. The results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior predictive performance, with coefficients of determination exceeding 0.90 at five of the six representative monitoring points (reaching 0.975 at PLA2) and mean absolute percentage errors below 7%. The model successfully reconstructs the spatial correlation structure of multi-point deformation and demonstrates robust performance under limited-data conditions and moderate noise levels (0%–10%). These findings confirm that the proposed framework delivers accurate, physically consistent, and uncertainty-aware deformation predictions under both normal and disturbed operating conditions, providing a reliable and extensible solution for digital twin-based dam safety monitoring and risk early warning. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: A hybrid model calibration framework for transient seepage prediction in levees using field monitoring data

Authors with affiliations: Bazdar H., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, 02155, MA, United States; Vahedifard F., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, 02155, MA, United States, Institute for Water, Environment, and Health, United Nations University, Richmond Hill, L4B 3P4, ON, Canada; Moaveni B., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Tufts University, Medford, 02155, MA, United States
Abstract: Accurate prediction of transient pore-water pressure (PWP) is essential for reliable assessment of levee performance and decision-making, as seepage-driven processes directly influence failure mechanisms such as slope instability, uplift, and internal erosion. Physics-based numerical seepage models are widely used in engineering practice, but their predictive accuracy is often limited by model parameter uncertainty, simplified boundary conditions, and unmodeled processes, particularly under transient hydrologic forcing. These limitations introduce uncertainty in evaluating levee performance under extreme events. This study develops a hybrid modeling framework that enhances predictive accuracy while preserving the physical consistency of numerical seepage models. The framework integrates transient finite-element (FE) seepage modeling, sensitivity-guided parameter calibration, and a data-driven residual-learning layer based on a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. The LSTM is trained exclusively to learn structured residual errors between FE predictions and field measurements and operates as an additive correction without modifying governing equations. Application to a field-instrumented levee demonstrates that while calibration improves overall agreement, systematic discrepancies persist under transient conditions. The residual-learning layer reduces prediction error by approximately 70%, lowering the RMSE from about 11 cm to approximately 3. Interpretability analysis using TimeSHAP confirms that residual corrections are governed primarily by physically meaningful drivers, including hydrologic forcing and recent system state. By reducing structured model discrepancy, the proposed framework improves transient seepage predictions while retaining a physics-based predictive baseline and providing transparency into the factors governing residual correction. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future sensor-integrated digital-twin applications as additional validation data become available. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Real-time simulation of reversible solid oxide cells for digital twins: exploration based on mechanism models and data-driven methods

Abstract: To address the conflict between physical fidelity and computational efficiency in vehicle-to-grid applications, this paper proposes a mechanism-data hybrid digital twin framework for reversible solid oxide cells. A quasi-two-dimensional dynamic model is developed using the control volume method to describe the axial multi-physics coupling. Crucially, to overcome the high computational burden of nonlinear node current solution in distributed models, which limits real-time execution, a PID-modulated current allocation algorithm is introduced into the node current allocation process. This method reformulates current allocation from a numerical solution problem into a closed-loop voltage-error regulation process. While maintaining stable convergence, it reduces the maximum average iteration order from approximately 105 to within 102. Consequently, the model achieves a real-time ratio of 6.21% under a 5 ms time step with 15 nodes, while maintaining a real-time ratio of 47.2% even under a 1 ms time step with 20 nodes. These results indicate that the model satisfies the real-time execution criterion under the tested millisecond-level time steps and node configurations. Hardware-in-the-loop tests further show that the model can maintain stable real-time operation during dynamic electrical interaction and output continuous dynamic responses of multi-physics state variables. To ensure fidelity, Sobol global sensitivity analysis is employed to reduce the number of uncertain parameters from 15 to 8. Data calibration is then conducted under 12 experimental conditions, keeping the cell voltage prediction error within 5%. Finally, the non-uniform distributions of internal electric, fluid, and thermal fields captured by the model provide a reference for understanding the coupled multi-physics evolution inside the cell. The proposed framework balances physical explainability, computational efficiency, and predictive accuracy, thereby offering a feasible solution for digital twin applications and real-time control strategy optimization of solid oxide cells. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd
