Title: From Descriptive to Predictive Analytics in Healthcare Service Operations: A Strategic Analysis of AI-Driven Digital Twins for Emergency Department Capacity Management
Affiliations: SiMLQ, Toronto, Canada; Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada; Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel; Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel
Authors with affiliations: Baron O., SiMLQ, Toronto, Canada, Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Jerusalem, Israel; Azaria S., Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv, Israel; Krass D., SiMLQ, Toronto, Canada, Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada
Abstract: Many modern business processes operate under congestion: stochastic demand, shared and limited resources, complex routing, and tight service-level constraints. From healthcare and public services to logistics, financial operations, and large-scale customer support, these systems exhibit nonlinear behavior where small disruptions propagate quickly and performance deteriorates sharply. This paper examines how Business Process Management (BPM) can evolve to address congestion-driven environments by integrating process mining, queueing theory, simulation, and machine learning and artificial intelligence (ML&AI) into digital twins. We discuss how descriptive analytics must move beyond static dashboards toward data-driven process models that reveal how processes actually unfold in practice—capturing routing variability, rework loops, synchronization delays, and resource contention. Process mining provides structural visibility; queueing-aware modeling explains performance; ML&AI supports prediction under uncertainty. Building on these foundations, predictive and comparative analytics enable counterfactual “what-if” evaluation of staffing, routing, prioritization, and scheduling policies before implementation. Finally, prescriptive analytics embedded within real-time digital twins allow organizations to intervene proactively—anticipating congestion, reallocating capacity, and mitigating cascading delays. Drawing on industrial deployments through SiMLQ, we demonstrate how combining process intelligence with congestion-aware operational modeling transforms BPM from retrospective analysis into continuous, real-time decision support. The implications extend across service industries where variability and resource contention define performance, resilience, and competitiveness. Emergency departments are not failing because clinicians lack commitment; they are failing because the operating system that coordinates demand, staffing, beds, diagnostics, specialist consultation, and inpatient transfers remains largely reactive. Digital twins that are based on extensive descriptive analytics can transform fragmented event data into a safe, continuously updated environment for prediction, counterfactual evaluation, and prescriptive action. The managerial implication is blunt: modern businesses, such as hospitals that rely only on after-the-fact statistics will remain trapped in decision blind spots. Businesses that build validated digital twins would move capacity management upstream, detect failure before it occurs, and redirect scarce resources to the highest-leverage bottlenecks in real time. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Modal parameters are increasingly used in vibration-based Structural Health Monitoring (SHM), Finite Element Model Updating (FEMU), and Digital Twin (DT) applications; however, nominally identical structures can exhibit different modal properties due to physical variability and uncertainties associated with modal identification. This study presents an experimental-statistical framework for characterizing these sources of variability through a large-scale repeated testing campaign comprising 400 vibration experiments on an Axial Piston Pump (APP) sub-assembly. Modal parameters were identified using input–output covariance-driven Stochastic Subspace Identification (SSI-IOCOV), combined with automated modal parameter extraction and tracking. Variability associated with component, assembly, and operator effects was characterized from repeated experimental measurements, while bootstrap resampling was used to quantify identification induced uncertainty under nominally fixed physical conditions. The resulting modal parameter distributions enable explicit comparison between experimentally induced variability and identification induced uncertainty, providing a statistically characterized baseline of nominal modal behavior. The results show that, for the investigated configurations, experimentally induced variability is consistently larger than the bootstrap derived identification uncertainty. Natural frequencies exhibit relatively consistent behavior and are primarily influenced by component variability, whereas damping ratio estimates show substantially greater dispersion and sensitivity. Accurate characterization of these uncertainty sources provides a basis for distinguishing structurally significant changes from normal variability arising from repeated testing and measurement conditions. Although demonstrated on an APP sub-assembly, the proposed framework is applicable to other mechanical structures and provides an experimental uncertainty basis for vibration-based SHM, subsequent probabilistic FEMU, and DT applications. © 2026

Title: Digital twins and nanomedicine: Predictive modelling for clinical translation

Authors with affiliations: Chowdhury S., BCDA College of Pharmacy & Technology, 78/1 Jessore Road (S), Hridaypur, West Bengal, Kolkata, 700127, India; Sarkar S., BCDA College of Pharmacy & Technology, 78/1 Jessore Road (S), Hridaypur, West Bengal, Kolkata, 700127, India; Das A., BCDA College of Pharmacy & Technology, 78/1 Jessore Road (S), Hridaypur, West Bengal, Kolkata, 700127, India
Abstract: The combination of digital twin technology and nanomedicine has emerged as a promising strategy for advancing predictive modelling and precision therapeutics. Nanomedicine offers significant opportunities for targeted drug delivery and controlled drug release; however, its broader clinical translation remains constrained by complex nano–bio interactions, interpatient variability, heterogeneous biodistribution, and uncertainties in predicting nanoparticle pharmacokinetics. Digital twins, conceptualized as continuously updated, patient-specific virtual representations that integrate real-world biological and clinical data, have the potential to address some of these challenges by supporting individualized computational simulations and treatment optimization. This review critically examines the integration of digital twin frameworks with nanomedicine, focusing on computational modelling of nanoparticle transport, protein corona dynamics, immune interactions, and biodistribution. It further evaluates predictive modelling approaches, including physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and hybrid mechanistic–AI frameworks, highlighting their respective strengths, limitations, and current validation status.Applications in cancer, cardiovascular, and neurological disorders, together with smart drug delivery platforms and biosensor-assisted monitoring systems, are also discussed. The review additionally examines current challenges associated with model validation, data standardization, interoperability, regulatory acceptance, and clinical implementation. Although clinically validated digital twin systems for nanomedicine remain limited, continued advances in computational modelling, multimodal data integration, experimental validation, and standardized regulatory frameworks may facilitate the future development of reliable digital twin-enabled precision nanomedicine © 2026 The Authors

Title: Artificial intelligence in orthopedics: current applications, challenges, and future directions

Abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence research in orthopedics has grown rapidly, yet a substantial gap remains between technical development and clinical translation. This narrative review summarizes current applications of artificial intelligence in orthopedic practice and highlights barriers to implementation. Main body: Current work converges on three domains: machine learning for structured perioperative risk prediction, deep learning for standardized musculoskeletal imaging, and large language models for workflow and decision support. Applications such as automated fracture detection, Kellgren–Lawrence grading for osteoarthritis, and transfusion risk modeling are approaching clinical maturity. However, routine adoption is limited by algorithmic opacity, performance degradation in new clinical environments, and poor fit within existing workflows. We argue that progress should shift from increasing model complexity toward rigorous evaluation, including external validation on independent cohorts. In addition, probability calibration and uncertainty estimation are important for trustworthy risk communication. Future directions may include multimodal “digital twin” approaches that integrate electronic medical records, imaging phenotypes, and intraoperative data into patient-specific trajectories. Conclusions: The clinical impact of artificial intelligence in orthopedics will depend on life-cycle governance and demonstrated net benefit, prioritizing reliability and implementation science over retrospective benchmark performance. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Recent advances and emerging trends in CFD applications for disinfection in water and wastewater treatment: A decade in retrospect
Affiliations: Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Kennesaw State University, Marietta, 30060, GA, United States; Carollo Engineers, Seattle, 98101, WA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Zhang J., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Kennesaw State University, Marietta, 30060, GA, United States; Neogi B., Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Kennesaw State University, Marietta, 30060, GA, United States; Wicklein E., Carollo Engineers, Seattle, 98101, WA, United States
Abstract: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) is widely used to analyze and optimize water and wastewater disinfection. This targeted structured review synthesizes approximately 110 peer-reviewed studies published during 2014–2025, with selected earlier studies retained for historical context. Applications spanning UV and UV-LED reactors, chlorination, ozonation, peracetic acid (PAA), advanced oxidation processes (AOPs), and emerging systems are evaluated using a decision-oriented right-fidelity framework that links the engineering quantity of interest to model fidelity, validation evidence, dominant uncertainty, and application readiness. Major advances include multiphysics coupling of hydrodynamics with radiation, reactive transport, and gas–liquid mass transfer; higher-fidelity turbulence treatment; uncertainty-aware validation; and CFD-trained surrogate models. Direct CFD–AI evidence is currently concentrated in surrogate and optimization studies, whereas physics-informed neural networks and digital-twin applications remain emerging or prospective for disinfection. Across technologies, the dominant uncertainty is process specific: optical and dose-response assumptions for UV, matrix-dependent kinetics for chlorine and PAA, and multiphase mass-transfer closures for ozone. The review provides practitioner guidance on model selection, minimum validation requirements, current reliability limits, and evidence needed for routine design, regulatory assessment, and operational decision support. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Towards efficient parametric state estimation with shallow recurrent decoder networks: Application to circulating fuel reactors

Abstract: The recent developments in data-driven methods have paved the way for new methodologies to provide accurate and robust full state reconstruction of engineering systems under any operating conditions. Such approaches can be attractive for next-generation nuclear reactors, which represent particularly challenging applications for sensing and monitoring due to the complexity of the strongly coupled physics involved and the extremely harsh environments. Data-driven techniques can combine different sources of information, including computational proxy models and noisy measurements on the system, to robustly estimate the state. This work leverages the novel Shallow Recurrent Decoder (SHRED) architecture to infer the entire state vector (both neutronics and fluid dynamics fields) of a circulating fuel reactor, the Molten Salt Fast Reactor. The standard architecture is extended to treat parametric time-series data, ensuring the possibility of investigating different scenarios and showing its capabilities to provide an accurate state estimation in various conditions. The proposed methodology adopts possible innovative sensing strategies in new-generation reactors, including out-of-core time-series neutron flux measurements alone, in-core sensing measuring the precursor concentrations or mobile probes advected by the fuel flow. The promising results of this work are further strengthened by the possibility of quantifying the uncertainty associated with the state estimation due to the considerably low training cost of the architecture. The ability of SHRED to deliver real-time, system-wide reconstruction highlights its potential for reactor monitoring, control, and digital twin development in next-generation circulating fuel systems. © 2026 The Author(s). Abstract: Sufficient testing under corner cases is critical for the long-term operation of vehicle-infrastructure cooperation systems (VICS). However, existing corner case generation methods are primarily AI-driven, and VICS testing under corner cases is typically limited to simulation. In this paper, we introduce an L5 “Interactable” level to the VICS digital twin (VICS-DT) taxonomy, extending beyond the conventional L4 “Optimizable” level. We further propose an L5-level VICS testing framework, IMPACT (Interactive Mixed-digital-twin Paradigm for Advanced Cooperative vehicle-infrastructure Testing). By enabling direct interactions between human operators and VICS entities, IMPACT introduces realistic human-related uncertainties into the testing loop and supports the human-in-the-loop generation of corner cases as a complement to AI-driven methods. Furthermore, the mixedDT-enabled “Physical-Virtual Action Interaction” facilitates safe VICS testing under corner cases, incorporating real-world environments and entities rather than purely in simulation. Finally, we implement IMPACT on the I-VIT (Interactive Vehicle-Infrastructure Testbed), and experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. The experimental videos are available at our project website: https://dongjh20.github.io/IMPACT. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Hybrid electric ships are emerging as mobile multi-energy assets that combine diesel generators (DGs), batteries, supercapacitors (SCs), fuel cells (FCs), renewable sources, and shore power through AC/DC or medium-voltage DC (MVDC) networks. Their energy management systems (EMS) must coordinate source dynamics, electrochemical degradation, transient buffering, DC-grid stability, lifecycle cost, carbon intensity, and operational safety under time-varying marine conditions. This review examines sustainable EMS for hybrid electric ships from an energy-system and engineering-deployment perspective. It frames shipboard EMS as a cross-domain coordination problem linking multi-energy architecture, source constraints, hydrodynamic load uncertainty, MVDC stability, validation evidence, and deployment pathways. The narrative synthesis indicates that coordination addressing lifecycle, stability, and validation requirements should be assessed alongside conventional fuel-saving power splitting. Rule-based and equivalent-consumption strategies remain transparent near-term baselines, whereas optimization-based methods are effective when models, forecasts, and solver timing are credible. Learning-assisted EMS can improve prediction and adaptation, but broader shipboard use should be supported by validated constraints, reliable state estimation, fallback logic, hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and power-hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) testing, and traceable validation evidence. The review identifies open ship-load benchmarks, degradation- and stability-aware dispatch, EMS–converter co-design, ship–port scheduling, lifecycle carbon accounting, validated digital-twin/HIL/PHIL workflows, and reporting requirements for certification-oriented shipboard EMS assessment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: iS3-based digital twin system for engineering geological information along rock tunnel axis
Affiliations: Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China
Authors with affiliations: Sun H., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China; Rui Y., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China; Dai Y., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China; Sheng D., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China; Zhu M., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China; Li X., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China; Zhu H., Department of Geotechnical Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Tongji University, Shanghai, China
Abstract: With the extensive development of tunnel engineering in complex geological environments, traditional approaches to geological information acquisition and management can no longer meet the demands of refined management and real-time decision-making. Based on the iS3 intelligent tunnel construction platform, this paper proposes a digital-twin-based geological information management method for tunnel alignments. The developed digital twin system integrates multi-source data fusion, geological model construction, and surrounding rock classification. By integrating borehole logs, geological cross-sections, and excavation-exposed information, the system constructs both the geometric model and the multidimensional geological model of the tunnel alignment using spline fitting and the k-nearest neighbors interpolation method. In addition, by combining large language models (LLMs) with knowledge graph technology, the system is able to automatically extract key geological information from tunnel face geological records and build a structured database. To address the uncertainty in surrounding rock classification, a probabilistic classification algorithm is further introduced. Taking the geological model as input, the algorithm evaluates surrounding rock grades based on multiple geological indicators in combination with cloud model theory. The proposed method is tested using the Wuji Tunnel as a case study. The results show that, when the tunnel axis is divided into 20 m intervals for surrounding rock classification decision-making, the accuracy reaches 91.1%. The system can efficiently handle complex geological information during tunnel construction, providing effective technical support for risk assessment and construction decision-making, and demonstrating strong potential for engineering applications. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A closed-loop framework integrating robotic inspection and digital twins for fatigue prognosis of in-service steel bridges
Affiliations: College of Civil and Transportation Engineering, Hohai University, Nanjing, China; Chemical and Materials Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada; School of Civil Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing, China
Authors with affiliations: Li X., College of Civil and Transportation Engineering, Hohai University, Nanjing, China, Chemical and Materials Engineering, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada; Fu Z., College of Civil and Transportation Engineering, Hohai University, Nanjing, China; Guo H., College of Civil and Transportation Engineering, Hohai University, Nanjing, China; Ji B., College of Civil and Transportation Engineering, Hohai University, Nanjing, China; Xu Z., School of Civil Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing, China
Abstract: Fatigue cracking threatens the safety of orthotropic steel decks (OSDs) in long-span bridges, yet current manual inspection lacks predictive depth. We present a closed-loop framework integrating autonomous robotic inspection, vision-based quantification, and finite-element fracture mechanics to enable adaptive fatigue prognosis. In laboratory validation, the robotic platform achieved a mean localization accuracy of 2.7 ± 0.8 cm, meeting structural precision requirements. Field deployment on an in-service cable-stayed bridge demonstrated that automated inspection reduced average time per girder from 124.6 to 50.4 minutes—a 59.6% reduction. Identified cracks were assimilated into a digital twin for adaptive state updating. Analysis of discrepancies between simulated and observed propagation paths—interpreted via stress intensity factor fields—highlighted significant mixed-mode fracture effects, particularly elevated Mode-II (shear) contributions, as a primary source of predictive uncertainty under in-service conditions. This integration of robotics and digital twins provides a scalable solution for automated maintenance. Beyond labor reduction, the framework establishes a data-driven path toward proactive life-cycle management, enhancing the structural resilience and long-term safety of critical transportation infrastructure. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Data challenges and metrological approaches in the agrifood supply chain: Data accuracy, data availability, and data privacy issues

Abstract: The agrifood supply chain is undergoing a profound digital transformation driven by the adoption of advanced sensing technologies, data analytics, and interconnected information systems. While these innovations create unprecedented opportunities to improve food safety, traceability, authenticity, and sustainability, they also introduce major challenges related to data accuracy, data availability, and data privacy and ethical governance . In this evolving landscape, metrology provides the scientific framework needed to ensure that digital data are reliable, comparable, and fit for decision-making. This review examines the principal data challenges affecting digital agrifood systems and discusses how metrological principles—including traceability, calibration, validation, uncertainty evaluation, and standardised measurement protocols—can be extended beyond traditional laboratory measurements to emerging digital technologies such as IoT, remote sensing, blockchain, Digital Twins, and artificial intelligence. By integrating these principles with FAIR data practices, digital agrifood ecosystems can improve data interoperability, transparency, and long-term reusability while supporting trustworthy data sharing and responsible governance. The review also highlights how research infrastructures such as METROFOOD-RI and governance initiatives such as DRG4FOOD provide complementary examples of implementing these principles in practice by combining metrological rigor with ethical and privacy-aware data governance. Overall, this review proposes a metrological perspective for addressing emerging data challenges and demonstrates how the integration of measurement science, digital technologies, and responsible governance can support trustworthy digital agrifood ecosystems, evidence-based decision-making, and more sustainable and resilient food systems. © 2026 The Authors.

Abstract: Product volatility and market uncertainty are driving manufacturing companies toward highly customized products and increasingly flexible, reconfigurable production systems. To address these challenges, advanced technologies such as Digital Twins (DT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and eXtended Reality (XR) are being adopted to enhance engineering design processes and reduce time-to-market. While Concurrent Engineering has historically improved product development efficiency, limited attention has been given to production system design, which remains critical to introduce new products rapidly. This research investigates how the Industrial Metaverse (IM), a comprehensive environment integrating DT, AI, and XR, can support production system design while aligning with Industry 5.0 principles of human centricity. The study focuses on the detailed design phase, where both hardware and software components are verified and tested. In this context, the IM is explored as a platform to actively engage human stakeholders through immersive and collaborative environments, enhancing the interaction in the virtual worlds for design reviews and training. The findings are based on lessons learned from the METABRAKE project, a collaborative academia-industry project aimed at developing and testing IM applications for product-production system concurrent engineering. Through a laboratory demonstration, the study highlights the capability of immersive technologies to improve design review and virtual training, while also identifying key challenges and lessons learned on technical integration and organizational processes. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Title: Uncertainty-aware deep reinforcement learning optimised construction fleet management: A digital twin approach
Affiliations: School of Mechanical Engineering and Mechanics, Eastern Institute of Technology, Ningbo, China; Faculty of Engineering and Applied Sciences, Cranfield University, Cranfield, United Kingdom; Department of Engineering, Durham University, DH1 3LE, United Kingdom; Faculty of engineering and physical sciences, University of Southampton, Southampton, SO17 1BJ, United Kingdom; School of Aerospace Engineering, Xiamen University, Xiamen, China

Abstract: The construction industry faces great challenges in optimising fleet management under dynamic and uncertain operational conditions. Existing methods either rely on static schedules or heuristic rules, which lack adaptability to uncertain operational conditions and fail to capture the complexity of real-world construction site dynamics, leading to imbalanced resource allocation, disruptions in construction progress, and further deteriorating operational cost uncertainty. This study develops a novel digital twin framework that integrates modelling, simulation, and deep reinforcement learning, specifically the Deep Q-Network (DQN), for optimising fleet management under highly dynamical and uncertain conditions. A simulator of the earthmoving process is developed in the digital world, by modelling the cooperation between excavators and dumpers. By following the physical–virtual–physical workflow of digital twins, real-world data is used to quantify operational parameters and their associated uncertainties. The uncertainties are then integrated into DQN training to generate optimal real-time scheduling strategies, enabled by a new reward design that balances multiple objectives. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed solution offers significant cost savings ranging from 1.41% to 9.71% while ensuring consistent decision-making, even under high uncertainty. This study also discusses how different levels of uncertainty impact operational productivity and costs. This work highlights the potential of the integration of deep reinforcement learning and digital twin approach, emphasising the necessity and impact of incorporating uncertainty in modelling and training to enhance predictive accuracy and decision-making. The proposed framework aims to advance sustainable and intelligent construction practices. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Motion control of an aquatic snake robot with actuator failures and environmental uncertainties using neural network super twisting sliding mode control
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Assam, Guwahati, 781039, India; Advanced Research and Technology Office, MathWorks, Natick, 01760, MA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Patel B.M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Assam, Guwahati, 781039, India; Valenti R.G., Advanced Research and Technology Office, MathWorks, Natick, 01760, MA, United States; Dwivedy S.K., Department of Mechanical Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati, Assam, Guwahati, 781039, India
Abstract: Snake robots, designed to mimic the motion of biological snakes which can be used as versatile applications in underwater operations like maintenance and surveillance. In this work, the snake robot is designed and simulated in the Simscape multibody environment in which the need for explicit mathematical modelling is not required. Because of the multi-link construction, the robot features multiple actuators, raising the possibility of actuator failure. Understanding the robot’s motion in the event of such failures is crucial. Hence, this work examines different scenarios of actuator malfunction. Motion control is achieved through a virtual holonomic constraints (VHCs) based approach, considering various uncertainties in underwater environments. To deal with these uncertainties, the model-based robust control approach known as sliding mode control (SMC) is applied to a simplified dynamic system, which is formulated through virtual holonomic constraints (VHC). A radial basis function (RBF) neural network estimates the model, which is then integrated into the SMC control strategy. To mitigate the chattering issue associated with SMC, the super twisting sliding mode control (STSMC) strategy is employed. Consequently, we propose the RBF-STSMC scheme for controlling the motion of a snake robot in underwater conditions during single or multiple actuator failures and uncertain environments. This proposed scheme is evaluated against existing control strategies. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Vibration of blades and towers in large offshore and floating wind turbines: Mechanisms, modelling credibility and mitigation pathways

Authors with affiliations: Zuo Z., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Cai C., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Wang X., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Jia N., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Sun X., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Zhong X., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Shi K., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China; Li Q., National Energy Wind Turbine Blade R&D Center, Institute of Engineering Thermophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China
Abstract: The upscaling of wind turbines (WTs) and the expansion of offshore and floating deployment are turning blade and tower vibration from a component-level structural response into a system-level reliability issue. Longer and more flexible blades, taller towers, reduced modal frequencies and platform-induced motions increase blade–tower–support coupling and make vibration prediction more sensitive to modelling assumptions. This review examines blade and tower vibrations in large offshore and floating WTs using a mechanism-informed framework. Six vibration categories are considered: buffeting, periodic and parametric excitation, stall-related self-excited vibration, classical flutter, vortex-induced vibration (VIV), and resonance or modal interaction. For each category, observable vibration signatures are linked to dominant energy pathways, structural degrees of freedom and operating conditions. Modelling approaches are evaluated according to the physical quantities they must capture credibly, including load statistics, phase relationships, time-periodic coefficients, aerodynamic damping, vortex lock-in, modal frequencies and uncertainty bounds. Mitigation strategies are organised by mechanism-specific intervention pathways, including added damping, frequency management, aerodynamic or surface modification, flow-disruption devices, and control or operational measures. Their engineering trade-offs are discussed in terms of power production, load redistribution, offshore accessibility, reliability, maintenance and life-cycle cost are discussed. Future priorities include floating-platform-induced coupling, mechanism-specific validation benchmarks, uncertainty-aware stability and fatigue assessment, digital twins, and life-cycle reliability of mitigation systems. © 2026

Abstract: Toxicology has accumulated many predictive tools - physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models, quantitative systems pharmacology (QSP) frameworks organ-on-chip systems, quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models, adverse outcome pathway (AOP) networks and machine-learning approaches. Yet predictive practice remains fragmented. Each tool captures a slice of biology; few capture the whole; none captures the patient. We argue that the concept of a digital twin - a continuously updated, mechanistically grounded, data-driven digital representation of an individual biological system - offers the missing organisational layer. We first trace the origin of digital twins from aerospace engineering through biomedicine into toxicology, emphasising how the defining properties (dynamic data assimilation at the pace a decision requires, multi-scale integration, hybrid mechanistic-statistical architecture, personalisation, predictive simulation) map onto existing toxicological methods. We then position PBPK and QSP as mature proto-twin components and name the architectural gaps - continuous data flow, uncertainty quantification, feedback-driven recalibration and regulatory-grade validation - that separate today's best models from a working twin. A four-layer architecture is proposed: data, mechanistic, AI and simulation. Six published systems are tested against the five conditions; none satisfies all five. We examine applications in drug development, personalised risk assessment, mass-poisoning response, chemical-biological-radiological-nuclear (CBRN) preparedness and antidote discovery for unknown toxins. Finally, we confront the translational gap: data heterogeneity, validation standards, interpretability, regulatory acceptance and ethical custody of patient-level models. Toxicology, we conclude, has most of the ingredients needed for digital-twin implementation; what remains is the integration work, two unresolved scientific problems and the institutional willingness to address them. Title: Physics-informed digital twin for optimal operation of solar air source heat pump-based district heating systems

Abstract: District heating systems (DHS) are increasingly required to support low-carbon building energy supply; however, conventional fossil-fuel-based DHS suffer from high energy consumption, thermal losses and limited flexibility under variable solar availability and heating demand. Solar air-source heat pump systems improve renewable heat utilization, but their practical operation is challenged by intermittent solar irradiance, nonlinear coupling among the solar collector, heat pump, thermal storage and load-side distribution loop and the need for accurate real-time state estimation and control. Existing rule-based and proportional–integral–derivative (PID) strategies lack predictive capability, while conventional model predictive control (MPC) and digital-twin approaches often rely on simplified linear or quasi-static models that cannot fully capture heat-pump nonlinearities, model uncertainty and thermodynamic constraints. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a physics-informed digital-twin district heating system (PI-DT-DHS) based on a physics-informed neural network (PINN) for a solar air-source heat pump. The proposed framework models the solar air heater, evaporator, condenser, thermal storage tank and load-side loop using coupled thermodynamic energy-balance equations, while the PINN embeds supervised reference-data fitting, physics residuals, boundary conditions, energy conservation and operational constraints into the learning process. The trained digital twin is further combined with a constrained optimization layer to minimize compressor power, auxiliary heating, load-temperature deviation and storage-temperature fluctuation under operational limits. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed PI-DT-DHS reduces compressor energy to 19.7kWh, auxiliary heating to 8.9kWh, storage loss to 2.4kWh and distribution loss to 2.0kWh, while increasing useful heat delivery to 39.5kWh compared with other district heating configurations. Title: Digital twin-based machine learning framework for predicting nonlinear seismic response of reinforced concrete shear walls using analytical data

Abstract: This study proposes a digital twin (DT) and machine learning (ML) framework to predict nonlinear pushover responses of reinforced concrete (RC) shear walls using analytically derived data. Two hundred SAP2000 layered shell models were analyzed, and monotonic lateral capacity curves were processed via SPO2FRAG for bilinear parameter extraction. Key response features—initial stiffness (K0), yield displacement (), and post-yield stiffness ratio ()were identified. Ten input variables including wall geometry, material properties, reinforcement ratios, axial load, and opening ratio were used to train Random Forest regressors for predicting the pushover curve descriptors. Model accuracy was validated using nested cross-validation, yielding mean test R2 values of 0.996 for, 0.995 for, and 0.925 for, while uncertainty measures (Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), 95% confidence intervals) supported robustness. The DT surrogate reconstructs pushover curves in under 2 seconds per specimen, supporting rapid parametric analysis and seismic scenario assessments without the need for repetitive finite element simulations. The study also documents model limitations and outlines guidance for extending the approach to shear-dominated walls and experimental validation. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Purpose of Review: This review explores the growing relevance of simulation in advancing next-generation forest operations and logistics. It addresses the critical question of how simulation methods, such as discrete event simulation, agent-based simulation, and hybrid simulation and modeling approaches, contribute to better decisions in forest engineering practice. We highlight the unique characteristics of simulation in forestry compared to other sectors, introduce its current applications, and examine methodological innovations that enhance forest operations management at operational, tactical, and strategic levels. Additionally, we assess the evolving role of simulation in forest engineering, specifying its transition from a primary focus on wood procurement to the integrated management of ecosystem services. Recent Findings: Recent applications demonstrate the value of simulation for forest engineering beyond traditional productivity analysis, now incorporating sustainability dimensions, risk mitigation planning, stakeholder coordination, and silvicultural practices to balance different objectives. Simulation has become a key method enabling better design of forest value chains from tree planting to harvesting and logistics, incorporating equipment interactions, occupational risk, and integration with real-time data. Recent advances combining simulation and optimization methods have proven particularly powerful for capturing complex stakeholder interactions and emergent system behaviors. Digital twin technologies and the integration with artificial intelligence represent emerging frontiers, while participatory modeling approaches show promise in bridging the gap between sophisticated analytical tools and practical field implementation. Summary: Simulation has become an important method in forest engineering for modeling complex trade-offs inherent in multifunctional forestry while addressing operational uncertainties. Key methodological advances in forest operations include improved access to better data, more powerful simulation software, integration with optimization and generative artificial intelligence, and the emergence of real-time adaptive systems. However, persistent challenges remain in data availability, stakeholder engagement, and translating model outputs into operational field realities. Future research must address uncertainties related to incorporating better datasets into the models and real-time data streams to increase the robustness of the outcomes. Simulation offers a transformative opportunity for education, equipping future forest engineers and wood supply chain managers with the skills and mindset needed to navigate increasingly complex decision environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Prospective risk scenario intelligence for industry 5.0: A data-driven framework using synthetic futures, deep learning, and counterfactual interventions
Affiliations: Department of Systems Engineering, École de Technologie Supérieure, University of Quebec, Montréal, Canada; Risk Analytics AI (RAAI), AZ, United States
Authors with affiliations: Gholamizadeh K., Department of Systems Engineering, École de Technologie Supérieure, University of Quebec, Montréal, Canada, Risk Analytics AI (RAAI), AZ, United States
Abstract: Industry 5.0 is conceptualized as an integration of human-centric design, artificial intelligence, digital twins, and cyber-physical systems, through which novel risk pathways are created where safety, security, human–AI interaction, and resilience become tightly coupled. Empirical incident datasets for these emerging configurations are not yet available, by which proactive risk assessment is hindered. A prospective scenario intelligence framework is developed to stress-test future risk states without reliance on historical accident data. Based on a systematic parameter taxonomy derived from the literature, 200,000 synthetic future operating states were generated using a structured generative model. These scenarios were analyzed by transformer-based tabular representation learning, deep embedded clustering for latent risk regime discovery, graph-attention networks for cross-domain co-assurance coupling, deep ensembles with conformal prediction for calibrated uncertainty, self-supervised neural risk ranking, and counterfactual intervention analysis. Seven interpretable risk regimes were identified, including digital-twin drift, security-dominant degradation, cyber-to-physical cascade, and resilient adaptive operation. High-priority scenarios were characterized by elevated multi-domain degradation with weak resilience. The largest simulated risk reductions were obtained through digital-twin recalibration and sensor data-fusion upgrades. The framework offers a prospective computational approach for proactive reliability analysis in Industry 5.0, by which conceptual risk knowledge is transformed into an uncertainty-quantified, model-based roadmap that requires future empirical validation before operational implementation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Quantum-Inspired Graph Neural Digital Twins for the sub-microsecond topological co-design and temporal degradation modeling of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin smart gels
Affiliations: Bajpai & Co. Research Private Limited (Bajpai Labs), Uttar Pradesh, Lucknow, India
Authors with affiliations: Bajpai K., Bajpai & Co. Research Private Limited (Bajpai Labs), Uttar Pradesh, Lucknow, India
Abstract: The clinical translation of lignocellulosic smart gels is constrained by empirical formulation screening, complex structure–property relationships, and uncertainty in degradation and therapeutic-release behavior. This study aims to determine whether a unified computational digital-twin framework can (i) optimize the crosslinking topology of cellulose-, hemicellulose-, and lignin-based matrices, (ii) predict their mechanical and temporal degradation behavior, and (iii) translate optimized formulations into real-time control parameters for microfluidic synthesis. To address these objectives, we develop a Quantum-Inspired Graph Neural Digital Twin (Q-GNDT) that represents molecular interactions as dynamic non-Euclidean graphs and formulates topological optimization as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem. A temporal graph-decay model couples pH-dependent hydrolysis, enzymatic cleavage, percolation loss, and drug diffusion to predict time-resolved degradation and release. The computational architecture is integrated with an edge-AI control model designed for sub-microsecond microfluidic actuation. Retrospective cross-validation against published experimental datasets from three independent studies yielded mean absolute errors of 2.1% for pore size, 2.9% for storage modulus, and 1.5% for drug-release kinetics, with an overall RMSE of 0.74%. An in-silico targeted-delivery case study further produced 4.1% initial burst release, 98.0% cumulative delivery, and near-linear release kinetics (R2 = 0.991). These results indicate that Q-GNDT can serve as a computational design and screening framework for narrowing the experimental search space of programmable lignocellulosic biomaterials. Prospective synthesis, biological testing, and in vivo validation remain necessary before clinical translation. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: A probabilistic physics-based framework for the development and continuous adaptation of lifecycle digital twins
Affiliations: Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; CMSoft, Inc., CA, United States; U.S. Air Force, United States
Authors with affiliations: Farhat C., Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and Institute for Computational and Mathematical Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, United States; Daeninck G., CMSoft, Inc., CA, United States; Harp D.I., U.S. Air Force, United States
Abstract: Digital twins are increasingly employed to support predictive analysis, decision-making, and monitoring of complex physical systems. However, existing implementations often rely either on high-fidelity models that are computationally prohibitive for real-time operation or on purely data-driven surrogates that lack physical interpretability and robustness outside their training domain. We present a unified, physics-based computational framework for digital twinning that addresses these limitations through hierarchical projection-based model order reduction, nonparametric probabilistic representation of model-form uncertainty, and data-driven calibration and updating. The framework spans a hierarchy of reduced-order models, from high-dimensional models (HDMs) to hyperreduced stochastic surrogates, enabling computationally efficient predictions while preserving the essential physics of the underlying system. It establishes a systematic progression from an HDM to a digital twin prototype (DTP) through projection and hyperreduction, and subsequently to an operational digital twin instance (DTI) through asset-specific stochastic calibration. To achieve real-time predictive capability while capturing unsteady nonlinear behavior, the framework incorporates a novel trajectory-based perturbation formulation supported by a database of physical matrices acting as localized tangent operators of the underlying nonlinear equations. Interpretable and non-interpretable sources of model-form uncertainty are represented through low-dimensional stochastic parameterizations, enabling efficient uncertainty propagation, statistical inference, and continuous data-driven updating in reduced-order spaces. The framework is validated using two aerospace applications. The first demonstrates an operational DTP for an F-16D aircraft executing aggressive, unsteady maneuvers under the United States Air Force HAVE MIRAGE project, delivering physics-consistent online predictions from real flight data at 20 Hz (0.05 s intervals) in a faster-than-real-time setting – achieving speedup factors up to 57 × ahead of real-time on a single CPU. The second application demonstrates a DTI for structural health monitoring, inferring Level-1 damage presence through changes in the predictive consistency and confidence intervals of the digital twin, utilizing a synthetic dataset representing progressive degradation states. Within this structural tracking context, the hyperreduced stochastic forward solver yields a two-order-of-magnitude speedup factor of approximately 272 × over the HDM, enabling near-real-time tracking on a single standard core. Together, these applications demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a computationally efficient, physics-consistent foundation for digital twinning across the lifecycle of complex engineering systems. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Physics-driven and data-driven hybrid digital twin framework for methanol fuel supply system based on dynamic Bayesian network

Abstract: Methanol has attracted increasing attention as a potential low-carbon marine fuel. However, the safe operation of methanol fuel supply systems is challenged by coupled hydraulic, thermal, and control dynamics, together with time-varying degradation and operational uncertainty. To address these challenges, this study proposes a physics-driven and data-driven hybrid digital twin framework based on a dynamic Bayesian network (PDH-DBN) for methanol fuel supply systems. The framework combines a conservation law-based physics-driven model, a temporal convolutional network (TCN)-based data-driven model, online Bayesian updating through particle filter, and adaptive model fusion. The physics-driven branch updates pump-related parameters online, while the data-driven branch updates correction parameters for the TCN outputs. The two branches are then fused adaptively using their current posterior residuals. The updated parameters are further used to construct pump health indices. The proposed approach was validated on a laboratory test bench under varying flow conditions and a preset pump fault. Under normal operation, the fused framework achieved RMSEs of 0.104–0.110 Hz for pump frequency, 0.022–0.031 bar for pressure, and 0.015–0.017 °C for temperature. Under the preset pump fault scenario, PDH-DBN effectively isolated primary-pump degradation. These results indicate that PDH-DBN can support accurate state estimation, adaptive fusion, uncertainty-aware health assessment, and pump-level fault isolation for methanol fuel supply systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Abstract: Digital Twin assisted mobile edge computing is emerging as a key enabler for sustainable city services that require low latency, energy efficiency, and resilient unmanned aerial vehicle and Internet of Things operation. These technologies promote urban sustainability by reducing energy/bandwidth overhead, strengthening resilience during mobility, and supporting equitable services through privacy-preserving coordination. However, prior work is fragmented across DT design, UAV-enabled edge architectures, task offloading and scheduling, service migration, federated learning, federated reinforcement learning, and semantic communication. This systematic literature review organizes the literature with a DT-centric taxonomy that captures DT roles, paired objects, synchronization strategies, deployment styles, decision scopes, learning paradigms, and semantic data handling. We consolidate evidence by function and compare objectives, metrics, and deployment realism. Key findings show that predictive and control-in-the-loop twins enable feasibility-aware offloading and proactive migration, but benefits depend on disciplined synchronization under limited control-plane budgets. Federated intelligence supports scalable coordination yet is constrained by non-IID data, client churn, and communication overhead, which motivates hierarchical federation and semantics-aware update reduction. Semantic communication further reduces bandwidth by transmitting only task-relevant meaning and supporting fidelity-controlled transmission and selective learning updates. We conclude with open challenges for city-scale deployment, including uncertainty-aware prediction, joint offloading migration control, scalable multi-twin coordination, standardized semantic metrics, and reproducible evaluation using realistic mobility, channel, and energy models. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Optimizing critical care capacity using fuzzy multi-objective digital twins and deep learning
Affiliations: University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria
Authors with affiliations: Nozari H., University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria; Yordanova Z., University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria; Milusheva V., University of National and World Economy, Sofia, Bulgaria
Abstract: Capacity management in intensive care units is one of the most complex challenges in the health system, requiring advanced decision-making approaches due to uncertainty in demand, resource constraints, and clinical sensitivity of decisions. This study presents an innovative framework for optimizing intensive care capacity, in which data-driven predictions, fuzzy modeling, and multi-objective decision-making are integrated within a dynamic digital twin. The proposed framework supports adaptive and uncertainty-aware decision-making by utilizing patient behavior prediction and continuous system status updates. Numerical results based on real and simulated data show that the proposed framework reduces the clinical risk index, admission delay, and workload imbalance, while providing a more controlled use of ICU capacity and faster recovery after demand shocks, compared to the fixed rule-based policy and the deterministic optimization model. The findings of this study show that integrating intelligent decision-making with digital twins can play an effective role in the development of decision support systems in the field of intensive care. © 2026 The Authors. Abstract: This study proposes a reinforcement learning-based dynamic evacuation guidance system for fire emergencies in multi-story buildings. The proposed framework integrates a cellular automata-based fire simulation with an agent-based evacuation simulation to model the coupled dynamics of fire spread and occupant movement. The fire simulation represents the spatiotemporal propagation of flames and smoke, including inter-floor spread through vertical shafts and the stack effect. The evacuation simulation models occupant behavior by incorporating walking speed reductions caused by smoke and crowd density, as well as probabilistic route choice using a mixed logit model to capture heterogeneous decision-making. Within this environment, a reinforcement learning agent dynamically controls directional restrictions at corridor junctions and exits. The agent observes crowd flow, crowd density, fire hazard scores, and exit information, and learns an evacuation guidance policy that minimizes both evacuation time and fatalities through interaction with the simulation environment. To ensure the relevance of the learned policy under realistic deployment conditions, the agent is additionally trained under a sensor uncertainty wrapper that models hazard-sensor noise, CCTV pedestrian detection misses, and measurement latency. Experiments were conducted on a three-story model under 26 fire scenarios with varying ignition locations, with all reinforcement learning agents evaluated under the full sensor uncertainty environment and compared against two deterministic baselines—a rule-based dynamic guidance and a strengthened shortest-path-based baseline that incorporates global path information. The proposed uncertainty-aware policy achieves average reductions of approximately 32% in total evacuation time and 58% in fatalities compared with the rule-based dynamic guidance, and approximately 20% and 42% in the same metrics compared with the strengthened shortest-path-based baseline, with statistical significance confirmed by paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm–Bonferroni correction (Holm-adjusted p<0.001). The results demonstrate that reinforcement learning can effectively learn adaptive evacuation guidance policies that consider both fire dynamics and crowd behavior under realistic sensor conditions. These findings support the use of simulation-driven AI decision support as one component of Safety Digital Twin-based safety management for complex buildings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Machine learning-enhanced nano-QSAR and multiscale modeling for predictive nanomedicine: applications in herbal therapeutics and neglected tropical diseases

Abstract: Nanomedicine has transformed targeted drug delivery, yet the complexity of nano-bio interactions continues to hinder rational nanoparticle design. Predictive computational approaches, particularly machine learning (ML), nano-quantitative structure-activity relationships (nano-QSAR), and multiscale modeling, emerge as essential tools for understanding and optimizing nanoparticle behavior across biological environments. This review synthesizes advances in nano-specific descriptors, classical and deep learning frameworks, physics-informed hybrid models, and simulations spanning quantum, atomistic, and tissue-level scales. We highlight two application domains where these strategies show distinct translational promise: herbal nanomedicine, where computational modeling supports the design of phytochemical-loaded nanoparticles with improved solubility, stability, and targeting, and neglected tropical diseases, where predictive tools enable optimization of macrophage targeting, parasite niche penetration, and performance under resource-limited conditions. Persistent challenges, including data scarcity, heterogeneity, limited reproducibility, and regulatory uncertainty, are critically examined. We propose future directions centered on standardized open datasets, foundation AI models, autonomous nanoparticle design, and patient-specific digital twin platforms. Collectively, these integrative computational strategies provide a roadmap for accelerating safe, effective, and context-adapted nanomedicine development. Integration of machine learning, nano-QSAR, and multiscale modeling enables predictive, rational design of nanomedicines for diverse disease applications. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Hidden rock mass state theory: A physics-informed state estimation framework for next-generation Digital Twins in open-pit rock engineering
Source title: International Journal of Rock Mechanics and Mining Sciences
Affiliations: Dokuz Eylul University, Engineering Faculty, Department of Mining Engineering, Izmir, Turkey
Authors with affiliations: Aksoy C.O., Dokuz Eylul University, Engineering Faculty, Department of Mining Engineering, Izmir, Turkey
Abstract: Rock-mass behaviour in large open-pit mines emerges from the coupled evolution of geological, structural, hydrogeological, geomechanical, and operational conditions. Although modern monitoring systems provide increasingly dense observations of deformation, groundwater response, seismicity, and operational change, these measurements primarily represent observable responses rather than the underlying physical condition governing rock-mass behaviour. This study introduces the Hidden Rock Mass State (HRMS) as a latent, time-dependent representation of this evolving physical condition. HRMS is mathematically represented through the Engineering Representation of the Hidden Rock Mass State (ERMS), comprising five interacting physical domains, and sequentially estimated through the Evolutionary Rock Mass State Observer (ERMSO), a physics-informed state-estimation framework for state-aware rock-mass Digital Twins. The framework explicitly separates physical state, external forcing, and observable response and is evaluated through intra-mine state discrimination, uncertainty and information-availability analyses, withheld observations, and independent perturbation-response datasets across six contrasting mining environments. Within the principal implementation environment, four sectors produced distinct multidomain ERMS configurations, with pairwise state distances ranging from 0.301 to 0.694. The principal state interpretation remained robust under alternative weighting assumptions and ±20% input perturbations across 1,000,000 Monte Carlo realizations; the two highest-state sectors retained their principal positions in more than 97% of realizations. Controlled omission of individual physical domains preserved the complete sector ordering in four of five cases, with a maximum ERMS deviation of 0.067. Independent deformation, inclinometer, and InSAR observations were physically consistent with the inferred temporal, spatial, and depth-dependent state evolution. Incremental predictive benchmarks further showed that independently characterized state information improved out-of-sample prediction beyond external forcing alone: hydrogeological state information reduced RMSE and MAE by 30.1% and 24.4%, respectively, relative to a rainfall-only model, while an independent dynamic benchmark produced corresponding reductions of 6.0% and 5.2% after conventional source–path variables were included. These results support HRMS as a physically structured latent-state framework in which rock-mass response is interpreted through the interaction between pre-existing physical condition and external forcing, providing a state-estimation basis for next-generation rock-mass Digital Twins. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Saltation-consistent event-aware digital twins for uncertainty transport in non-smooth dynamical systems
Affiliations: Sir Geoffrey Leigh Academy, Kent, Dartford, United Kingdom; Institute of Physics, London, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Mosekari S., Sir Geoffrey Leigh Academy, Kent, Dartford, United Kingdom, Institute of Physics, London, United Kingdom
Abstract: Non-smooth mechanical systems challenge prediction not only because their trajectories contain impacts, frictional transitions, and unilateral constraints, but because these events reorganize state propagation, sensitivity, uncertainty, and control authority. Existing digital-twin, hybrid-systems, Bayesian-estimation, and reduced-order frameworks each address part of that difficulty, yet they are usually developed on separate mathematical layers and therefore become least reliable precisely where engineering decisions are most event-sensitive. This paper introduces an event-aware mechanics and inference architecture for non-smooth dynamical systems in which event surfaces are treated as first-class transport interfaces rather than as numerical exceptions. Starting from a high-fidelity hybrid mechanical model with unilateral contact, friction, and measure-valued impulses, we derive saltation-consistent transport laws for sensitivities and covariance, formulate forced Bayesian correction at mechanically determined event times, and establish reduced-order error bounds that isolate jump mismatch as a distinct approximation channel. The resulting framework couples full-order mechanics, event-aware uncertainty propagation, online parameter updating, and reduced-order approximation within a single mathematically consistent architecture. Benchmarks involving impact, stick–slip, and shock-response dynamics show that event-aware transport preserves post-event state accuracy, concentrates parameter information in short event windows, and improves reduced-order fidelity during discontinuity-dominated transients. The central advance is the identification of event surfaces as the structural interfaces through which mechanics, inference, uncertainty transport, and control are coupled in non-smooth digital twins. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Model updating plays an important role in obtaining a more accurate finite element model (FEM) based on measured vibration data. Based on the updated FEM, it is more convenient to carry out further analysis, e.g., structural health monitoring, digital twin, and so on. Bayesian model updating methods are attracting more attention since they can provide rigorous models and evaluate the uncertainty of the updated results. However, in the real application, it still has some problems such as computational efficiency and accuracy. In this paper, a two-stage Bayesian function combined with MCMC algorithm is proposed and used to perform model updating of a real complicated long-span cable-stayed bridge. The two-stage Bayesian function can automatically consider the heteroscedasticity of each utilized modal degree and it allows for incomplete modal information for model updating. Before conducting model updating, two different sensitivity analysis functions are used for local and global sensitivity analysis of bridge model. A set of interaction process between different computation tools has been established to improve computational speed by using an improved stopping criterion. The updated results are demonstrated for both model classes, and ultimately a Bayesian model class evidence was used to judge their superiority. The proposed method was verified by a numerical example and then applied in the updating of the bridge. The experimental results show that the model updating method successfully corrects initial FEMs with reverse mode order errors using incomplete modal information. Simultaneously, the results exhibit a relatively low level of uncertainty. Furthermore, the Bayesian model class selection algorithm proves that new sensitivity analysis functions are superior. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Institution of Structural Engineers.

Abstract: The increased occurrence of extreme weather events, cyber-physical disturbances, and electrification requires distribution systems to sustain critical services and recover quickly under adverse conditions. Meanwhile, the penetration of DERs, digitally controlled assets, and decentralized energy markets is transforming the traditional distribution networks into active and flexible systems. Virtual power plants (VPPs) and peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading are two types of complementary flexibility, but their coordinated role in resilience-oriented distribution systems operation has not been sufficiently synthesized. This review investigates the incorporation of distribution systems resilience, VPP aggregation, DER and battery energy storage system (BESS) coordination, and centralized/decentralized energy trading based on around 160 peer-reviewed studies. This review offers an in-depth synthesis of the resilience metrics, VPP architectures and control strategies, P2P and transactive-energy mechanisms, and optimization approaches for the distribution systems with DERs. Besides the synthesis of the literature, a scenario-based numerical assessment of the coordinated operation of DERs and BESS under single and multi-fault conditions is performed utilizing the IEEE 33-bus radial distribution system (RDS). The four optimization methods GA, GWO, HPOA, and COA are evaluated using 30 matched experimental runs, and the difference of performance is compared by Wilcoxon signed-rank and Friedman tests. The results show that the coordinated VPP operation enhances the load restoration and decreases the energy not served (ENS), while it provides voltage support and accelerates the recovery during the outage conditions considered. The integrated resilience-aware operation further shows the complementary role of DER/BESS coordination and P2P energy trading in enhancing the technical and economic performance. The review highlights important gaps in coupled uncertainty and cascading-failure modeling, network-aware transactive-energy coordination, cyber-secure VPP operation, scalable multi-VPP control, resilience-oriented market valuation, interoperability and experimental validation. Future research should target integrated and scalable cyber-physical-economic frameworks with AI-assisted adaptive control, digital twins, distributed and federated VPP coordination, resilient P2P markets, larger-system validation, and hardware-in-the-loop and field demonstrations. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Jiang S.J.; Xu Y.L.; Li S.M.
Title: Digital twin-informed spatiotemporal graph neural network for buffeting response prediction of a long-span bridge
Affiliations: Department of Bridge Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China; State Key Laboratory of Bridge Intelligent and Green Construction, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China
Authors with affiliations: Jiang S.J., Department of Bridge Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China; Xu Y.L., Department of Bridge Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China, State Key Laboratory of Bridge Intelligent and Green Construction, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China; Li S.M., Department of Bridge Engineering, School of Civil Engineering, Southwest Jiaotong University, Chengdu, China
Abstract: Conventional buffeting analyses of long-span bridges rely on wind tunnel tests and numerical simulations, involving many parameters of uncertainties and suffering from high computational cost. To address these limitations and provide a real-time buffeting response prediction, this study proposes a digital twin-informed spatiotemporal graph neural network (DTI-STGNN) method. This method is composed of three parts: (1) establish a digital twin for buffeting analysis of long-span bridges and generate a dataset from the digital twin, which can cover various wind and structural conditions; (2) design graph convolutional layers, temporal convolutional layers, and loss function of DTI-STGNN and train it using the dataset generated by the digital twin; and (3) develop a hybrid model combining long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer to achieve accurate short-term wind speed prediction based on historical wind speed data and then predict the corresponding buffeting response of the bridge using DTI-STGNN. The proposed DTI-STGNN method is finally applied to a real suspension bridge as a case study. The results of the case study show that compared to traditional LSTM and gated recurrent unit models and conventional buffeting analysis methods, the DTI-STGNN method possesses high accuracy and real-time prediction capacity, strong generalization capability, and physical consistency features, offering a new approach for real-time buffeting response prediction and safety assessment of long-span bridges. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Bolted-joint tightening affects both structural integrity and line performance in EV chassis assembly, yet production torque tables are often conservative to accommodate variability in joint mechanics and shop-floor conditions. This study uses a deployable digital-twin workflow to reduce torque variants while jointly considering mechanics constraints, AGV-related logistics, and cost/OEE objectives. The workflow couples (i) a torque–preload joint model with vibration and fatigue checks, (ii) an uncertainty-calibrated, value-aware LSTM for quality-risk prediction from torque–angle signatures and context, and (iii) a multi-objective PSO variant for mixed discrete–continuous search with feasibility-first handling. Candidate torque tables are admitted only after verification-twin re-evaluation, which serves as a release gate. In an industrial study covering 5,524 vehicles (Feb 2024–Jan 2025), torque specifications are reduced from 23 variants to 8 (− 65.2%) while keeping the observed reject rate within a ≤ 0.05% cap and meeting Goodman safety ≥ 1.5. Standardization reduces end-effector changeovers by 31% and AGV idle time by 14% at a 42 s takt without increasing fleet size. Cross-platform transfer is evaluated on three EV platforms, and ablations are reported with statistical tests and effect sizes alongside V&V metrics. Reproducibility is supported by a complete nomenclature, fully specified algorithms, and a shareable synthetic dataset with scripts that regenerate all figures and tables. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: A physics-guided digital twin framework for synthetic gamma-ray spectrum generation and validation in radiation monitoring applications

Abstract: The limited availability of labelled gamma-radiation data constrains the development and evaluation of machine-learning methods for radiation-monitoring applications, particularly under shielded or otherwise difficult-to-reproduce conditions. This study presents a physics-guided Digital Twin framework integrating Geant4-based Monte Carlo radiation transport, automated scenario orchestration, detector-response aggregation, structured synthetic-data generation, and multiple explicitly separated levels of assessment. Eight radionuclide-labelled source classes were represented by characteristic monoenergetic gamma emissions ranging from 0.051 to 2.610 MeV. Simulations covered four shielding materials-lead, stainless steel, concrete, and polyethylene-at thicknesses of 0, 1, 2, 5, and 10 cm, resulting in 160 source-material-thickness configurations. The simulated detector responses reproduced the expected dependence of photon transmission on energy, shielding material, and absorber thickness. After incorporating counting-statistical uncertainties, the fitted linear attenuation coefficient for 1.25-MeV 60Co-labelled photons in lead was 0.618 ± 0.042 cm-1, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.535 - 0.700 cm-1. The corresponding NIST XCOM reference value of 0.680 cm-1 lies within this interval. A limited detector-level experimental assessment was performed using independently acquired NaI(Tl) spectra. A multi-peak blind spectrum was assigned to material containing the 232Th decay chain before disclosure of the source identity, and the assignment was subsequently confirmed by the data provider. This result is reported as a proof-of-concept case rather than a statistical estimate of identification accuracy. An independent UAV radiation-survey dataset containing 3,722 observations across ten flight transects was additionally analysed. It demonstrated a strong and spatially stable relationship between integral gamma activity and estimated 137Cs activity r=0.990, R2=0.980. These UAV results provide an application-level reference but are not interpreted as direct validation of Geant4-generated spectra. The proposed framework provides a transparent and extensible basis for physics-guided synthetic-data generation while explicitly distinguishing attenuation verification, limited detector-level spectral assessment, and application-level consistency analysis. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Adaptive task planning based on physiological state estimation and state uncertainty improves performance in human–robot collaboration
Affiliations: Robotics Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States; Robotics Department, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States
Authors with affiliations: Rafter A., Robotics Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States; Tilbury D.M., Robotics Department, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States; Barton K., Robotics Department, Mechanical Engineering Department, University of Michigan, 2505 Hayward Street, Ann Arbor, 48109, MI, United States
Abstract: Human–robot collaboration combines the strengths of humans and robots to enhance productivity, flexibility, and safety. A task planner can use knowledge of relevant human and robot states to optimize overall task performance. Digital twins use models and real-time data to estimate these human and robot states. In our study, we implement a system of digital twins in which state information from a human–robot collaborative system is used to inform task reallocation in response to disruptions in team performance, with the goal of maximizing overall team throughput. The case study involves an assembly task in which three humans (one real, two simulated) work with a dual-arm robot. Humans are responsible for performing assembly operations, while the robot delivers parts. In aggregate, the digital twins predict the throughput of the human–robot collaborative system and detect disruptions, such as when the predicted throughput drops below a threshold. When a disruption is detected, the task planner reallocates tasks among agents based on their estimated capacity to maintain performance. The study examines how overall throughput is affected by varying levels of uncertainty in the predicted states of the human–robot collaborative system. In addition, the study explores how the task planner considers varying levels of human stress to allocate tasks and improve performance. The results of a study with 40 participants show that incorporating human stress estimates into task planning improves team performance, and that lower uncertainty values also improve team performance, but with a smaller effect. Together, these two factors improve throughput on average by 5.3% compared to a planner that uses high uncertainty and omits human stress estimates. These findings demonstrate that incorporating even simple physiological indicators and principled uncertainty filtering can significantly enhance task allocation decisions, offering a scalable approach to embedding human-aware intelligence into collaborative robotic systems. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Strategy selection of competitive ports and the information value of digital twin in the construction of green shipping corridors
