Abstract: With the promotion of decarbonization initiatives, many ports are building green shipping corridors (GSCs), which involve the adoption of clean energy and the development of supporting infrastructure between ports. However, uncertainties in clean energy supply costs pose challenges for strategic decision-making. In response, digital twin (DT) technologies, increasingly emphasized in port planning and management, help address these uncertainties by enhancing the availability and quality of information for decision-making. This study considers the information value of DT in GSCs construction, and uses game theory to analyze the strategy selection of two competitive ports in construction of GSCs. We find, first, when the traditional energy adoption ratio is small and in a certain interval, the port with GSCs obtains benefits and gives its opponent without GSCs an interesting free-rider effect thus forming a win–win outcome. Therefore, the practices that both ports conduct GSCs and only one port conducts GSCs can form two interesting win–win outcomes. Besides, when the traditional energy adoption is very small, i.e., below a certain threshold, the port with GSCs has huge competition advantages, thus only one port conducting GSCs will yield a win-lose outcome. Second, under perfect information with DT, many of the win–win outcomes observed under imperfect information are replaced by win-lose results. This suggests that access to accurate clean energy cost information diminishes the free-rider effect of the opponent without GSCs. Third, counter-intuitively, when the market size is large, DT may be over-invested if both two ports adopt DT, and information asymmetry may be better. These findings offer practical implications for port managers considering GSCs construction strategies under conditions of competition and information asymmetry. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Abstract: As a core component in steel production, the steel strip is prone to surface defects during the continuous production process due to its complex conditions. To achieve high-precision real-time monitoring of its surface quality and efficient quality control, the steel strip surface defect detection method is proposed based on uncertainty region fusion and digital twin (DT) model establishment. Specifically, the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) and Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD) models pretrained on public defect datasets are used for independent surface detection, obtaining initial defect regions with confidence scores and uncertain detection results. To address single-model detection uncertainty and enhance detection accuracy, the decision-level uncertainty region fusion method is designed to fuse initial regions and uncertainty information based on region overlap and confidence, acquiring maximum reliable defect regions for surface defect recognition and localization. Different from existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) steel strip defect detection methods, the proposed method innovatively introduces uncertainty perception and diagonal equal-area decision-level fusion. It effectively reduces unreliable bounding box predictions and single-model detection bias and further realizes high-confidence defect data interaction and virtual–real synchronization with digital twin framework. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, the public datasets and experimental steel strip defect datasets are utilized with several defects. The results demonstrate that the proposed method yields consistent and significant improvements in detection accuracy, recall, and overlap rate on both the public Northeastern University (NEU) dataset and the self-built dataset, which verifies the value for steel strip quality control and intelligent manufacturing. Title: A systematic review and thematic analysis of physics-informed machine learning in construction and infrastructure systems

Abstract: This study conducts a systematic review and thematic analysis to explore how physics-informed machine learning (PIML) can enhance reliability in infrastructure assessment and construction management. Previous studies are classified based on state estimation, digital twin updating, performance prediction, deterioration prediction, multi-hazard response analysis, and maintenance and inspection decision support. Embedding governing physical laws in the learning process ensures that models adhere to mechanical principles. The analysis shows that PIML can enhance prediction stability, decrease data needs, and allow for the identification of concealed structural and construction parameters through inverse methods. Importantly, integrating mechanics into data-driven models transforms machine learning from a curve-fitting tool into a verification-compatible analysis method. Constraining predictions with physical laws reduces unrealistic outputs; enables extrapolation to unobserved hazard scenarios such as earthquakes, winds, and floods; and facilitates estimation of deterioration states needed for risk-informed maintenance planning. The reviewed literature shows that these capabilities enable operational digital twins that continuously update infrastructure conditions using real-time monitoring data. However, there are persistent challenges, including computational expenses, inadequate uncertainty quantification, limited multi-physics integration, and the lack of benchmark datasets and regulatory approval. This review concludes that PIML offers a pathway to next-generation artificial intelligence in construction and infrastructure systems by bridging monitoring data and engineering mechanics. As a reliability engine within digital twin frameworks, PIML supports predictive maintenance, performance-based design, and resilience-oriented management of existing and future infrastructure systems. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Design of large-scale floating offshore wind turbines: A review of advances and challenges
Affiliations: School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Huaneng Clean Energy Research Institute (CERI), Beijing, 102209, China
Authors with affiliations: Gu Q., School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Li H., Huaneng Clean Energy Research Institute (CERI), Beijing, 102209, China; Cheng Z., School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China; Huang D., School of Energy and Power Engineering, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, Shanghai, 200093, China
Abstract: Reliable design of floating offshore wind turbines requires balancing energy production, structural reliability and cost under coupled interactions among aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, structural dynamics and turbine control. This review examines horizontal-axis floating turbines, focusing on how blade, floater, mooring and control design affect system response. Physical tests, numerical models and data-assisted methods are evaluated in terms of predictive accuracy, computational cost and validation evidence. Platform motion alters the relative rotor inflow, while control strategies that suppress platform motion can increase fatigue loads under certain operating conditions. Reported fatigue changes therefore remain specific to the turbine configuration, environmental conditions and operating state. Environmental uncertainty, experimental scaling and limited field data constrain validation; predictive accuracy depends on the representation of the governing physical mechanisms and the reliability of environmental and structural inputs. A validation procedure is proposed comprising five groups of cases covering basic model checks, aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, coupled response and field comparisons. Machine learning and digital twins can support load estimation and maintenance planning, with performance evaluated under conditions excluded from calibration and training. Research priorities thus include coordinated structural and control optimization, uncertainty propagation in lifetime fatigue prediction, and independent model validation under fault and shutdown conditions. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Active Learning for Data-Driven Reduced Models of Parametric Differential Systems with Bayesian Operator Inference
Affiliations: Department of Mathematics, Brigham Young University, 275 TMCB, Provo, 84602, UT, United States; Centre for Mathematical Sciences, Lund University, Box 118, Lund, 22100, Sweden; Oden Institute for Computational Engineering and Sciences, The University of Texas at Austin, 201 E 24th St., Austin, 78712, TX, United States

Abstract: This work develops an active learning framework to intelligently enrich data-driven reduced-order models (ROMs) of parametric dynamical systems, which can serve as the foundation of virtual assets in a digital twin. Data-driven ROMs are explainable, computationally efficient scientific machine learning models that aim to preserve the underlying physics of complex dynamical simulations. Since the quality of data-driven ROMs is sensitive to the quality of the limited training data, we seek to identify training parameters for which using the associated training data results in the best possible parametric ROM. Our approach uses the operator inference methodology, a regression-based strategy which can be tailored to particular parametric structure for a large class of problems. We establish a probabilistic version of parametric operator inference, casting the learning problem as a Bayesian linear regression. Prediction uncertainties stemming from the resulting probabilistic ROM solutions are used to design a sequential adaptive sampling scheme to select new training parameter vectors that promote ROM stability and accuracy globally in the parameter domain. We conduct numerical experiments for several nonlinear parametric systems of partial differential equations and compare the results to ROMs trained on random parameter samples. The results demonstrate that the proposed adaptive sampling strategy consistently yields more stable and accurate ROMs than random sampling does under the same computational budget. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Title: Digital twin-driven zero-shot fault diagnosis of axial piston pumps using fluid-borne noise signals

Abstract: Axial piston pumps are crucial components in fluid power systems, where reliable fault diagnosis is essential for ensuring operational safety and efficiency. Traditional data-driven methods require extensive labeled fault data, which is often impractical to obtain for high-value pumps, while model-based diagnosis is affected by simulation fidelity and parameter uncertainties. To address this limitation, this study develops a calibrated-source zero-shot fault diagnosis framework using fluid-borne noise signals. The source generator is an inverse-transient-analysis-calibrated digital twin derived from our prior fluid-borne-noise modeling work, which uses healthy pressure measurements to synthesize pressure-ripple and outlet-flow-ripple fault signals for classifier training; experimental fault samples are excluded from training and used only for target-domain testing. Directly measured pressure ripples and outlet-flow ripples estimated by a physics-informed neural network are evaluated as separate diagnostic branches in both one-dimensional and synchrosqueezed time–frequency forms. The implemented learning model is a convolutional neural network classifier for zero-shot fault diagnosis of axial piston pumps. Among the tested temporal, residual, and transformer-style backbones, a compact wide-kernel convolutional neural network with a subsequence-length first-layer kernel gives the best one-dimensional pressure-ripple performance. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping visualizations indicate that this kernel scale helps the model focus on complete pressure-ripple events rather than isolated local details. The flow-ripple branch provides a more mechanism-oriented view of leakage-related faults, although its accuracy is limited by virtual-sensing uncertainty. Low-fidelity domain-adaptation comparisons further show that distribution alignment can improve clean-condition performance but degrades under strong noise. Overall, the results indicate that reliable zero-shot pump diagnosis requires synthetic fault data with sufficient source-domain fidelity and a classifier whose receptive field is consistent with fluid-borne-ripple physics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Uncertainty-aware digital twin-driven fault-tolerant control for autonomous underwater vehicles using temporal fusion transformer-based fault diagnosis

Abstract: Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) operate in challenging marine environments. The actuator faults, propulsion degradation and environmental disturbances can significantly compromise mission safety and tracking performance. Existing studies have primarily focused on either fault diagnosis or fault-tolerant control as separate tasks. A limited attention has been given to integrating fault diagnosis, predictive digital twins and uncertainty-aware control within a unified framework. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel uncertainty-aware digital twin-driven fault-tolerant control (UA-DT-FTC) framework that integrates the Temporal Fusion Transformer with Confidence-Aware Learning (TFT-CAL) for fault diagnosis; a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) based Digital Twin for one-step-ahead state prediction; dual-source uncertainty estimation; and a severity-confidence-adaptive predictive fault-tolerant control strategy. The proposed controller continuously adjusts the digital twin compensation according to both the estimated fault severity and the confidence of the fused uncertainty measure through a severity-confidence adaptive gain and fault-adaptive predictive gains, thereby improving tracking performance under uncertain operating conditions. To the best of the authors' knowledge, publicly available studies using the selected AUV benchmark dataset have primarily focused on fault identification, whereas its integration into a complete digital twin-assisted fault-tolerant control framework has not been previously reported. Experimental evaluation on a publicly available AUV dataset comprising five operating conditions demonstrates that the proposed diagnosis module achieves approximately 97.57% classification accuracy and 97.43% macro-F1 score. The performance was also validated through five-fold cross-validation. The LSTM-based Digital Twin provides one-step-ahead state predictions whose reliability is explicitly quantified through prediction residuals. In closed-loop control, the proposed UA-DT-FTC framework achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated controllers, reducing the tracking root mean square error (RMSE) and integral absolute error (IAE) by approximately 6.7% and 6.5%, respectively, compared with the conventional digital twin-based fault-tolerant controller, while maintaining robust performance under Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis. These results demonstrate that the proposed integration of TFT-CAL fault diagnosis, an LSTM-based Digital Twin, dual-source uncertainty estimation, and a severity-confidence adaptive predictive fault-tolerant control strategy provides an effective and reliable solution for improving the fault tolerance, robustness, and operational safety of autonomous underwater vehicles. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), enabled digital twins are emerging as a transformative paradigm for precision medicine, enabling dynamic, patient-specific modeling across clinical care, drug development, and population health. Digital twins provide computational representations of biological systems, while generative AI enhances their capacity for data synthesis, prediction, and simulation under uncertainty. Despite rapid technological progress, the clinical translation of these systems remains limited by challenges in validation, safety, interpretability, and regulatory oversight. In this work, we present a structured analysis of generative AI–powered digital twins in healthcare, spanning patient-level modeling, clinical trials, and preclinical drug discovery. Beyond reviewing existing applications, we introduce a clinical-grade evaluation framework encompassing validation strategies, uncertainty calibration, safety monitoring, and synthetic data governance. By articulating both opportunities and unresolved barriers, this study provides a roadmap for the responsible deployment of generative AI–enabled digital twins in precision medicine. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Machine learning for rarefied gas transport in vacuum and micro/nano systems: Demonstrated capabilities, deployment requirements, and a research roadmap
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, 01003, MA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Roohi E., Department of Mechanical and Industrial Engineering, University of Massachusetts Amherst, Amherst, 01003, MA, United States
Abstract: Machine learning (ML) now serves several distinct roles in rarefied-gas modeling. Learned components can be embedded in kinetic solvers, and surrogate models can distribute the cost of an expensive calculation over repeated queries. Fast forward models can support parameter inference from measurements. Published studies report complete-solver acceleration of a kinetic Fokker–Planck method, a reduction in the runtime of ab initio direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC), percent-level errors at withheld flow conditions, and improved accuracy near shocks through physics-based representations. These results establish useful capabilities within stated test ranges, although they do not support unrestricted extrapolation. This Perspective classifies these uses according to the reference solver, training data, physical constraints, deployment range, and online task. The classification covers deterministic kinetic methods, DSMC, particle Fokker–Planck solvers, moment methods, molecular and ab initio models, and free-molecular test-particle simulation. The article distinguishes kernel, complete-solver, and lifecycle costs and describes implementation paths for conductance design, Knudsen-pump optimization, gas–surface inference, and vacuum-system digital twins. It also proposes a benchmark manifest based on microchannel mass flow, Knudsen pumps, vacuum conductance, and 70-degree blunted-cone experiments. Reliable deployment requires physical constraints, evaluation that accounts for sampling noise, propagation of accommodation uncertainty, and comparison with experiments. Kinetic solvers therefore remain the source of physical structure and certification even when ML changes how often and where those solvers are used. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Interface authorization in flexible automated mine ventilation duct production lines is difficult because heterogeneous users and services access safety-critical resources under time-varying cyber-physical risk that static RBAC/ACL rules cannot capture. This study presents HGRAD, a heterogeneous-graph risk-adaptive access control framework for industrial cyber-physical systems. HGRAD models each access event as a dynamic graph with four node types: user nodes encode operator identity, role, and history; interface nodes represent exposed PLC/MES/service access points and protocol/load states; resource nodes denote commands, records, or work-order objects with different sensitivities; and physics-informed risk nodes provide conservative structural-risk proxies for critical resources. A Temporal-HGT encoder and relation-specific hierarchical attention capture temporal context, structural semantics, and abnormal-path salience, while an intervention-inspired log-based filter, adversarial perturbation, Shapley audit weighting, and MC-Dropout uncertainty estimation support adaptive authorization rather than fixed-threshold decisions. In the TON_IoT benchmark mapping, the physics-informed node is derived only from benchmark-log proxy signals, including access intensity, operation criticality, freshness, and resource criticality; it is not generated by real mine ventilation sensors, plant-side finite-element outputs, or field digital-twin measurements. HGRAD achieves the strongest validation and held-out benchmark performance among compared baselines. The results are therefore benchmark-level proof of concept for access-control design, not evidence of completed industrial deployment or field-validated mine-safety performance. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Digital twin-driven deep learning and multi-agent reinforcement learning for energy management of smart microgrids

Abstract: The increasing integration of electric vehicles (EVs) and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology introduces significant operational challenges in modern power systems, mainly due to the high uncertainty of renewable generation and rapidly varying demand profiles. Conventional energy management approaches are often based on simplified system models or centralized optimization schemes, which struggle to capture system dynamics in real time and scale effectively under highly stochastic and large-scale operating conditions. This paper proposes a unified framework that can simultaneously provide accurate prediction of uncertain resources, real-time system representation, and adaptive decentralized decision-making for large-scale EV coordination. In this regard, this paper proposes an integrated framework combining Digital Twin Technology (DTT), Deep Neural Networks (DNN), and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) for real-time EV charging and discharging optimization. This integration enables coordinated prediction, decision support, and distributed control within a data-driven framework, improving adaptability compared to conventional standalone approaches. Within this framework, EVs are dynamically adapted with uncertain resources enabling efficient local energy management in which a 22.3% reduction in operational cost and a 38% decrement in battery aging, compared to the Intelligent Battery Life Enhancement Method is achieved © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Temporal-digital twin-network enabled Out-of-Order synchronized control for production-intralogistics considering disturbance propagation

Abstract: Dualistic production and intralogistics (DPiL) have inherently intricate spatio-temporal coupling relationships. Meanwhile, the occurrence of disturbance propagation further amplifies such complexity, aggravating operation control difficulty. This novel problem is summarized as the dualistic production and intralogistics synchronized control problem (DPiLSynC) considering disturbance propagation. Traditional production planning and control (PPC) methods overlook the impact of disturbance propagation, significantly compromising system stability. Fortunately, digital twin (DT) technology promises rapid identification of disturbances by physical-virtual interaction. The adverse effects of disturbances may diffuse across the manufacturing system, causing operational disruptions. But analyzing the spatio-temporal characteristics of disturbance propagation is challenging due to the unclear connection-interaction mechanism of multiple DT models in manufacturing systems. This paper proposes a temporal-digital twin-network (T-DT-N) enabled Out-of-Order (OoO) synchronized control approach. Firstly, the modified OoO framework with disturbance propagation analysis is designed to reconstruct the operation logic of DPiL. Secondly, T-DT-N is developed to reveal the spatio-temporal evolution patterns of disturbance propagation by introducing the temporal network to model connection-interaction relationships of DT models. Thirdly, OoO synchronized control using propagation analysis results is proposed, involving three distinct control phases, each considering multiple factors aiming to achieve resilient DPiL operation. Computation results indicate this approach achieves shorter order makespan, shopfloor throughput time, and waiting time, while decreasing the percentage tardy. Furthermore, it exhibits stability across varying queue lengths and uncertain levels, thereby validating its application in a dynamic environment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), as core devices for hydrogen energy utilization, play an increasingly strategic role in transportation electrification, distributed power generation, and large-scale energy storage. However, the inherent strong multi-physics coupling, complex nonlinear degradation, and high sensitivity to operating conditions of PEMFC impose significant challenges on its cost, durability, and efficiency. Machine learning (ML) provides new opportunities to address these challenges and accelerate intelligent PEMFC development. This review examines ML applications across the full lifetime of PEMFCs, covering material design, manufacturing and quality control, system state management and control, and digital twin (DT) development. Beyond summarizing recent progress, it critically compares ML approaches in terms of data requirements, interpretability, computational cost, robustness, generalization, and uncertainty quantification, while highlighting emerging physics-informed ML, hybrid physics-data-driven models, self-adaptive DTs, and deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Three major challenges are identified: (1) data scarcity, heterogeneity, and insufficient standardization; (2) limited physical consistency, interpretability, generalization, and uncertainty quantification; and (3) computational, real-time, and safe-deployment requirements. Overall, integrating data, physical knowledge, and intelligent decision-making can advance ML-enabled PEMFCs from isolated prediction and optimization toward reliable, adaptive, and full-lifetime intelligent operation. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Twin-Branch Probabilistic Stress Estimator (TB-PSE): A digital twin approach for large-scale structural static responses analysis
Affiliations: State Key Laboratory for Manufacturing and Systems Engineering, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an, 710049, China; Department of Energy, Polytechnic University of Milan, Milan, 20156, Italy; MINES Paris-PSL, CRC, Sophia Antipolis, France

Abstract: Digital twin technology enables real-time monitoring and predictive analysis of complex structural systems. However, traditional finite element analysis (FEA) remains computationally expensive for real-time applications, while existing deterministic machine learning models often lack robust uncertainty quantification. This paper presents a Twin-Branch Probabilistic Stress Estimator (TB-PSE) specifically designed for digital twin-enabled large-scale structural static responses analysis, with application to liquid rocket engine frame static testing. The TB-PSE architecture employs a dual-branch neural network structure in which each branch utilizes multi-layer residual connections to independently predict the mean and standard deviation of stress distributions across all structural nodes. By formulating stress prediction as a probabilistic process rather than deterministic estimation, the proposed method captures inherent uncertainties in structural response and provides confidence intervals for critical stress assessments. Experimental validation conducted on a 24-step static test of rocket engine frame structures demonstrates that TB-PSE improves stress-field estimation accuracy while providing uncertainty information for risk-informed assessment of safety–critical aerospace structures. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Authors: Qiu C.; Zhou W.; Yang L.; Peng Y.; Wang K.
Title: Closed-loop intelligent quality control for robotic welding: A survey on architecture, technologies, and system integration
Affiliations: School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China
Authors with affiliations: Qiu C., School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Zhou W., School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Yang L., School of Automation, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Peng Y., School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China; Wang K., School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing University of Science and Technology, Nanjing, China
Abstract: Weld quality formation involves strong multi-physics coupling under multiple sources of uncertainty. The conventional open-loop paradigm—pre-set parameters followed by post-weld inspection—therefore cannot deliver timely in-process intervention. Recent advances in multi-modal sensing, deep learning, advanced control, and digital twins have made closed-loop quality control technically feasible, yet integrating these isolated technologies into an end-to-end system remains a major challenge. Existing reviews predominantly address single functional layers and lack systematic analysis of cross-layer integration, engineering maturity, and fair evaluation protocols. We propose a unified analytical framework for robotic arc welding: a five-layer closed-loop architecture (Perception–Modeling–Decision–Execution–Assessment) coupled with three nested feedback loops (fast/medium/slow). We then review key technologies across all layers in a concept-centric manner: multi-modal sensing organized by physical observables and fusion hierarchy; physics-driven, data-driven, and hybrid modeling with trade-off analysis; hierarchical control from PID through MPC, ADRC, and reinforcement learning; and assessment covering inspection, diagnostics, and knowledge feedback. A Technology Readiness Level (TRL) assessment of over 40 technologies yields a maturity matrix with a pronounced “ends-high, middle-low” pattern. Inter-layer interface analysis exposes a critical asymmetry: the forward path from perception to execution is largely established, whereas the backward knowledge path from assessment to modeling/decision remains severely fragmented. Finally, we identify common pitfalls in method comparison and propose a two-tier comparison framework with a minimum reporting standard. We lay out a systematic roadmap for moving robotic welding from isolated single-layer demonstrations toward deployable and evolvable industrial closed-loop systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Abstract: Accurate prediction and risk assessment of time-varying wall deflection during staged braced excavations remain challenging due to evolving system behavior and multiple sources of uncertainty. To address this issue, an evidence-optimized physics-informed digital twin framework is developed for stage-wise probabilistic prediction, sequential Bayesian updating and risk assessment. A high-fidelity finite element model is employed as the physics-based baseline to generate training data for a sparse Gaussian process regression surrogate. Physically interpretable composite kernel structures are designed to encode covariance assumptions for the coupled effects of soil parameters, wall depth, and excavation stage, and are ranked using Bayesian model evidence. The resulting surrogate balances predictive accuracy, model parsimony, and physical interpretability. During the online phase, monitoring data are assimilated stage by stage to update selected soil parameters and depth-dependent discrepancy terms, while posterior predictive distributions are used to quantify uncertainty. The proposed framework is validated through two representative braced excavation cases: the Taipei National Enterprise Center excavation and the launching shaft of the Wuhu Yangtze River-Crossing Tunnel. Results show that sequential data assimilation drives progressive posterior contraction of key parameters and improves the agreement between predicted and measured wall-deflection profiles. The posterior distribution of maximum wall deflection is further transformed into exceedance probabilities and stage-wise risk levels, enabling posterior predictive risk inference during excavation. Through evidence-supported selection of physically interpretable kernel structures, the proposed framework provides a closed-loop digital twin for probabilistic prediction, risk assessment, and early warning in staged braced excavations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Training LLMs with Reinforcement Learning over Digital Twin Representations for Reasoning-Intensive Surgical VideoQA
Affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States
Authors with affiliations: Shen Y., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States; Zhang H., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States; Unberath M., Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, United States
Abstract: Surgical video question answering requires multi-step reasoning across semantic, spatial, and temporal dimensions. Existing methods architecturally compress videos into discrete token representations and couple visual perception with reasoning. This approach fragments continuous spatial-temporal relationships and has been shown to restrict multi-step reasoning capabilities. We introduce a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that trains large language models (LLMs) to decouple perception from reasoning by operating over digital twin representations constructed from surgical foundation models. Additionally, we introduce hierarchical representations across frame, temporal window, and procedure levels with probabilistic uncertainty estimates. Finally, we propose a novel reward that combines format validation with accuracy assessment through clinical plausibility evaluation and uncertainty-aware calibration for training. To demonstrate the capabilities of this approach, we introduce REAL-Colon-Reason, a colonoscopic benchmark with 2000 question-answer pairs across three complexity levels. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on REAL-Colon-Reason and two existing surgical VideoQA benchmarks REAL-Colon-VQA and EndoVis18-VQA. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Digital twin-in-the-loop energy management for grid-edge flexibility in electrified residential buildings
Affiliations: SWTCH Energy Inc., Toronto, Canada; School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Canada
Authors with affiliations: Tai C., SWTCH Energy Inc., Toronto, Canada; Guo J., SWTCH Energy Inc., Toronto, Canada; Li C., SWTCH Energy Inc., Toronto, Canada; Fattahi J., School of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Ottawa, Ottawa, Canada
Abstract: We present an integrated framework for coordinating residential electrified loads in multi-unit residential buildings (MURBs) using heat-pump digital twins in the loop (DTiL), reinforcement learning (RL), and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization (DRO). The framework is designed to support MURBs as flexible grid-edge resources under uncertain and stressed operating conditions, including weather-driven demand variability. The heat-pump DTiL combines a reduced-order thermal balance, a coefficient-of-performance (COP) power map, and a learned disturbance channel and is synchronized with streaming telemetry through an event-aware observer to produce horizon forecasts of heat-pump electrical demand. These local short-horizon predictions are used alongside an RL policy that proposes EVSE charging schedules, after which a tractable convex DRO reformulation is used to obtain schedules that remain feasible under uncertainty in non-EV demand and EV availability while satisfying sub-feeder and main-panel ampacity limits. The DTiL framework couples online demand prediction with robust schedule correction, allowing the controller to adapt to time-varying building conditions without relying solely on nominal forecasts. Experiments quantify DT prediction accuracy, robust scheduling feasibility, and reliability–utilization trade-offs under weather-sensitive load variation. In an 8-unit residential pilot, the approach achieved electrical-power error of 35.9-45.3 W and scheduling efficiency of 91% across robustness settings. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Risk-informed design of methane sensor networks using a prescriptive digital twin approach

Abstract: This study presents a prescriptive digital twin framework for the optimal design of methane sensor networks in industrial facilities under uncertain operating conditions. The proposed approach integrates high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics simulations, artificial neural network-based surrogate modeling, Bayesian probabilistic inference, and multi-objective optimization to support severity-weighted risk-informed decision-making. CFD simulations are used to generate detailed methane dispersion data under varying leak scenarios and environmental conditions, capturing the effects of facility geometry, wind dynamics, and turbulence. An ANN surrogate model is developed to provide rapid prediction of key performance metrics, including methane concentration and time-to-detection. Uncertainty in leak characteristics and atmospheric conditions is explicitly modeled and updated using Bayesian inference through an ensemble Kalman Filter, enabling continuous refinement of predictions. The sensor placement problem is formulated as a constrained multi-objective optimization problem and solved using the NSGA-II algorithm to identify Pareto-optimal configurations that balance detection probability, response time, deployment cost, and severity-weighted risk. The results show that methane dispersion is strongly influenced by flow structures such as recirculation zones and high-velocity corridors, which significantly affect detection performance. The proposed framework achieves a higher detection probability (up to ∼96–97%) and a reduced time-to-detection compared to uniform and heuristic placement strategies under equal cost conditions. Moreover, severity-weighted risk analysis identifies high-risk leak scenarios and hazardous regions, while Bayesian updating improves robustness, reduces prediction uncertainty, and enables adaptive risk-informed sensor placement. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: Toward trustworthy and explainable AI-driven industrial fault diagnosis: A data-to-deployment review

Abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis has achieved high benchmark accuracy, yet performance often deteriorates across machines, operating regimes, sensors, and time. This structured narrative review examines the literature through three connected concerns: the credibility of diagnostic evidence, the suitability and transferability of learning methods, and the assurance needed for industrial use. The reviewed evidence indicates that data leakage, class imbalance, sensor instability, and untested domain shift can make complex models appear more reliable than they are. Traditional machine learning remains valuable when physically meaningful features are stable and labeled data are limited. Deep learning is more suitable for complex raw, sequential, image, or multimodal signals, while transfer learning is useful only when source-target compatibility and negative transfer are evaluated. Explainability can support model checking and maintenance decisions, but explanations also require validation for fidelity, stability, physical plausibility, and usefulness to engineers. The literature further supports a staged route to deployment, progressing from independent validation and shadow operation to advisory use, bounded automation, and gradual fleet integration. Near-term research priorities should strengthen independent validation, uncertainty calibration, efficient edge deployment, and human evaluation. Long-term opportunities include safe lifelong adaptation, reliable fleet-level learning, validated digital twins, and human-centered automation. Overall, trustworthy fault diagnosis should be assessed across the full diagnostic lifecycle rather than inferred from benchmark accuracy alone. © 2026 The Author(s).

Title: Low-head pumped hydro energy storage for inverter-dominated power systems: Post-2022 advances in contra-rotating turbomachinery, offshore deployment and grid-supportive control
Affiliations: Department of Electrical Engineering, Universitas Brawijaya, Malang, 65145, Indonesia; Hangzhou Regional Center (Asia-Pacific) for Small Hydro Power (HRC), Hangzhou, 310012, China; Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, Auburn University, 36849, AL, United States

Abstract: The rapid expansion of inverter-based renewable generation intensifies the need for long-duration energy storage capable of delivering both energy shifting and verifiable ancillary services. Low-head pumped hydro storage (LH-PHS) broadens pumped-storage deployment to lowland, coastal, offshore, and constrained sites, but its feasibility depends on high-flow hydraulic design, transient-safe operation, and power-electronic control. The evidence base comprises 103 sources, including 59 references added beyond the original 44-source seed set; 56 of these additions are dated 2021–2026. Four findings emerge. First, within the expanded coded post-2022 turbomachinery, performance-prediction, and transient subset, contra-rotating reversible pump-turbines (CR-RPTs) represent 10 of 29 studies (34%), while conventional and variable-speed pump-as-turbine (PAT) and other single-runner pathways account for 16 studies (55%); CR-RPTs are therefore best viewed as a specialized high-control-authority option rather than a universal dominant pathway. Second, commercial PATs offer lower cost and wider availability, and recent variable-speed models report prediction errors generally within 10% across broad speed-ratio ranges, although reliable head-flow-efficiency mapping under off-design conditions remains difficult. Third, CR-RPT experiments report peak hydraulic efficiencies of approximately 86–92%, offshore/coastal concepts report round-trip efficiencies above 70–72%, and grid-service-oriented control has achieved full-reserve activation rise times below 3.92 s in turbine mode and 0.23 s in pump mode. Fourth, neural networks, support vector regression, reduced-order models, and digital twins are emerging as computationally efficient surrogates for performance prediction, monitoring, and control, but their transferability, uncertainty, and physical interpretability remain limitations. LH-PHS is consequently best understood as an adaptive co-design problem linking hydraulic stability, machine selection, converter/control architecture, multi-timescale scheduling, lifecycle impacts, and stakeholder acceptance. Explicit grid-forming LH-PHS demonstrations remain largely absent. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies.

Abstract: Ecological substrates have emerged as multifunctional slope protection materials with dual engineering stability and ecological restoration benefits, yet their large-scale and long-term application remains constrained in harsh slope environments characterized by steep terrain, arid climates, freeze–thaw cycles, and severe land degradation. The complex coupling of hydromechanical and biological processes in extreme field conditions leads to insufficient systematic understanding of the optimal design criteria and in-situ performance evolution of ecological substrates, restricting their reliable engineering promotion.This critical review comprehensively synthesizes recent advances in ecological substrates from the perspectives of material composition, functional mechanisms, design principles, construction technologies, maintenance strategies, and performance evaluation, with an explicit focus on surface soil erosion and erosion-induced shallow landslides. Particular attention is given to the coupled physical–chemical–biological processes governing substrate behavior and the interactions among substrate properties, vegetation development, and environmental stressors. Based on the existing literature, an integrated framework is proposed to link material design, ecological adaptation, hydrological regulation, monitoring, and long-term performance assessment. The review identifies four major challenges that currently limit the broader application of ecological substrates in harsh environments, including insufficient understanding of early-stage performance, incomplete knowledge of hydro–mechanical–biological coupling, uncertainty in long-term root–substrate evolution, and limitations of existing life-cycle assessment approaches. Future research priorities include the development of low-carbon and bio-based materials, mechanistic studies across multiple scales, intelligent design and digital twin technologies, standardized databases and evaluation systems, and policy support for green infrastructure. These advances are expected to promote the transition from empirical design toward more predictive and sustainable vegetated slope protection. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Digital twins and physics-informed machine learning for safe agro-industrial waste valorization: Bioactive recovery, food-grade standardization, and regulatory readiness
Source title: Trends in Food Science and Technology
Affiliations: Bioprocessing Laboratory, Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural Areas, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, 400076, India
Authors with affiliations: Sahu C.K., Bioprocessing Laboratory, Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural Areas, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, 400076, India; Arora A., Bioprocessing Laboratory, Centre for Technology Alternatives for Rural Areas, Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, 400076, India
Abstract: Background: Agro-industrial residues are promising sources of phenolics, pigments, polysaccharides, proteins, and other functional ingredients, but food-grade valorization remains constrained by feedstock heterogeneity, sensor uncertainty, empirical scale-up, solvent and energy burdens, and contaminant co-extraction. Scope and approach: This review critically evaluates digital twins and physics-informed machine learning (PIML) as a safety-bounded framework for residue valorization. It examines process analytical technology, laboratory assays, soft sensors, unit-operation models, model predictive control, techno-economic assessment, life-cycle assessment, and regulatory audit trails. Particular emphasis is placed on coupling target-bioactive recovery with the transport and concentration of pesticides, mycotoxins, metals, residual solvents, and process impurities. Key findings and conclusions: PIML can embed transport, reaction, rheological, and degradation constraints into learning architectures, thereby improving extrapolation from sparse and drifting food-process datasets. Digital twins can extend these models into synchronized cyber-physical systems that optimize recovery while enforcing calibrated uncertainty, contaminant boundaries, explainability, traceability, and dossier-ready comparability for EFSA Novel Food, FDA GRAS, Codex, and related pathways. Persistent barriers include sensor fouling, calibration drift, missing benchmark datasets, computational latency, interoperability gaps, and limited toxicological validation. A staged maturity roadmap is proposed, from data shadows to qualified autonomous twins. An updated search through 6 June 2026 identified adjacent reviews, but no publicly indexed source jointly formalized PIML-constrained unit-operation twins, coupled bioactive-hazard states, uncertainty-bounded release invariants, and regulatory comparability. However, DT/PIML should be implemented as staged, risk-based decision-support systems, not universal replacements for conventional optimization, because scale-transfer uncertainty, rare-event coverage, and computational burden determine whether industrial use is justified. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: A data-driven dynamic Bayesian network for health monitoring and maintenance decision support of marine diesel engines

Abstract: Performance monitoring and maintenance decision-making are critical components of machinery management for ensuring the safety, reliability, and operational efficiency of maritime systems. Recent advances in sensor technologies, data transmission capabilities, machine learning, and knowledge management have accelerated the transition from traditional fixed-interval maintenance towards condition-based and predictive maintenance strategies in the maritime industry. However, the health assessment of large two-stroke marine diesel engines remains challenging due to the presence of multiple interdependent operational parameters and their temporal uncertainties under varying sea and operational conditions. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel data-driven Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) framework for the health monitoring and maintenance decision support of large two-stroke marine diesel engines. The proposed framework integrates 15 operational parameters within a unified probabilistic model to capture temporal degradation and quantify health uncertainty through dynamic probabilistic reasoning. The framework was validated using operational data from a six-cylinder MAN B&W 6S50MC-C main engine. A five-day case study showed that cylinders 4 and 6 remained in the AMBER health state, while cylinder 5 was predicted to deteriorate from GREEN to AMBER after two days of operation, demonstrating the model's capability to predict health degradation trends. Sensitivity analysis identified Total Base Number (TBN) and iron content as the most influential indicators affecting engine health. Furthermore, water mist catcher performance, fuel viscosity, and exhaust temperature deviation exhibited the largest temporal variations, with average deviations of 4.31%, 3.91%, and 3.37%, respectively. The results demonstrate that the proposed DBN framework effectively captures temporal dependencies and operational uncertainty, enabling dynamic health assessment and risk-informed maintenance decision-making. By integrating multiple interdependent degradation factors within a unified probabilistic framework, the proposed approach provides an effective tool for condition-based maintenance and establishes a practical foundation for future maritime digital twin and intelligent maintenance applications. Abstract: Underground hydrogen storage is increasingly positioned as a long-duration flexibility option for renewable-dominated energy systems. Dependable deployment, however, is constrained by coupled uncertainties spanning multiphase flow, pore-scale interfacial physics, reactive transport, and potential microbiological effects. To improve the applicability and generalisability of physics-informed artificial intelligence for underground hydrogen storage, we conducted a PRISMA 2020 systematic literature review of studies published from 2020 to 2026. The Scopus and Google Scholar searches retrieved 1071 records. After deduplication, 872 unique records remained, and 676 full texts were assessed for eligibility. From these, 51 primary studies relevant to PI-AI for UHS were retained for synthesis after an evidence-quality appraisal gate, comprising 49 UHS-explicit studies and 2 methodologically adjacent studies, retained for transferable PI-AI insights. We examined the complexity of applying physics-informed learning across pore-to-field scales and how this complexity contributes to barriers to transferability, reproducibility, and decision readiness. Specifically, we synthesised evidence across five themes: pore-scale interfacial physics; reactive transport, sorption, and biogeochemistry; reservoir-scale surrogate architectures; uncertainty and data assimilation readiness; and multi-objective design and operational optimisation. Each study was also coded by task, model family, uncertainty practice, and validation strength. Only 9 of the 51 included studies (17.6%) reported predictive intervals or distributions consistent with quantified predictive uncertainty (UQ-A), and just one of these reported fully calibrated empirical-coverage checks, identifying uncertainty quantification as the most consequential evidence gap in the reviewed corpus. Title: Dataset on the reproducibility of UHPC mechanical properties under a fixed recipe with controlled production variability
Affiliations: Department of Measurement and Control Engineering, University of Kassel, Kassel, Germany; QuantumFusion GmbH, Kassel, Germany; MAITERIA UG, Kassel, Germany
Authors with affiliations: Rezazadeh F., Department of Measurement and Control Engineering, University of Kassel, Kassel, Germany; Abrishambaf A., QuantumFusion GmbH, Kassel, Germany; Zimmermann G., MAITERIA UG, Kassel, Germany; Kroll A., Department of Measurement and Control Engineering, University of Kassel, Kassel, Germany
Abstract: A dataset was collected to investigate the reproducibility of ultra-high performance concrete (UHPC) quality under controlled variability, since UHPC mechanical properties can vary even when using a fixed mix formulation in production. This dataset is the first open-access dataset in the UHPC community to take a holistic view of the UHPC production process and associated production variability, featuring a relatively large number of systematically designed experiments under a fixed recipe. A reference UHPC recipe, designed for a 28-day compressive strength of 120 MPa, was used to produce 150 experimental records, while the quality, storage conditions, and dosing accuracy of raw materials, along with mixing parameters and curing conditions, were systematically varied to emulate real-world production environments. For each batch, five fresh UHPC properties and the average mixer power were recorded, and compressive and flexural strengths at 24 hours and at 28 days were measured using standardized methods under controlled laboratory conditions. By linking process variability to mechanical outcomes under the fixed reference recipe, the dataset supports reproducibility analysis in UHPC production and provides reusable data for machine learning, uncertainty modeling, and digital-twin development. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: A Hybrid physics-informed digital twin for offshore wind-farm flow prediction: integrating CFD simulations with deep regression forest and probabilistic surrogate models
Source title: Journal of Engineering and Applied Science
Affiliations: Department of Smart O & M and IoT, Nantong Institute of Technology, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China; Nantong Huarong Construction Group Co., Ltd, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China
Authors with affiliations: Wu X., Department of Smart O & M and IoT, Nantong Institute of Technology, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China; Yin L., Nantong Huarong Construction Group Co., Ltd, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China; He T., Department of Smart O & M and IoT, Nantong Institute of Technology, Jiangsu, Nantong, 226002, China
Abstract: The marine-atmosphere dynamics are nonlinear and multiscale, which poses a computational challenge for accurately describing the flow field around offshore wind turbines. Using advanced data-driven surrogate models and CFD simulations, this study presents a hybrid physics-informed digital twin framework to predict wind farm behavior under stochastic environmental conditions with high accuracy. In this work, we propose a framework that simultaneously integrates spatiotemporal dependencies, physical constraints, and probabilistic uncertainties by combining Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), Deep-Gaussian Process Regression (Deep-GPR), Extreme Gradient Boosting Algorithm (XGBoost), and a transformer-based regression model called CFD-Former. PINNs incorporate Navier–Stokes equation residuals into the training process to ensure physical consistency, while XGBoost and Deep-GPR improve model generalizability to different inlet flow conditions. Hybrid surrogate models are trained on data from CFD calculations with different wind direction and speed conditions. The generated digital twin is able to predict the velocities measured at the meteorological tower within an uncertainty of 10% and reproduce the high resolution flow patterns due to CFD with a mean absolute deviation below 1%. This novel approach uses deterministic simulation and intelligent inference to predict offshore wind farm performance in a scalable and physically based manner, possibly enabling adaptive operation and reliability assessment. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: A digital twin approach for aircraft fatigue crack prediction considering overload retardation effect
Affiliations: College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; College of Civil Aviation, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China
Authors with affiliations: Zhang H., College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; Li W., College of Civil Aviation, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; Li Y., College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China; Li H., College of Aerospace Engineering, Nanjing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Nanjing, 210016, China
Abstract: Aircraft structures endure variable flight loads and environmental conditions that promote fatigue-crack initiation and propagation at critical locations, thereby threatening structural reliability. Accurate crack-growth prediction is challenged not only by uncertainties in material properties and load histories but also by overload retardation, in which an overload-induced plastic zone temporarily reduces the subsequent crack-growth rate. To address these challenges, this paper develops a digital-twin framework named DPUP, which integrates Data, Physics, Uncertainty, and Prediction modules to enable real-time tracking and prognosis of fatigue cracks under overloads. Specifically, the Data module collects and processes flight-load data, physical-test data, and inspection data; the Physics module incorporates global-local multiscale finite-element modeling with three-dimensional M-integral analysis to obtain crack length dependent stress-intensity factors, and then couples the NASGRO model with the Modified Generalized Willenborg model to capture overload retardation effects; the Uncertainty module characterizes variability in fatigue crack-growth parameters and the overload factor, while the Prediction module assimilates crack-inspection observations through a particle filter to dynamically update the crack state and uncertain parameters. The DPUP framework is validated using fatigue crack-growth data from a 2024-T3 aluminum-alloy lower-wing-skin specimen subjected to TWIST spectra truncated at Levels I and III. Results show that the NASGRO-MGW model captures spectrum-dependent overload retardation, while particle-filter assimilation progressively improves crack-growth predictions and updates the uncertain material and overload parameters. Overall, the DPUP framework provides a physically interpretable approach for aircraft-specific crack-growth tracking under variable-amplitude loading and offers a practical basis for remaining-life assessment, adaptive inspection planning, maintenance decision-making, and mission planning. © 2026 Elsevier Masson SAS.

Title: Uncertainty-aware digital twins for safe operation and active fault-tolerance in degrading heterogeneous pumping systems

Abstract: Conventional deterministic controls often fail in fluid systems under mechanical degradation due to epistemic uncertainties, leading to constraint violations. While passive fault diagnosis has advanced, autonomous risk-averse decision-making post-degradation remains lacking. To bridge this gap, this study proposes an Adaptive Probabilistic Digital Twin (APDT) framework. Utilizing Uncertainty Quantification (UQ), the APDT establishes mathematical guardrails based on the Probability of Feasibility, actively preventing physical boundary violations under deep uncertainties. Furthermore, the framework dynamically reconstructs system mappings online to adapt to non-stationary asymmetrical degradation, overcoming the limitations of static models. An embedded Trust-Region mechanism ensures smooth state transitions by preventing actuator fatigue. Crucially, trajectory analysis reveals an emergent “strategic offloading” behavior: the APDT autonomously shifts operational loads from degraded to healthy units. This acts as an active fault-tolerant mechanism, mitigating stress on deteriorating components to prevent sudden failures while maintaining robust output. Ultimately, the APDT offers a reliable, physics-compliant paradigm for the active safety management and life-extension of cyber-physical systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Toward quality-assured intelligent welding processes for aerospace structures: From process monitoring to digital closed-loop manufacturing

Abstract: Aerospace welding is moving beyond preset-parameter automation toward process-integrated quality assurance. In this setting, material response, process observability, adaptive action, and traceable evidence must operate as coordinated functions rather than as separate technologies. This review applies a reproducible structured search covering January 2000 to July 2026, supplemented by earlier landmark sources, and classifies the literature as direct aerospace demonstration, transferable non-aerospace evidence, or conceptual enabling technology. High-strength aluminum alloys, titanium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, thermoplastic composites, and dissimilar joints are examined alongside friction stir, high-energy-beam, hybrid, and composite welding routes. The analysis then addresses one-, two-, and three-dimensional sensing, multimodal spatiotemporal alignment, defect and performance prediction, adaptive control, and digital-twin architectures. Evidence is comparatively mature for local sensing, defect recognition, and offline optimization. By contrast, validation remains limited for out-of-distribution reliability, physics-constrained transfer across materials and processes, millisecond-scale virtual-real closure, and certification-grade links between process signatures and residual strength or fatigue life. The proposed roadmap assigns high-fidelity models to offline learning and validation, reduced-order or surrogate models to online state estimation, and uncertainty-aware decisions to auditable safety limits. This synthesis defines the conditions required for intelligent welding to progress toward deployable, quality-assured closed-loop manufacturing of aerospace structures. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of The Society of Manufacturing Engineers.

Title: An Edge-First Digital Twin–Driven Cyber–Physical Home System for Resilient Aging-in-Place
Affiliations: School of Urban Construction Engineering, Chongqing Technology and Business Institute, Chongqing, 400085, China
Authors with affiliations: Wang Z., School of Urban Construction Engineering, Chongqing Technology and Business Institute, Chongqing, 400085, China; Hu X., School of Urban Construction Engineering, Chongqing Technology and Business Institute, Chongqing, 400085, China
Abstract: Aging-in-Place monitoring in small, high-density apartments faces three persistent engineering constraints: severe occlusions, strict privacy requirements, and unstable home networks. Under these conditions, cloud-centered closed-loop schemes become unreliable, while alerts are often difficult to verify. To address these issues, this paper proposes an Edge-First Digital Twin-based Cyber-Physical Home System (DT-CPHS), in which uplink semantic synchronization is explicitly decoupled from downlink local control. The system uploads only low-dimensional semantic state vectors and evidence metadata, while alert auditing and replay are supported through an event-sourced Twin Event Log. To improve robustness under occlusion and conflicting sensor indications, DT-CPHS adopts decision-level multi-source fusion based on Dempster–Shafer evidence theory. In parallel, a connectivity-aware local rule engine provides deterministic offline fallback, together with hysteresis-based anti-flapping and seq-based backfill for consistency maintenance. A full-stack prototype was implemented in a real apartment using non-intrusive heterogeneous sensing (mmWave radars, wearable, PIR/door sensors) and a low-cost gateway (Raspberry Pi 4) with HA/Node-RED/MQTT. Experimental results validate four engineering goals. First, for offline survivability, local safety actions maintained 100% availability during WAN outages with bounded latency (Offline median 276 ms, P95 358 ms), whereas Online mode showed a pronounced long tail (median 734 ms, P95 1452 ms, max 1.87 s). Second, for occlusion robustness, the proposed fusion achieved 95.0% recall under heavy occlusion (vs. 60.0% for radar-only), and 95.6% overall recall across 180 fall trials. Third, for false-alarm control, continuous monitoring under frozen thresholds yielded 0.67 FP/day over 72 h (1/0/1 across three days). Fourth, for deployability and efficiency, semantic synchronization remained at the KB/s level (mean 4.2 KB/s, P95 12.6 KB/s), while 72-h profiling showed stable overhead (CPU P95 ≈ 25%, memory drift ≈ + 0.15 MB/h). In addition, a preliminary usability pilot (N = 8) suggests that evidence-chain explanations reduce caregiver decision time (8.9 → 3.1 s) and improve trust (2.8 → 4.3). These results indicate that DT-CPHS provides a practical path toward resilient, privacy-aware, and explainable home monitoring under compact in-home deployment constraints. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Abstract: Electric vehicles are crucial in the transition to sustainable transportation. Specifically, in the coming years, the number of electric trucks is expected to increase significantly due to regulations and an anticipated lower total cost of ownership (TCO). As a result, electric truck adoption is growing, bringing challenges to fleet managers due to range limits and uncertain energy usage. This work introduces an AI-powered Digital Twin (DT) framework, TwinERGY, to predict the energy consumption for battery-electric trucks at the pre- and intra-trip stages. Three sequence-to-sequence models are compared for the pre-trip scenario to determine trip-level energy consumption. We utilize a conditional diffusion model for real-time probabilistic estimation of power and time elapsed, initialized on the pre-trip model’s output and conditioned on historical intra-trip inputs. Combined with the pre-trip model’s output using Bayesian fusion, it aims to reduce end-trip energy consumption estimation uncertainty with every lapsing segment. The results show that the framework can aid in reducing uncertainty and contribute to more confident decision making during fleet management. Going a step ahead, we also provide explanations of the obtained results, uncovering the important features affecting energy consumption. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Physics-informed large models for wind and solar forecasting: A carbon-aware framework for decarbonized power systems

Abstract: The large-scale integration of wind and solar power is essential for power-sector decarbonization, but their variability creates persistent challenges for forecasting, reserve allocation, storage scheduling, curtailment, and emission-aware operation. This review synthesizes recent advances in statistical, deep-learning, transformer, foundation-model, probabilistic, and physics-informed renewable forecasting, with emphasis on physical consistency, uncertainty, computational requirements, real-time applicability, and system-level operational value. We propose the Physics-Informed Large Model Carbon-Aware (PILM-CA) framework, a conceptual architecture linking physical renewable dynamics, physics-informed large-model forecasting, grid-operational decision support, and carbon-aware optimization. Unlike accuracy-centric forecasting frameworks, PILM-CA explicitly represents the pathway through which forecast uncertainty can affect commitment, reserves, storage, fossil backup, curtailment, and consequent carbon intensity. Published evidence indicates that these effects are system-dependent rather than universal; therefore, the framework distinguishes evidence-supported components from conceptual cross-layer relationships requiring operational validation. Probabilistic forecasting metrics, extreme-event resilience, digital-twin deployment, technology readiness, and climate adaptation are also critically examined. The review identifies research priorities for scalable, physically coherent, uncertainty-aware forecasting that supports both decarbonization and resilience in high-renewable power systems. © 2026 The Authors

Abstract: This study presents an automated 3D scan-to-model framework for historic buildings using point cloud data. An enhanced PointNet++ architecture enables component-level semantic segmentation and progressive surface segmentation. Geometric fitting couples RANSAC with NURBS to preserve surface continuity and achieve high-fidelity modeling of complex timber components without template libraries. To ensure interpretability and reliability, an integrated accuracy–uncertainty scheme is introduced, applying residual statistics and Jacobian-based covariance propagation to quantify residual distributions between point clouds and fitted surfaces, as well as uncertainty in normal orientations. Experiments on a representative Tibetan historic timber structure demonstrate millimeter-level geometric accuracy and yield error maps and uncertainty indices. The framework delivers geometric fidelity and completeness of detail, and provides a unified basis for accuracy and reliability verification, thereby supporting HBIM integration, structural assessment, and future digital twin development for heritage conservation. Title: Spatial–temporal event compiler: Look-around reasoning for uncertainty-aware synchronization in digital twin-driven manufacturing systems

Abstract: Personalized production is widely adopted in discrete manufacturing due to its ability to meet diverse customer requirements through flexible combinations of components. However, it also poses significant challenges to production synchronization, which requires all necessary operators, tools, materials, and industrial robots to be available within the prescribed time and space. In complex multi-stage manufacturing processes, execution deviations can accumulate into operation-level uncertainty, namely the risk that an operation cannot start, proceed, or finish as scheduled because the required resources and execution conditions are no longer aligned. Such uncertainty undermines resource utilization and may trigger cascading delays across the entire process. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a spatial–temporal event compiler (STEC) framework comprising digital, knowledge, and reasoning engines for compiling and analyzing manufacturing events. Specifically, the state information of digital models is compiled into a spatial–temporal event graph, which is continuously updated through a multi-clock alignment scheme that aligns distinct planning, scheduling, and execution time scales. Within the reasoning engine, a look-around reasoning approach is developed to capture historical consistency, the current execution context, and near-future evolution trends by integrating look-backward, look-present, and look-forward perspectives, thereby enabling uncertainty assessment. Furthermore, an LLM-based synchronization mechanism is incorporated into the framework to provide status reports through multi-turn interactions, allowing managers to query the current execution status and assess potential downstream impacts for timely intervention. Finally, a case study demonstrates that STEC improves the accuracy and stability of uncertainty identification. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Generative adversarial networks with Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification for structural health monitoring: Fibre Bragg grating data augmentation comparison in Hawk T1A aircraft
Affiliations: Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Authors with affiliations: Peiro A., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom; Impraimakis M., Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Bath, Bath, BA2 7AY, United Kingdom
Abstract: The signal generation capabilities of a novel data augmentation framework are examined in aerospace structures. First, the framework learns class-conditional temporal and spectral characteristics of the measured structural responses. It uses conditional generative adversarial network training and Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty quantification as a Bayesian approximation. This step enables stochastic signal synthesis and uncertainty quantification. Second, the generated responses are rigorously compared against experimental measurements across time, frequency, uncertainty, variability, and feature domains to assess physical realism, statistical consistency, and distributional fidelity. Finally, the synthetic data are evaluated to determine whether they should be incorporated into a supervised damage classification workflow. The framework is validated on the full-scale benchmark dataset from a BAE Systems Hawk T1A aircraft tested at the University of Sheffield’s Structural Dynamics Laboratory for Verification and Validation. The test involves acceleration, fibre Bragg grating strain, and nonlinear dynamic response measurements. The results demonstrate that the model accurately captures dominant structural dynamics, it guides on signal use for classification improvement based on uncertainty characteristics, and it provides meaningful uncertainty estimates linked to signal complexity and excitation characteristics. Importantly, the framework offers a realistic generative modelling plan as a robust digital twin component for data-driven structural health monitoring, supporting resilient decision-making for condition assessment in safety-critical aerospace systems. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: This paper presents the application of a generalized Active Disturbance Rejection Control (GADRC) framework applied to an electric flow heater model as a representative heat source process. The proposed approach incorporates partial process knowledge into both the control law and the Extended State Observer (ESO). In contrast to classical ADRC, where all internal dynamics are treated as an aggregated disturbance, the known and unknown components of the process are explicitly separated. The known dynamics are derived from a simplified first-principle model of the heater that does not require system identification, with parameters obtained directly from technical documentation of the heater. These known terms are embedded in the control law and observer structure, while the ESO estimates only the residual model uncertainty and not measurable disturbances. Simulation results obtained using a nonlinear digital twin of the electric flow heater demonstrate improved disturbance rejection and robustness compared to classical ADRC under model parameters uncertainties and in the presence of measurement noise. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Abstract: Axial-vibration experiments on time-varying-mass rods are difficult to design because element activation or deactivation creates short transition intervals that fixed space-filling designs can miss. This study proposes Agentic Sampling with Adaptive Surrogate and Element Birth–Death digital twin (ASAS-EBD), a bounded agentic soft-computing method for allocating high-fidelity evaluations around these events. The method couples an element-birth–death finite element digital twin with a graph-temporal surrogate that returns an eight-dimensional Gaussian response distribution. A neuro-fuzzy critic converts predictive uncertainty, reconstructed-equilibrium residual, design-space diversity, transition risk, and evaluation cost into a state-dependent acquisition score. The planner selects one action from Latin-hypercube, Sobol, residual-biased, and transition-risk candidate pools, records the resulting response, updates the surrogate, and repeats until the accuracy-calibration stopping rule or evaluation budget is reached. Evidence comes from a completed in-house rod campaign and its synchronized digital-twin workflow. Three open vibration datasets define additional excitation, noise, modal-range, and mass-state regimes; they are used as regime sources rather than as direct rod-response labels. In the pooled comparison, ASAS-EBD attains 0.98% modal-frequency mean absolute error, 2.85% response normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE), 0.038 expected calibration error, 0.936 empirical 95% coverage, and termination after 145 high-fidelity evaluations. Relative to the strongest recent physics-informed baseline, the corresponding reductions in NRMSE and evaluations are 22.9% and 23.7%. ASAS-EBD also gives the lowest NRMSE in each of four reported regimes; however, with only four regime-level pairs, the exact two-sided Wilcoxon test is not significant (p=0.125). The results therefore support sample-efficiency on the reported benchmark while leaving multi-fixture and direct external-response validation as necessary next steps. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.
